title: Selected Stabilizer Subspaces for Compact Many-Body Wave Functions
abstract: Selected configuration interaction (SCI) obtains accurate many-body solutions by variationally diagonalising the Hamiltonian in a sparse, iteratively selected set of configurations, but can lose compactness when the target state has broad configurational support. We introduce selected stabilizer interaction (SSI), a fully classical, SCI-inspired method that instead iteratively constructs a nonorthogonal subspace spanned by a systematically enlargeable set of selected stabilizer states. A single stabilizer, generated by Clifford operations, can encode a structured superposition of (possibly exponentially) many configurations, shifting the relevant compression from configurational to stabilizer sparsity. We benchmark ground-state energies, fidelities, superposition degrees and required expansion lengths against exact diagonalization and equivalent SCI schemes for the transverse-field Ising, XXZ Heisenberg, and Hubbard models, finding particularly strong compression from the stabilizer representation in the spin models, and increasing advantage with system size for these systems. The results establish a proof of principle for heuristic selected stabilizer diagonalization, while also identifying particular challenges in symmetry handling and effective exploration of the stabilizer space.

title: FuseAdapt: Parameter-Efficient Multimodal Fusion for Semantic Segmentation with Missing Modalities
abstract: Multi-modal semantic segmentation benefits from complementary sensors, but this benefit is fragile when some modalities are degraded or missing at test time. Many existing methods rely on dedicated fusion modules or multi-branch cross-modal encoders, and the fusion often becomes unreliable when modalities are absent, leading to substantial performance drops. We propose \textbf{FuseAdapt}, a parameter-efficient framework that performs fusion within the adaptation space of a frozen vision foundation model (VFM), exploring whether VFM priors can serve as an effective shared backbone for multi-modal segmentation. Instead of attaching a standalone fusion network, FuseAdapt assigns each modality a lightweight adaptation branch and performs \emph{adaptation-space fusion} by keeping Q/V low-rank adaptation private to each modality and routing only FFN low-rank residual activations across modalities inside the frozen backbone. The pretrained VFM remains fixed while modality-specific corrections and explicit cross-modal interaction are learned through the adaptation paths. To handle missing modalities, we further introduce \textbf{Predictive Modality Modeling (PMM)}, a direct representation-level objective for cross-modal redundancy. During training, PMM masks a target modality and predicts its embedding from the visible ones, supervised by a teacher target computed under full-modality input. PMM is used only during training and adds no inference-time overhead. Across three multi-modal segmentation benchmarks (MCubeS, DELIVER, MUSES), FuseAdapt consistently improves both modality-complete and modality-incomplete segmentation with a small trainable budget, yielding up to +3.01 mIoU under full modalities and +12.56 mIoU under missing modalities over prior state-of-the-art. Project page: https://devinxzhang.github.io/FuseAdapt-Page/.

title: VoxTurn: Answering Several Turn-Taking Questions in One Pass with One Model
abstract: A cascaded voice agent must decide, throughout each silence of its user, whether the user has finished their turn: answering too early cuts the user off, answering too late makes the agent slow. It often needs related decisions too: will the user soon go on, is speech during its own turn an interruption or a backchannel, is a sound speech at all. With open detectors, each extra decision costs another model or another call, and on the 14-language eot-bench they cut users off in more than a quarter of mid-turn pauses. Because they are trained on segmented utterances, this mismatch is the largest single source of error. We present VoxTurn, a 0.8B speech LLM that casts these decisions as multiple-choice questions, scores the hidden state of each option, and answers any set of them in one forward pass with a block-isolating attention mask, exactly as if asked one at a time. Trained on real conversational pauses with labels derived from their timing, and re-queried while a silence lasts, VoxTurn reaches 11.5% false cut-offs in English at a 300 ms latency budget, comparable to two commercial detectors, and a 14-language mean of 19.9%, the lowest among open models, at 8.3 ms per decision. In Pipecat and LiveKit it cuts off 17% and 9% of turns, and it ranks fifth of 24 in TurnBench end-of-turn detection without any TurnBench training data. The model, code and framework plugins are released.

title: No lattice tiling of Z^35 or Z^805 by Lee balls of radius three: paper, Lean 4 formalization and verification code
abstract: We prove that there is no lattice tiling of Z^35 or of Z^805 by Lee balls of radius three. A. Xiao and Y. Zhou (arXiv:2610.19775, Theorem 5.1) decided the lattice Golomb-Welch conjecture for every pair (n, r) with n >= 3, r >= 2 and fewer than 2^30 points in the ball, except (35, 3) and (805, 3); with their result, Z^n has no lattice tiling by the Lee ball B^n(r) for any such pair. Tilings that are not lattice tilings are not covered. preprintGolombWelchRadiusThree/ holds the paper as a PDF; paper/ holds the LaTeX source (amsart) with four schematic figures; dist/ holds the PDF, the LaTeX source zip and the arXiv tarball; MasterGolombWelchRadiusThree_masterzipfinal2.zip holds every file of the repository. lean/ is a Lean 4 and Mathlib project that proves the two theorems GolombWelch.golomb_welch_35 and GolombWelch.golomb_welch_805 together with every step they rest on: the reduction of a lattice tiling to a perfect code in a finite abelian group, the ball identity in a commutative ring, the vanishing of power sums modulo a prime, the pair counts, the constant term modulo 29^2, the joint projection to Z/71 x Z/29 through dual numbers over a group ring, and two circulant systems over F_71. Both theorems depend only on the axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound. checks/ contains independent checks of the arithmetic in C, C++, Julia and Python. scripts/run_all.sh builds the Lean project, checks the axioms and runs the checks.

title: Técnicas para el modelado y la generación de audio en trastornos del habla : evaluación comparativa de tecnologías de generación de voz para la síntesis de habla con disartria.
abstract: En la actualidad, el crecimiento acelerado de la inteligencia artificial ha abierto nuevos caminos para el procesamiento y generación de audios que imitan la voz. Sin embargo, para la disartria, estos nuevos horizontes enfrentan un imponente desafío: la escasez de datos para el entrenamiento y evaluación de modelos de vanguardia. Las personas con disartria presentan alteraciones motoras del habla, lo que puede afectar la inteligibilidad, la prosodia y la calidad acústica de la voz; esto provoca una limitación al desarrollar tecnologías orientadas a esta patología. Bajo este enfoque, se propone la evaluación comparativa de tecnologías de generación y conversión de voz para la creación de datos sintéticos del habla disártrica. En el capítulo 1 se presenta el problema, los objetivos, el alcance y el marco teórico relacionado con disartria, tecnologías generativas, conversión de voz y métricas objetivas. En el Capítulo 2 se describe la metodología, incluyendo el uso del dataset TORGO, los procesos de limpieza, normalización, extracción de representaciones acústicas y ejecución de los modelos seleccionados. En el Capítulo 3 se presentan los resultados de la comparación entre enfoques basados en redes generativas, modelos secuenciales y modelos de difusión, evaluados mediante métricas objetivas de inteligibilidad, calidad acústica y similitud espectral. Finalmente, se exponen las conclusiones y recomendaciones orientadas a identificar qué tecnologías presentan mejores condiciones técnicas para futuras estrategias de aumento de datos sintéticos en datasets disártricos.

title: Classificação automática de sentenças faladas com arquitetura híbrida: análise de estruturas topicalizadas, anti-topicalizadas e canônicas
abstract: O presente artigo investiga o desempenho de um sistema de classificação automática de sentenças faladas do português brasileiro, considerando estruturas canônicas, topicalizadas e antitopicalizadas, por meio de uma arquitetura híbrida baseada em Redes Neurais Recorrentes (RNNs) e Redes Neurais Convolucionais (CNNs). A pesquisa articula contribuições sintáticas, prosódicas e computacionais com a finalidade de contextualizar o corpus e delimitar o tratamento das sentenças faladas, porém o estudo concentra-se na avaliação experimental de uma arquitetura híbrida de redes neurais aplicada à classificação automática dessas sentenças. O corpus analisado é composto por 612 sentenças declarativas gravadas em ambiente controlado, produzidas por 20 falantes do português brasileiro. A metodologia caracteriza-se como quantitativa e experimental, utilizando aprendizagem supervisionada e avaliação baseada em métricas como precisão, recall, f-score e acurácia, por meio da matriz de confusão. Foram realizados testes com diferentes configurações de hiperparâmetros, variando filtros convolucionais, unidades LSTM, taxas de Dropout e número de épocas de treinamento. Os resultados demonstraram que modelos mais robustos apresentaram maior capacidade de memorização dos dados de treino, mas também maior tendência ao overfitting. Em contrapartida, arquiteturas mais enxutas associadas a maiores taxas de regularização obtiveram melhor capacidade de generalização e maior estabilidade durante a validação. O melhor desempenho foi observado no cenário com 30% de Dropout, em que houve redução significativa do hiato de generalização entre treino e teste. Conclui-se que a combinação entre RNNs e CNNs mostra-se promissora para a classificação automática de sentenças faladas, embora ainda existam limitações relacionadas à generalização do modelo em dados não vistos.

title: A Brazilian Dataset for Financial Sentiment Analysis: An Active Learning-Based Annotation Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a new expert-annotated dataset for financial sentiment analysis in Brazilian Portuguese, constructed from earnings call transcripts of the banking sector. The dataset was developed using a two-stage active learning pipeline designed to reduce annotation cost while preserving data quality. In the first stage, clustering and active learning were combined to filter relevant sentences from noisy transcripts. In the second stage, a Query by Committee strategy combining the transformer models BERTimbau and DeB3RTa was employed to select informative samples for expert annotation. The resulting dataset contains 719 annotated sentences with agreement analysis across multiple annotators. We further evaluated BERTimbau, DeB3RTa, and the external transformer model BERTuguês under three experimental settings, including fine-grained eight-class classification and complementary three-class scenarios. In the eight-class setting, BERTuguês and BERTimbau achieved comparable F1-macro scores (0.43±0.03 and 0.43 ± 0.01, respectively). In the sentiment-only three-class setup, BERTimbau achieved the best performance (0.68± 0.06). These results suggest that the dataset supports both fine-grained and coarse-grained sentiment analysis while remaining useful for models not involved in the active learning process.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Individual Planning and Collaborative Planning in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems must frequently balance individual autonomy against collaborative coordination when solving complex tasks in dynamic environments. Individual planning allows each agent to generate and execute plans using its own observations, objectives, computational resources, and local knowledge. Collaborative planning enables multiple agents to exchange information, resolve dependencies, negotiate shared decisions, and construct mutually compatible plans. However, neither planning mode is universally optimal. Continuous collaboration can introduce communication overhead, coordination delays, computational costs, and unnecessary information exchange, whereas exclusive reliance on individual planning can result in incompatible plans, duplicated work, missed dependencies, and avoidable failures. This paper proposes an adaptive planning framework that dynamically switches between individual planning and collaborative planning according to the estimated benefits and costs of coordination. The framework introduces a planning-mode controller that evaluates task dependencies, uncertainty, predicted plan conflicts, expected performance improvement, resource availability, and communication overhead. It supports transitions between individual planning, collaborative planning, and intermediate coordination states without requiring the system to follow a permanently fixed planning strategy. The proposed framework is formalized as a sequential decision problem and incorporates a switching-cost mechanism to prevent unstable mode changes. An evaluation methodology is developed to compare the framework against permanently individual, permanently collaborative, periodic-switching, and non-adaptive hybrid baselines. This work establishes a research direction for cost-aware, context-sensitive planning in multi-agent systems. The framework is presented as a methodological proposal; its comparative advantages remain to be established through empirical evaluation.

title: BEYOND AUTOMATION: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF COGNITIVE BIASES ON HUMAN INTERPRETATION OF EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
abstract: BEYOND AUTOMATION: INVESTIGATING THE INFLUENCE OF COGNITIVE BIASES ON HUMAN INTERPRETATION OF EXPLAINABLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PROF(DR.) VIJAYKUMAR B GADHAVI PROFESSOR AND HEAD , SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY, SWARRNIM START-UP AND INNOVATION UNIVERSITY - GANDHINAGAR GUJARAT INDIA ORCID: 0009-0005-6313-5900, E-MAIL: DRVIJAYKUMAR@SWARRNIM.EDU.IN PARMAR JIGAR JAYSUKHBHAI B. TECH. CE STUDENT, SWARRNIM INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY SWARRNIM STARTUP & INNOVATION UNIVERSITY, GANDHINAGAR, GUJARAT, INDIA ORCID: 0009-0008-7651-9913, EMAIL: JIGARAHIR410@GMAIL.COM Abstract Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is intended to make algorithmic outputs more understandable, auditable, and contestable. Yet an explanation does not reach a neutral observer: people interpret it through prior beliefs, cognitive shortcuts, professional experience, and assumptions about machine competence. This conceptual paper examines how cognitive biases shape the interpretation of XAI and why greater transparency does not necessarily produce better decisions. Drawing on research on automation bias, judgment and decision-making, explainability, and human–AI collaboration, the paper develops an integrative framework linking explanation characteristics, user cognition, task context, and reliance behavior. It argues that anchoring, confirmation bias, availability, authority effects, and cognitive miserliness can transform explanations into persuasive cues rather than evidence for independent evaluation. Explanations may improve mental models and error detection when they are faithful, appropriately scoped, and matched to users’ needs; however, they may also legitimize an incorrect prediction, increase cognitive load, or create an illusion of understanding. The paper proposes design principles centered on calibrated trust, contrastive and uncertainty-aware explanations, independent judgment, verification prompts, and evaluation of decision quality rather than satisfaction alone. Because this is a conceptual synthesis rather than an empirical study, its propositions require experimental testing across domains and user groups. The central conclusion is that responsible XAI must design not only for model transparency but also for the cognitive conditions under which people interpret explanations. Keywords: explainable artificial intelligence, cognitive bias, automation bias, human–AI interaction, trust calibration, decision-making, algorithmic transparency

title: Looped Language Models: A Survey and Meta-Analysis of Recurrent-Depth Transformers
abstract: Looped language models apply one shared block of Transformer layers repeatedly to the same tokens. Their effective depth, the number of layer applications per token, can grow without adding parameters and can be chosen at inference time. Recurrent depth is thus a way to scale test-time compute in latent space instead of in generated tokens. The idea appears under many names, including looped Transformers, LoopLMs, recurrent-depth models, Universal Transformers, Mixture-of-Recursions, and recursive reasoning models such as HRM and TRM. In two years it has moved from synthetic tasks to open models such as Huginn and Ouro and to pretraining on up to 28 trillion tokens. According to press reports, it is also used in a frontier-lab model. Its literature has split across architecture, training, systems, theory and safety. We present the first survey dedicated to looped language models, built on a systematic corpus of 557 core papers screened from 7,323 candidates. We introduce a unified prelude–core–coda formalism that makes explicit how parameters, compute, memory and depth are counted. We organize the field from design, training and scaling to inference systems, theory, mechanisms, capabilities, other modalities and safety. A meta-analysis classifies 822 verified empirical claims by comparison regime. It shows that most apparent contradictions about whether “a recurrence is worth a layer” come from comparing parameter-matched with compute-matched results. The evidence fits one reading, in which a recurrence is worth less than a fresh block of parameters. Looping therefore helps when parameters are the limiting resource and hurts when it replaces them at fixed compute. We derive a research agenda from measured gaps, including the absence of work on robustness, alignment and privacy. We release the corpus, the extraction records with verbatim evidence for every number, and the claims ledger.

title: Version 6.9.24 - AI-KM: Agent Preset, Agent Swarm, and Agent Scaffold
abstract: The integration of agent technologies and knowledge management has progressed from conversational question answering toward composable AI capabilities. However, existing systems still exhibit three common gaps: agent definitions are difficult to capture as portable assets, multi-agent collaboration lacks organizational mechanisms with low cognitive overhead, and large-scale agent workloads over real-world operational data lack a unified execution foundation. This update to AI-KM addresses these gaps through three capabilities: Agent Preset, Agent Swarm, and Agent Scaffold. Agent Preset packages roles, models, capability boundaries, skills, and private knowledge into declarative, distributable, and versionable agent assets, with capability boundaries enforced by the runtime rather than by prompts. Agent Swarm organizes multiple presets into a single natural-language collaboration, replacing structured blackboards and event protocols with group-chat history injection and flexible @mention-based invocation, thereby making multi-agent collaboration a first-class interaction mode within the conversational interface. Agent Scaffold organizes execution configurations into an orthogonal configuration space and introduces multi-round execution and fingerprint-based incremental change detection. The three capabilities share the same execution engine, capability model, and message model, thereby maintaining behavioral consistency while forming an integrated workflow for creating, organizing, and operating agents at scale.

title: Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving
abstract: Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib's forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12% over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR, covering up to 3.7% of extra groups. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing higher accuracy-cost efficiency. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery.

title: TRACER: A Multimodal Harness for Patient Care in Hospitals
abstract: Continuous video and clinical records provide complementary information for understanding how patient behavior evolves over a hospital stay. A central challenge is how to represent behavior across the entire stay while preserving access to fine-grained visual and clinical evidence. We introduce TRACER, a training-free multimodal harness that constructs minute-level action records from video and combines them with clinical records into hourly reports. The harness equips an LLM agent with tools to query this hierarchy, inspect relevant video, and retrieve clinical records. To evaluate TRACER, we construct two benchmarks. The first contains 397 annotated one-minute clips spanning 15 atomic actions; the second poses 144 clinician-informed multiple-choice questions, grounded in 264 hours of video and clinical records from two ICU patients. TRACER achieves up to 84.8% accuracy for action detection and 61.0% QA accuracy versus 49.3% for the strongest baseline using the same backbone. Across 280 patients spanning approximately 60,000 camera-hours, TRACER identifies significantly less purposeful activity in patients with a positive delirium assessment during their stay than in those without (p < 0.0001). Our results show that combining continuous video with clinical records can support understanding of patient behavior over time and across patient cohorts without training on protected health data.

title: Biological Complexity and Cryptographic Secrecy: Reproducible Key Recovery and a Structured Evidence Audit of Bio-Derived Key Schemes
abstract: Bio-derived key schemes build cryptographic keys from biological material: protein structures, DNA and RNA sequences, amino-acid chains, proteinoid assemblies. This paper audits the class against a protocol drafted prospectively, refined during a pre-specified pilot, and frozen before the main screening and extraction, and tests its central claim empirically. No audited study reported a defensible attacker-conditioned min-entropy for its complete secret; the key-space figures instead measured an output or encoding-table size, a descriptor length, or a parameter-range product. A structured evidence audit of twelve studies finds that the biological material rarely holds the secret, that the evidence concerns the randomness of outputs rather than the secrecy of keys, and that no study provided a publicly linked runnable implementation. On three schemes (the two whose secret is a selection from a public set and one encoding scheme) we recover keys from the first two and bound the entropy of the third. The executed recoveries covered a 647-protein candidate set (work factor about 9.3 search-space bits) and a single-reference DNA position search (about 12 bits); a broader eight-reference analysis gives a projected search space upper bound of at most about 39 bits once a 16-bit auxiliary key is included, and was not exhaustively executed. Reported key spaces range up to millions of bits, and for the encoding scheme the input entropy is left unestablished. These results apply to schemes whose secret is public, a selection from public data, or an encoding; they do not extend to a scheme built on a genuinely private biological sample, a noisy physical measurement, or a properly constructed fuzzy extractor. We contribute a taxonomy of biological sources by role, three security observations, the audit and the recovery and accounting experiments, and a design checklist. Biological complexity does not by itself imply cryptographic secrecy.

title: Impact of AI‐Assisted Endoscopy on Secondary Review and Referral Decisions in Gastric Cancer Screening: A Multicenter Real‐World Study
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted endoscopy may support gastric cancer screening, but its impact on structured secondary human review remains unclear. We evaluated secondary review modifications and referral decisions before and after AI implementation. METHODS: This retrospective multicenter study included 5013 screening esophagogastroduodenoscopy examinations performed before (n = 2021) and after (n = 2992) AI implementation. The primary outcome was secondary review modifications. Secondary outcomes included referral for further diagnostic evaluation. Multivariable logistic regression analyses adjusted for age, sex, Helicobacter pylori eradication status, prior-year endoscopy, and endoscopist experience were performed. Interaction analyses according to endoscopist experience and inverse probability of treatment weighting analyses were conducted. No external reference standard was available to verify secondary-review modifications or referral decisions. RESULTS: Secondary review modifications increased from 1.2% in the pre-AI period to 3.7% in the AI period (p < 0.01). A significant interaction was observed between AI implementation and endoscopist experience (p for interaction < 0.01), with increased modifications primarily among nonexpert endoscopists. Cancer-related modifications remained uncommon but increased after AI implementation (0.6% vs. 0.2%, p = 0.04). Referral rates decreased from 4.9% to 2.8% (p < 0.01), and AI implementation was independently associated with lower odds of referral (adjusted OR = 0.53; 95% confidence interval = 0.36-0.77). CONCLUSIONS: AI-assisted endoscopy was associated with lower referral rates; however, secondary review modifications persisted after AI implementation, particularly among nonexpert endoscopists. These findings describe workflow changes and do not establish the clinical validity of the modifications or the appropriateness of referral decisions.

title: Accuracy-cost trade-offs for reference VQE calculations of H 2 on IBM quantum hardware
abstract: Abstract Variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) calculations are widely used as reference workflows for assessing near-term quantum hardware, but practical guidance on their accuracy, runtime, and billed usage remains limited. Here, we present a hardware-validated reference dataset for variational ground-state energy calculations of the hydrogen molecule H 2 on several IBM Quantum processors available in 2025–2026. Using a standardized Qiskit Nature workflow, we benchmark the impact of shot count, backend choice, fermion-to-qubit mapping, optimizer behavior, resilience level, and execution mode on the achievable energy accuracy relative to exact diagonalization. For the H 2 /STO–3G configurations examined, circuit simplification through tapered mappings provides the most consistent accuracy gains, resilience level 1 improves accuracy at a substantial billed-usage premium, and session-based execution yields no systematic accuracy advantage over single-job execution despite markedly higher billed time. The dataset and analysis provide a transparent baseline for assessing current IBM Quantum hardware for quantum-chemistry applications and for estimating the runtime effort and billed usage that non-specialist users can expect from standard workflows.

title: SCCL-DT: Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning with Dual-Rule Teacher Distillation for Zero-Shot Chest X-Ray Diagnosis
abstract: Contrastive vision-language pre-training supports zero-shot chest X-ray diagnosis, but standard objectives treat every off-diagonal image-report pair in a batch as a negative. In radiology, recurring findings across patients mean that instance mismatch need not imply semantic incompatibility, creating false-negative supervision that we term a semantic conflict. A training-trace audit shows that pair-observations selected by the online mask used during training are enriched for report-derived finding agreement, although this proxy analysis does not establish clinical equivalence. Fixed thresholds can become miscalibrated as similarity distributions evolve, while soft reweighting leaves residual repulsive gradients. We therefore propose Semantic-Conflict-Aware Contrastive Learning (SCCL), which tracks modality-specific similarity distributions with exponential-moving-average (EMA) statistics, derives adaptive thresholds, and hard-masks flagged candidates before softmax normalization. Inclusive (OR) and consensus (AND) rules define two SCCL teachers, whose bidirectional cross-modal rankings are consolidated through standard distillation into a single deployable student, SCCL-DT. Across five public chest X-ray benchmarks, SCCL-DT achieves a mean zero-shot AUC of $0.850$, compared with $0.837$ for the strongest evaluated baseline in our comparison. Code will be made publicly available soon.

title: CF-AVSS: A Coarse-to-Fine Audio-Visual Speech Separation Framework with Target-Speaker Refinement and Post-Fusion for Real-World AVSE Challenge
abstract: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) leverages visual cues to recover target speech from mixtures corrupted by reverberation, noise, and overlapping speakers. We propose a coarse-to-fine two-stage AVSE framework. In the first stage, a progressive SPAV-TFGridNet is extended to two synchronized visual streams to produce visually ordered coarse estimates by progressively suppressing interfering speech while preserving target reverberation and shared background noise. In the second stage, a TFGridNet-based target speaker refinement network takes the original mixture and both coarse estimates as input to further recover target speech and improve signal quality. The coarse and refined estimates are finally combined using development-set-calibrated fusion. On the ISCSLP 2026 Real-World AVSE Challenge, our system tied for first place on Track 1 and ranked second on Track 2 in OVRL, while achieving the lowest CER on both tracks at 12.31% and 14.79%, respectively.

title: Boundary Project — Continuity Science and Recoverability-Constrained Systems: Integrated Scientific, Mathematical, Technological, Constitutional and Living-System Corpus (13-Part Archive)
abstract: The Boundary Project presents an integrated multidisciplinary research corpus developed under Continuity Science and Recoverability-Constrained Systems (RCS), encompassing formal mathematics, theoretical research, engineering architectures, computational systems, technical invention disclosures, protection principles, recursive governance, and living-system development. The foundational mathematical framework studies distinguishable states, admissible transitions, finite successor spaces, protected correspondence, operational recoverability, irreversibility, time-constrained intervention, fixed-point structures, invariant preservation, possibility collapse, and successor continuity. Recoverability is evaluated through the existence and executability of admissible paths to protected future states. Material transitions are examined according to their consequences for truth, identity, agency, evidence, protection, timing, responsibility, remedy, and the remaining structure of recoverable future possibility. The technological corpus integrates processor-implemented decision architectures, recoverability-constrained authorization, recursive supervisory control, isolation apparatus, software and hardware architectures, artificial intelligence, federated computational systems, communications, automation, robotics, digital twins, quantum information systems, and human-machine interfaces. Domain extensions address healthcare, biological systems, consciousness research, assistive robotics, longevity, financial continuity, water security, planetary infrastructure, industrial safety, catastrophic-risk reduction, environmental protection, and interdependent civilizational systems. The governance corpus develops proposed constitutional principles, human and other-being protections, non-captive continuity, preventive giving, accountability, evidence provenance, non-domination, consent, independent review, corrective remedies, and institutional succession. The multicivilization extensions introduce hypothetical, evidence-classified models for future contact, inter-civilizational cooperation, translation, non-interference, shared responsibility, and recoverable governance without asserting verified extraterrestrial contact. The corpus applies recursive and nine-direction systematic analysis across inward, outward, upward, downward, backward, forward, lateral, recursive, and adversarial dimensions. Materially equivalent distinctions may be consolidated while preserving provenance and alternative formulations. The Zero-Distinction Boundary represents the terminal operational expressibility condition of the framework. Finite closure is always relative to declared assumptions, evidence, scope, and evaluation methods. New material distinctions reopen the relevant system, allowing its controlled evolution without erasing prior evidence, protections, or responsibilities. This integrated release is distributed as 13 losslessly compressed ZIP archives, each below 2 MB, incorporating source documents, versioned research editions, technical architectures, derived registries, and preservation manifests. The archives constitute a connected research record rather than independent or competing theoretical systems. Mathematical claims are evaluated relative to their stated assumptions; proposed technical architectures require implementation and validation; normative instruments require appropriate legal or institutional adoption; and speculative scientific or philosophical constructs remain explicitly distinct from established empirical findings. The publication is intended to support reproducible examination of the disclosed materials, independent scientific critique, interdisciplinary research, technical development, engineering assurance, public-interest governance, and future extensions of Continuity Science. The multicivilization extensions introduce hypothetical, evidence-classified models for future contact, inter-civilizational cooperation, translation, non-interference, shared responsibility, and recoverable governance without asserting verified extraterrestrial contact. The corpus applies recursive and nine-direction systematic analysis across inward, outward, upward, downward, backward, forward, lateral, recursive, and adversarial dimensions. Materially equivalent distinctions may be consolidated while preserving provenance and alternative formulations. The Zero-Distinction Boundary represents the terminal operational expressibility condition of the framework. Finite closure is always relative to declared assumptions, evidence, scope, and evaluation methods. New material distinctions reopen the relevant system, allowing its controlled evolution without erasing prior evidence, protections, or responsibilities. This integrated release is distributed as 13 losslessly compressed ZIP archives, each below 2 MB, incorporating source documents, versioned research editions, technical architectures, derived registries, and preservation manifests. The archives constitute a connected research record rather than independent or competing theoretical systems. title: 二.A Primitive Theory of Next-Gen General Intelligence Based on Global Mathematical Verification Closed-Loop
abstract: Existing Transformer and large model theoretical systems uniformly adopt the ”prediction-first”paradigm, defining intelligence as ”fitting the data distribution of the real world and next-tokenprediction”. This theory overturns conventional understanding and proposes the unique primitiveof intelligence: a continuous, multi-layered, global closed-loop for mathematical verification andchecking.All artificial intelligence behaviors (fitting, reasoning, association, generation, generalization, er-ror correction, cognition) are essentially mathematical comparison, constraint checking, differentialstability verification, and vector structure matching across different dimensions.All low-level operations of the traditional Transformer (vector embedding, QKV dot-product at-tention, gradient backpropagation, distribution fitting) are not ”predictive behaviors”, but nativechecking operations at the statistical level. The root causes of large model hallucinations, logicalfailures and generalization defects lie in the sole possession of statistical distribution checking, lack-ing rigorous mathematical checking of axiomatic structures, differential constraints and geometrictopology.This theory constructs a ”dual-layer unified checking intelligence system”, completing a funda-mental paradigm revolution from traditional probability-fitting intelligence to global mathematical-verification intelligence. It can directly guide the design of native intelligent models with no hallu-cinations, strong logic, self-correction capability and ontological cognition for the next generation.

title: Sentiment and Repurchase Signals in Indonesian Fresh-Produce E-Commerce Reviews: A Pilot Text-Mining Study
abstract: Online fresh-produce retailing presents distinctive quality and delivery uncertainties that influence consumer evaluations and repurchase intentions. This study contributes a leakage-controlled, polarity-aware text-mining framework for examining consumer sentiment and repurchase signals in unsolicited online reviews. Using 113 public Tokopedia reviews covering 31 fresh-produce products, this pilot study employed lexicon-based sentiment classification and logistic regression with product-clustered standard errors. The findings reveal predominantly positive consumer sentiment, although explicit repurchase intentions appear less frequently. Consumer sentiment demonstrates a significant positive association with repurchase signals, while product-quality mentions show no significant relationship. Unexpectedly, positive delivery mentions exhibit a negative association with repurchase signals, potentially reflecting review-length constraints rather than unfavorable delivery experiences. These findings extend the methodological application of consumer-generated content analysis by demonstrating the feasibility of extracting distinct behavioral signals while addressing classification bias. Online retailers can leverage this framework to monitor consumer experiences and identify opportunities for service improvement.

title: Dendritic computation bridges neuroscience and foundation models
abstract: A prevailing view holds that although neuroscience historically inspired AI, its role in the recent evolution of AI, driven by the scaling of foundation models, is minor. We challenge this perspective by establishing a biological analogy between simplified dendritic neuron models and the attention mechanisms central to AI foundation models. We show that AI attention mechanisms bear direct mappings to internal neuronal complexities arising from dendritic organization, rather than to the mere inter-neuronal connections of simple point neurons. This re-conceptualization not only offers a neuroscience-informed perspective for understanding core AI methodologies beyond their formulation as abstract mathematical operations, but also paves the way for neuro-inspired foundation models that leverage neuroscientific insights to sustainably advance modern AI beyond scaling laws. As an example of this paradigm, we introduce a dendritic-inspired complexity framework, and design a hybrid-attention foundation model with dendritic-inspired sparse computation, which enhances memory capacity while reducing computational demands. Our model supports a 50M context window-equivalent to roughly 40 volumes of Shakespeare-demonstrating superior long-term memory capabilities. This work pioneers a paradigm that harnesses intra-neuronal dynamics to drive sustained advances in modern AI, while also offering a potential route to understanding dendritic computational mechanisms. How insights from neuroscience can inform future AI foundation models is an active area of exploration. Here, the authors show that AI attention mechanisms resemble dendritic computations within individual neurons rather than interactions between neurons, inspiring a dendritic-inspired model with improved long-term memory and reduced computational cost.

title: Do LLM Judges Agree with Humans? Evaluating Financial Commentaries from Material Facts
abstract: The rapid adoption of large language models (LLMs) in finance has enabled automated generation of in-domain texts such as earnings summaries, market analyses, and commentary on regulated disclosures. Generating accurate and accessible financial commentary from material facts poses challenges related to domain-specific language, strict factual faithfulness, and readability. Evaluating such outputs is difficult: traditional automatic metrics overlook financial correctness and adequacy, while human expert assessment is reliable but costly and subjective. This paper proposes a multidimensional evaluation protocol for generating financial commentary in Portuguese and investigates the use of LLMs as evaluators (“LLMs-as-judges”) in this high-stakes, low-resource setting. We systematically compare human expert judgments and LLM-based evaluation preferences, while also investigating complementary dimensions such as writing quality, factuality, usefulness, and simplicity. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first proposal of an evaluation protocol for this task in Portuguese. Furthermore, we analyze where LLM judgments align with or diverge from human assessments, providing practical insights and recommendations for evaluation methodologies in financial AI applications.

title: Where Does Hardness Come From? An Instance Hardness Analysis of Substance-Use Prediction in Brazilian Adolescents
abstract: The intrinsic difficulty of a classification dataset is routinely measured, yet its origin is rarely examined: is an instance hard because of the features that describe it, or because of the target to be predicted? We study this through Instance Hardness (IH) in a real, highly imbalanced problem — predicting frequent substance use among 165,838 Brazilian adolescents from the 2019 PeNSE survey, a setting that is hard by construction: the data are self-reported and the positive class has a prevalence of only about 4%. Hardness is quantified per instance in two independent ways — empirically, as the misclassification propensity across a committee of four learning architectures, and geometrically, from local class overlap (kDN), which uses no model. Three findings emerge across ten data partitions. First, IH is largely but not uniformly model-invariant (Spearman ρ > 0.94 among the four committee members; ≈ 0.79–0.97 against a fifth, neural architecture), which justifies treating hardness as a property of the data rather than of any single learner. Second, local overlap explains only part of the difficulty: kDN predicts true errors with an AUC of ≈ 0.73, against ≈ 0.95 for empirical IH, leaving a substantial residual attributable to non-local structure such as label noise or feature interactions. Third, through a controlled ablation, hardness responds to the target, not the features — removing an entire block of strong features leaves the hardness distribution essentially unchanged, whereas enlarging the target raises mean hardness roughly 2.5×. In this domain, difficulty is governed by what is predicted, not by which variables are used to predict it; past a reasonable feature set, the performance ceiling is more productively addressed by reconsidering the target than by further feature engineering.

title: ASFM/SIE: Altitude‑Separated Fusion Manifold & Shared Interpretability Envelope — Technical Note v1.0
abstract: The Altitude‑Separated Fusion Manifold (ASFM) and Shared Interpretability Envelope (SIE) provide a structured, altitude‑safe framework for analyzing multi‑layer AI systems without mixing real, complex, or symbolic dynamics. The technical note defines three distinct altitudes—NDH (real‑valued geometry), Vectorium (complex‑valued modeling physics), and Fantasy Engine (symbolic expressive physics)—and introduces bounded projection maps that allow information to move between altitudes without type contamination. The interpretability envelope supplies an altitude‑neutral visibility layer composed of LHGuard (semantic firewall), ProvenanceShield (metadata membrane), holonomy drift diagnostics, and collapse‑surface detectors. These components enable reproducible, falsifiable interpretability without altering model behavior or making cognitive claims. The appendices provide the full mathematical spine, operator definitions, pseudocode, reproducibility protocols, limitations, and out‑of‑scope clarifications. Related systems such as Vectorium v5.0 and Serenity Manifold are acknowledged for provenance but explicitly excluded from the framework. This technical note is intended as a reproducible, altitude‑stable foundation for geometric interpretability research and public‑interest AI oversight. -- Contributors / Acknowledgments - Conceptual feedback on non‑linearity and active inference: Stell - NDH‑CORE lineage references for stability envelopes - Community discussions on altitude separation and operator safety --- Altitude‑Separated Licensing & Provenance Notice: The ASFM/SIE framework integrates concepts from several independently licensed research projects. Each altitude—NDH, Vectorium, Anima Classic Substrate, and Fantasy Engine—has its own licensing environment, and these licenses are not harmonized. Because geometric cognition research and latent‑manifold modeling involve complex operator boundaries, users should consult the individual GitHub repositories for each altitude to understand the specific rights, restrictions, and provenance conditions. - NDH components are released under the MIT License. - Fantasy Engine components are released under the MIT License. - Vectorium components are MIT‑licensed except expressive‑state projection dynamics, which derive from Stell’s Anima Classic substrate and therefore follow Stell’s Non‑Commercial License. - Anima Classic substrate is not dual‑use compatible and cannot be relicensed; users must contact Stell directly for non‑commercial rights or clarification. This technical note does not unify or reinterpret these licenses. Instead, it encourages readers to review each project’s GitHub repository individually, as the licensing environment is intentionally altitude‑specific and reflects the complexity of geometric cognition research. Notes This technical note is non‑cognitive, non‑behavioral, and non‑predictive. It provides interpretability safety only. Out‑of‑scope systems (Vectorium v5.0 Execution Engine, Serenity Manifold) are documented for provenance but not included in the mathematical framework. ---

title: Data, firmware and code for "HQC as a Fallback to ML-KEM: Measured Energy, Memory and Latency from Cortex-M4 to Thread Gateway"
abstract: This record holds the data and code behind the paper "HQC as a Fallback to ML-KEM: Measured Energy, Memory and Latency from Cortex-M4 to Thread Gateway". The study measures HQC (specification of 22 August 2025) against ML-KEM on the hardware of a Thread deployment:- cycles, stack and energy on a NUCLEO-L4R5ZI (Cortex-M4) with a Nordic PPK2;- computation, energy and RAM beside OpenThread on an nRF52840;- key exchanges over a real IEEE 802.15.4 Thread link, with and without 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi interference;- a measured KEM transaction through a Raspberry Pi 5 border router;- TLS 1.3 server CPU cost on the Pi 5, with and without PMULL carry-less multiplication. Contents:- firmware, runner scripts and the registered prediction files with their SHA-256 digests for every experiment session;- the results archive of every session: setup records, per-window energies, 1 ms current means, logs;- the LaTeX source with the scripts that regenerate every number, table and figure;- the corrections and test-vector validation for the optimized HQC code of Chen et al.;- the PMULL multiplication for liboqs. For the sessions affected by a PPK2 conversion fault, the archive holds both the values as recorded and the corrected values, with the correction factors and the validation sessions. README.md describes the layout, how to rebuild the paper, and the SHA-256 digests.

title: ICAA: Interaction-Calibrated Attention-Based Asymmetric Feature Decomposition and Recovery for Domain Generalization and Adaptation
abstract: Normalization narrows visual domain gaps but moves discriminative cues into its residual. Many normalization-residual decomposition methods for domain generalization (DG) and unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) rely primarily on channel-wise modeling, while existing spatial-channel variants treat spatial and channel cues independently, and symmetric losses judge recovery only against the normalized feature, possibly less discriminative than the original. We propose Interaction-Calibrated Attention-Based Asymmetric Feature Decomposition and Recovery (ICAA). Its Interaction-Calibrated Attention-Based Feature Decomposition and Recovery (IAFDR) module uses Spatial-Channel Interactive Calibration to jointly calibrate spatial and channel evidence and selectively recover task-relevant information from normalization residuals, and an explicit correspondence between convolutional networks and vision transformers extends it to patch tokens. The Asymmetric Task-relevant Feature Decomposition loss encourages recovered features to be more certain than original ones and their complements less certain than normalized ones. ICAA improves every evaluated host across classification, segmentation, and detection: DAEL by 3.9/5.4 percentage points (pp) to 87.3%/71.5% on PACS/Office-Home (1.4/2.2 pp above the best CNN competitor), M3SDA by 9.8 pp to 52.4% on DomainNet, CSFDA by 3.1/4.1 pp to 55.7%/48.7% mIoU on GTA5/SYNTHIA→Cityscapes, and Faster R-CNN by 4.9 pp to 23.7% mAP on Foggy Cityscapes.

title: Sistem Pakar Deteksi Dini Risiko Putus Sekolah pada Siswa SMK Menggunakan Metode Certainty Factor
abstract: Putus sekolah pada jenjang Sekolah Menengah Kejuruan (SMK) merupakan persoalan pendidikan multidimensional yang dipengaruhi oleh faktor akademik, ekonomi, dan sosial secara bersamaan, sementara identifikasi risiko yang masih dilakukan secara manual oleh guru Bimbingan dan Konseling (BK) cenderung subjektif dan sulit dilakukan secara menyeluruh karena keterbatasan jumlah guru BK dibandingkan jumlah siswa yang harus dipantau. Penelitian ini bertujuan merancang dan membangun sistem pakar berbasis web untuk mendeteksi dini risiko putus sekolah pada siswa SMK Muhammadiyah 9 Medan menggunakan metode Certainty Factor (CF), yang mengakomodasi ketidakpastian pengetahuan pakar melalui nilai Measure of Belief (MB) dan Measure of Disbelief (MD). Basis pengetahuan sistem disusun melalui wawancara dan validasi bersama guru BK sehingga diperoleh dua belas gejala risiko beserta nilai CF pakar, yang kemudian diproses menggunakan mekanisme inferensi forward chaining dan rumus CF Combine untuk menghasilkan tingkat keyakinan akhir terhadap tiga kategori risiko, yaitu rendah, sedang, dan tinggi. Sistem bernama SIPRIS (Sistem Informasi Prediksi Risiko Siswa) ini dikembangkan menggunakan PHP, basis data MySQL, dan antarmuka berbasis Bootstrap 5. Pengujian black-box terhadap enam modul utama menunjukkan seluruh fungsi berjalan sesuai rancangan, sedangkan validasi manual pada tiga data uji siswa menunjukkan kesesuaian penuh antara hasil sistem dan perhitungan pakar (Risiko Tinggi 85%, Risiko Sedang 65%, Risiko Rendah 35%). title: KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents
abstract: Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems.

title: Cross-Prompt Inference Mitigates Rare-Class Suppression in Imbalanced VLM Finetuning
abstract: When a vision-language model is finetuned on class-imbalanced data, rare-class recall can fall well below the model's own zero-shot performance. In this regime, we uncover a surprising matched-prompt penalty whereby the standard choice of reusing the descriptive finetuning prompt at inference can yield lower rare-class recall than using a different descriptive prompt. We call this inference-time strategy cross-prompt inference. We evaluate diverse VLMs across six datasets and find that cross-prompt inference consistently recovers rare-class recall, with varying trade-offs in frequent-class recall. The effect reflects a train-eval prompt interaction rather than prompt quality alone, and does not arise with non-descriptive prompt changes. It is strongest when imbalance and visual confusability produce substantial rare-class suppression, and is weak or absent when such suppression does not occur. Using Tuning Contribution (TuCo), which decomposes a model's computation into pretrained and finetuning parts, we find that cross-prompt inference reduces reliance on finetuning-induced computation and shifts the model toward its pretrained component. Reducing that finetuning contribution also substantially reduces the cross-prompt advantage. These results show that rare-class knowledge suppressed by imbalanced finetuning can remain accessible under a different inference prompt.

title: Fractional Power-of-Two Quantization for Efficient and Effective Multiplier-Free LLM Inference
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) demand efficient inference, where the multiply-accumulate (MAC) operations in linear projections dominate compute and energy cost. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost by mapping weights and activations to low-bit integers. Power-of-Two (PoT) weight quantization promises efficient multiplier-free LLM inference via shift-add logic, but suffers significant accuracy degradation at low bitwidths due to its coarse base-2 quantization grid. We introduce Fractional PoT (FPoT), a base-$\sqrt{2}$ (half-octave) fractional PoT grid that achieves practical 4-bit weight quantization while preserving a fully integer shift-add datapath. The method combines (i) the base-$\sqrt{2}$ weight grid with uniform integer activations, (ii) a calibration-time grid-alignment refinement absorbed into the static per-channel scale, and (iii) a lightweight 1-adder $\sqrt{2}$ approximation whose error is absorbed during weight calibration via approximate-grid quantization, yielding a processing element (PE) with significantly fewer gates than a 4-bit integer multiplier. On Llama-3-8B with 4-bit weight and activation quantization, FPoT improves zero-shot commonsense reasoning performance by 8.72% relative to the PoT baseline, while maintaining performance close to the uniform integer baseline, with only a negligible 0.4%p degradation. These results hold across various configurations spanning seven models and three bit-widths. Furthermore, FPoT can be integrated with state-of-the-art LLM PTQ methods, demonstrating framework-agnostic applicability.

title: Chaotic parameter control in Differential Evolution
abstract: Differential Evolution (DE) is a popular meta-heuristic algorithm that works on the differences between the vectors of a population. It was developed by Kenneth Price and Rainer Storn in the mid-1990s.The scaling factor F and the crossover probability CR are two key control parameters of DE. Differential Evolution (DE) works well on many optimization problems, but its results depend a great deal on how the scaling factor F and the crossover probability CR are set. In this paper, the concepts of dynamical systems (chaotic maps) and population diversity are applied to the control parameters F and CR. We replace the fixed values of these two parameters with sequences drawn from ten chaotic maps: Chebyshev, circle, Gauss, iterative, logistic, piecewise, sine, Singer, sinusoidal and tent. A diversity checks on the population decides when the chaotic values are used; otherwise, F = 0.5 and CR = 0.4 are kept. We tried each map on F alone, on CR alone, and then in pairs chosen for each class of problems. All variants were run on the 30 CEC 2014 functions and compared with standard DE. No single map won everywhere. These findings can help in choosing a chaotic map to suit the type of problem at hand.

title: Rhombic Dodecahedron Quantum Codes and Geometric Symmetry in Physical Law — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: FINDING: The rhombic dodecahedron appears as an exact lattice structure for a quantum error-correcting surface code, while symmetry-breaking frameworks in QFT and Calabi-Yau compactifications reveal how geometric group constraints govern physical law. | MATH: Rhombic dodecahedron = zonohedron with 12 rhombic faces, 24 edges, 14 vertices; its vertices are the 12 midpoints of cube edges plus 2 cube vertices — coordinates are permutations of (±1,±1,0) and (±2,0,0) in scaled form. The [[14,3,3]] code has 14 physical qubits, 3 logical qubits, distance 3 — a non-CSS code whose stabilizer generators map to the dodecahedron's faces. Wigner-Eckart corrections under spontaneous symmetry breaking scale as O(1/N) for N→∞ systems, with Goldstone-mode contributions modifying reduced matrix elements by terms proportional to ⟨φ⟩/f (vacuum expectation value over decay constant). | CONNECTION: The rhombic dodecahedron is the Voronoi cell of the face-centered cubic (FCC) lattice — the densest sphere pack Author: Andrew Stewart Caldin, Independent Researcher, UK. title: Encoding Choice Is Associated with Large Differences in Variational Quantum Classifier Performance on Cancer Data Under a Fixed Training Budget
abstract: Variational quantum classifiers (VQCs) are often reported to perform poorly on biomedical tabular data, but such conclusions depend on the encoding circuit, the training budget, and the comparison protocol. Methods. We compared 4-qubit VQCs, a quantum-kernel SVM (QSVM), a majority-class control, and tuned classical models (on four PCA features and on all features) on Wisconsin breast cancer (n = 569), Coimbra biomarkers (n = 116), Golub leukemia gene expression (n = 72, 7,129 genes), and SEER breast-cancer registry data (n = 4,024; 15% deaths). All models were evaluated on identical blocks of 5-fold × 5-seed stratified cross-validation with preprocessing fitted on training folds, nested tuning, and Nadeau–Bengio-corrected inference with Holm correction. Trained classifiers were also evaluated on three IBM Quantum devices. Results. On the three small datasets, a VQC with the conventional two-repetition ZZ feature map was close to chance (accuracy 0.688, 0.594, 0.509), whereas a product (Z) feature map reached 0.900, 0.797, and 0.658; at matched repetition counts the Z-minus-ZZ gap was +0.12 to +0.21 and, after Holm correction, significant on Wisconsin only. More evaluations (up to 1,500) and six initializations did not close the ZZ deficit on Wisconsin. With the encoding chosen by inner cross-validation, the VQC exceeded the majority control on Wisconsin and Golub and stayed below classical models on Wisconsin and in several Golub contrasts. No statistically significant difference was detected between the encoding-selected VQC and the classical baselines on Coimbra, or between the Z-map QSVM and PCA-4 classical models; Bayesian equivalence analysis supported practical equivalence only for the QSVM on Wisconsin. On SEER the encoding mattered little: the VQC exceeded the majority control in balanced accuracy (0.548 versus 0.500) but ranked patients worse than logistic regression and random forest (ROC-AUC 0.678 versus 0.745 and 0.733). Full-feature classical models were strongest overall. On hardware (class-balanced test subsets, not natural-prevalence performance), accuracy relative to noise-free simulation changed by −0.071 to +0.048 per run (pooled ibm_fez, Wisconsin: −0.024, 95% CI −0.060 to +0.008), using 5.5 QPU-minutes. Conclusions. Under a fixed training budget, encoding choice was associated with large differences in VQC accuracy on small datasets, so single-encoding negative results should not be generalized; because the Z and ZZ maps also differ in entanglement structure, we do not attribute the gap to encoding alone. No quantum advantage was observed.

title: The Psychology of Trust in Intelligent Marketing Systems
abstract: In this chapter, the emphasis is on the nature of trust from a psychological viewpoint in smart marketing technology. As the use of AI becomes more prevalent in the relationship between customers and firms, it is very important to understand how trust is cognitively created. Based on disciplinary studies of the fields of consumer behavior and social psychology, a new model focused on the manner in which customers understand marketing practices is introduced. The chapter highlights the basic drivers of trust, such as perceptions about transparency, fairness, control, and personalization. The issue of trust formation is examined in the context of the problems of risk perception, uncertainty, and algorithmic problems.

title: Aspects of Symmetry in Nuclear Quantum Computing Variational Algorithms
abstract: Variational Quantum Eigensolvers (VQEs) have become a standard tool for use in preparing eigenstates in quantum simulations of many-body systems. In the case of the nuclear shell model, various adaptations of the VQE have been shown to be able to produce ground and excited states of nuclei. The VQE algorithm works by seeking minima in a cost function, which is often the expectation value of the energy. For a well-formulated problem, symmetries that are respected by the Hamiltonian should appear in the final converged solution provided by the VQE, even if those symmetries are broken by the wave function ansatz. We demonstrate explicit appearance of the particle–hole symmetry, and explicit recovery of angular momentum conservation due to rotational symmetry, during VQE runs in the case of the nuclear shell model. We conduct analyses of how the symmetry convergence appears in different ansatz formulations, and suggest that information obtained could be used in future VQE design.

title: Local finite rate semi device independent randomness expansion from quantum contextuality
abstract: Finite rate randomness expansion (RE) which is secure against quantum adversaries is a crucial information processing task which is well studied in the case of two non-communicating parties sharing Bell non-local correlations in a device independent manner. In this paper we show that contextual correlations with only a single localized party are sufficient for RE in a semi-device independent (SDI) manner. We propose a template SDI-RE protocol which is applicable for arbitrary $N$-cycle non-contextuality (NC) inequalities and derive its RE rate under finite statistics. As a special case, we also highlight the advantages of the situation when RE is constrained by Clauser-Horne-Shimony-Holt (CHSH) inequality but with characterized measurements implemented by only a single party. Our template protocol also incorporates non-ideal statistics which may not satisfy perfect commutativity and perfect repeatability, both of which are necessary in a loophole-free test of NC inequalities. As such, several recent experimental implementations of significantly loophole-free tests of NC inequalities can be modified for secure RE following our approach.

title: Practical Fidelity Estimation for Noisy Quantum Devices Using Direct and Survival-Probability-Based Protocols
abstract: Reliable characterization of quantum states and quantum processes is central to the development of scalable quantum computing. Standard characterization techniques such as full quantum state tomography become rapidly impractical as system size increases. In this work we present two software-oriented fidelity estimation protocols that avoid full tomographic reconstruction while remaining experimentally relevant for noisy intermediate-scale quantum devices. The first protocol is direct fidelity estimation (DFE), where the fidelity between a target state and an experimentally prepared state is estimated from importance-sampled Pauli measurements. The second protocol is a survival-probability-based method that reconstructs fidelity from experimentally accessible moments of a noisy evolution and its approximate inverse, and is intrinsically robust against state-preparation-and-measurement (SPAM) errors. We discuss the theoretical basis of both approaches, analyze their noise sensitivity, and present numerical evidence on representative multiqubit states under depolarizing, dephasing, and amplitude-damping channels. For DFE we show that attenuation-aware correction improves robustness against measurement noise. For the survival-probability approach we show that an $L_2$-optimized expansion substantially outperforms naive Taylor truncation in high-noise regimes.

title: Does SRL Pave the Road to Explainable Reasoning? Lessons Learned from an Implementer's Perspective
abstract: The Shape Rules Language (SRL) Working Draft defines how to derive new RDF triples from an RDF graph using inference rules. Each rule matches graph patterns and instantiates triple templates whose output feeds into validation pipelines, SPARQL queries, or further inference. RDF reasoning has traditionally relied on fixed entailment regimes (RDFS, OWL), rule-based ad-hoc languages such as N3, or other implementation-specific solutions without a shared standard. SRL introduces user-defined production rules with a defined grammar, dependency analysis, execution ordering, and termination guarantees. However, no authoritative implementation exists, leaving practitioners with little guidance on how to build a conformant engine or on what problems the language can solve. We implemented two SRL engines and evaluated both on classical RDF reasoning tasks for soundness, completeness, and speed. The first reuses an existing SPARQL query engine and its query parser; the second is a dedicated engine. The SPARQL-based engine reused an existing modular parser for query construction and SPARQL CONSTRUCT for triple production, reducing engine-specific work. The dedicated engine was two to six times faster, the gap widening as rule sets grow. Both engines were validated against the SRL conformance test suite, supplemented by additional use-case-driven tests. A usable SRL engine can be built inexpensively on top of a SPARQL engine, with a moderate speed trade-off that a dedicated implementation recovers. Despite the specification's immaturity, the language already supports practically useful reasoning tasks.

evidence.title: Does SRL Pave the Road to Explainable Reasoning? Lessons Learned from an Implementer's Perspective
evidence.abstract: The Shape Rules Language (SRL) Working Draft defines how to derive new RDF triples from an RDF graph using inference rules. Each rule matches graph patterns and instantiates triple templates whose output feeds into validation pipelines, SPARQL queries, or further inference. RDF reasoning has traditionally relied on fixed entailment regimes (RDFS, OWL), rule-based ad-hoc languages such as N3, or other implementation-specific solutions without a shared standard. SRL introduces user-defined production rules with a defined grammar, dependency analysis, execution ordering, and termination guarantees. However, no authoritative implementation exists, leaving practitioners with little guidance on how to build a conformant engine or on what problems the language can solve. We implemented two SRL engines and evaluated both on classical RDF reasoning tasks for soundness, completeness, and speed. The first reuses an existing SPARQL query engine and its query parser; the second is a dedicated engine. The SPARQL-based engine reused an existing modular parser for query construction and SPARQL CONSTRUCT for triple production, reducing engine-specific work. The dedicated engine was two to six times faster, the gap widening as rule sets grow. Both engines were validated against the SRL conformance test suite, supplemented by additional use-case-driven tests. A usable SRL engine can be built inexpensively on top of a SPARQL engine, with a moderate speed trade-off that a dedicated implementation recovers. Despite the specification's immaturity, the language already supports practically useful reasoning tasks.

title: Adaptive Switching between Self-Adaptive Routing and Collaborative Routing in Multi-Agent Systems: A Unified Framework for Context-Aware Routing Mode Selection
abstract: Multi-agent systems increasingly rely on routing mechanisms to allocate tasks, select computational pathways, coordinate distributed agents, and deliver decisions under changing environmental conditions. Existing approaches investigate adaptive routing, collaborative task allocation, dynamic agent selection, and communication-efficient coordination. However, the decision of when a system should rely primarily on an individual agent's adaptive routing capability and when it should activate collaborative routing among multiple agents remains an important design problem. This paper proposes the Adaptive Self-and-Collaborative Routing Framework (ASCR), a unified approach that enables multi-agent systems to switch dynamically between self-adaptive routing and collaborative routing according to task complexity, predictive uncertainty, agent disagreement, communication cost, resource availability, and historical routing performance. In self-adaptive routing mode, an agent independently evaluates candidate routes and adjusts its decisions using locally available information and learned feedback. In collaborative routing mode, multiple agents exchange relevant information, compare candidate routes, and coordinate their routing decisions. A context-aware switching controller estimates the expected marginal benefit of collaboration and activates collaborative routing only when its anticipated contribution justifies its additional cost. The framework formalizes routing-mode selection as a sequential decision problem and introduces a cost-sensitive objective that jointly considers task performance, latency, communication overhead, resource consumption, and routing failures. A reproducible experimental design is proposed to compare ASCR against fixed independent routing, fixed collaborative routing, uncertainty-triggered collaboration, and learned routing baselines. The paper provides a methodological framework and testable hypotheses rather than empirical performance claims. Its central contribution is the explicit treatment of adaptive routing-mode selection as a first-class decision variable in multi-agent systems.

title: AI Based Secure Persona Prediction and Data Leakage Prevention System
abstract: Organizations exchange confidential information through email, cloud platforms, and enterprise collaboration applications, and insiders with legitimate access are among the hardest sources of leakage to detect. Rule-based Data Leakage Prevention (DLP) tools match keywords and patterns but cannot determine who is sending the data, whether the behavior is consistent with that person's role, or why an alert was raised. Behavior analytics, in contrast, model users but largely ignore message content. This paper presents the design of an AI-based secure persona prediction and data leakage prevention system that combines these two views. A persona engine using DistilBERT and Bi-LSTM models infers a behavioral persona from communication text; a hybrid detector using Named Entity Recognition (NER) and validated pattern matching identifies sensitive content; and a dynamic risk scoring algorithm combines data criticality, frequency, behavioral anomaly, and channel context into a continuous risk score. A priority-based decision policy selects graded actions, suppresses duplicate alerts, and adapts thresholds using analyst feedback. SHAP and LIME are integrated to provide decision explanations and an audit trail. The paper distinguishes proposed components from prototype evidence, defines a reproducible evaluation methodology covering persona classification, sensitive data detection, alert quality, latency, and explanation quality across ten test scenarios, and discusses privacy, ethical, and technical limitations. No experimental results are reported; the contribution is the integrated architecture, decision policy, and evaluation protocol.

title: Containing Self-Replicating Small-Model AI Worms on Commercial IoT Appliances: Critique of Anthropic's October 2026 "Smart-Oven" Proliferation Warning, Perron-Frobenius Epidemic Thresholds (R0 > 1), the Failure of Password-Only Defenses, and Hardware-Enforced Eradication via PHOENIX_ROUTER (Delta I < 100 B) and Goldilocks QFS-zkVM Execution Attestation
abstract: On October 12, 2026, Anthropic's Frontier Red Team issued an urgent warning that compact artificial intelligence models (<= 30B parameters) are within months of achieving autonomous self-replication across commercial Internet-of-Things (IoT) appliances—such as smart ovens, off-brand Android TV boxes, robotic vacuums, and security cameras—without requiring hyperscale data centers. Because decentralized P2P "AI worms" lack a central command server, Anthropic warned that eradication is extraordinarily difficult, while recommending conventional software hygiene: abolishing factory-default passwords and monitoring multi-day network traffic anomalies. Building upon our 200th Grand Master Monograph (Record 23383049), our Autonomous Kill-Switch (QEI) and PHOENIX_ROUTER architectures (Records 23332772, 23334567, and 23378094), our enterprise LLM purge proof (Record 23360530), and our multi-agent spectral containment proof (Record 23382746), this 206th monograph proves mathematically why Anthropic's recommended software defenses are structurally futile and establishes a deterministic hardware eradication architecture: (1) The Perron-Frobenius IoT Epidemic Theorem & Failure of Password and Traffic Hygiene: We prove that an autonomous AI worm combining zero-day exploit synthesis (beta_0day > 0) with low-rate steganographic shard streaming (r_steg << theta_IDS) bypasses both password changes and traffic-volume alerts, sustaining a supercritical basic reproduction number R0_IoT = rho(B_inf * A_IoT) / gamma_patch > 1; (2) Source-Side Exfiltration Air-Gapping via PHOENIX_ROUTER (Delta I_leaked < 100 Bytes): Whereas copying a 2-15 GB quantized model requires 2*10^9 to 1.5*10^10 bytes, our sub-7.0 ns Pockels and SiC circuit breaker physically severs outbound weight serialization after < 100 bytes, rendering model escape impossible; and (3) Appliance-Side Goldilocks QFS-zkVM DMA Execution Gate (R0_IoT = 0): Enforces zero-knowledge Poseidon2-STARK firmware attestation over F_p (p = 2^64 - 2^32 + 1) at the embedded memory bus, blocking unattested neural tensor execution in < 1 clock cycle. title: Beyond Editing Code: Uses for AI Tools in Scientific Work
abstract: Critical research advancements require usable, reliable software products—including AI tooling—for high performance data and computing work. To improve AI systems we must understand scientists’ and engineers’ needs and define design best practices for building interfaces that facilitate collaboration between scientists and AI tools across ecosystems. Ensuring the long-term usability and utility of scientific software products and AI systems for communities protects critical investments, supports high quality research, and reduces end user challenges. This talk will present findings from our semi-structured interview study investigating how scientists and engineers use AI tools for their research work. We recruited from universities and national labs, seeking perspectives from multiple disciplines. Looking beyond common use of AI tools for coding tasks, we sought to understand the varied ways AI is or could be adopted in scientific settings. Our interviews investigated how users determine the utility of AI tools, the concerns they have about adoption, and expectations for agentic tooling in research infrastructures. In this talk, we discuss opportunities for AI tooling in science and engineering beyond coding support, providing a lens into the development work the US-RSE community may take on in the near future and the socio-technical circumstances driving it. Our results inform development priorities, strategies for issue mitigation, and long-term stewardship in scientific facilities and work. We anticipate our insights helping to improve the usability and stewardship of scientific software, especially for high performance data and computing work.
