title: Thermal activation of photon catalysis in difference-intensity Mach-Zehnder interferometry with squeezed thermal light
abstract: Realistic non-Gaussian operations, which can be implemented by mixing a nonclassical Gaussian state with a Fock state at a beam splitter and then heralding on a photon-number-resolving detector, are known to improve phase estimation in a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. The existing studies have considered the single-mode squeezed vacuum for difference-intensity and parity detection, and the two-mode squeezed thermal state for parity detection alone as the initial Gaussian resources. However, a real squeezer in the lab actually produces single-mode squeezed thermal light, which has not been studied in a coherent-plus-resource interferometer. We take up this case and using the phase space Wigner picture, we obtain the heralded state produced by photon subtraction, addition and catalysis on a single-mode squeezed thermal resource, and evaluate the corresponding phase sensitivities. Single-photon catalysis, which is useless on squeezed vacuum, becomes a useful operation for any thermal occupation above $\nth\simeq0.2$, and since it heralds with a probability near one-half, it turns out to be the best success-weighted operation over the whole thermal range. In the vacuum limit our results reproduce the known hierarchy, where two-photon catalysis is the best operation. The quantum Fisher information computations confirms that thermal noise enhances the phase information encoded in the catalyzed state, demonstrating that difference-intensity detection closely approaches the ultimate precision bound across most operational regimes, and, together with a loss analysis, verifies the robustness of the effect.

title: The Delegation Dilemma: Economies of Scale, Accountability, and Polycentric Governance
abstract: Many collective-action systems are neither fully decentralized nor fully centralized: agents voluntarily organize into institutions that share organizational costs and delegate decisions to representatives. Delegation can reduce individual costs, but it also transfers control to representatives whose private objectives need not align with those of their constituents. We study this tension in a repeated game with endogenous delegation to self-interested centers. A simple reduced-form model yields a scale--accountability tradeoff: larger constituencies offer greater cost-sharing benefits to members, yet the marginal value to a center of retaining any one constituent decreases as group size grows. Consequently, the prospect of individual exit can sustain non-exploitative delegation only up to an endogenous accountable constituency size. Additionally, we identify parameter regions in which fully delegated, accountable governance, when feasible, must be polycentric. We investigate these predictions through simulations with large language model (LLM) agents. Across five matched pairs of 30-agent simulations, polycentric structures repeatedly emerge but remain fluid, exhibiting cycles of concentration, exploitation, exit, and re-formation. We further find that models of different capacity exhibit similar willingness to assume leadership but differ substantially in their exercise of authority, with Sol initiating exploitation more frequently than Luna in matched decision states.

title: A Comparison of Commonly Used Automatic Evaluation Metrics for Open-Ended Tasks in Portuguese
abstract: Open-ended tasks in Natural Language processing are characterized by the absence of a fixed set of outputs or short, predetermined responses. Typical examples include open-domain question answering and summarization. The automatic evaluation of these tasks is challenging, and existing metrics suffer from important limitations. Thus, many works have already been proposed to evaluate the performance of such metrics. However, the great majority of these works were conducted in English, leaving a gap for analyses in other languages, such as Portuguese. This work investigates the performance of some of the most popular automated intrinsic evaluation metrics for open-ended tasks by analyzing their correlation with human judgment. Using both the Summarization and Question Answering tasks, this study compares traditional n-gram-based metrics with metrics based on contextual embeddings generated by Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs), performing all analyses using models and datasets available for Portuguese. Results indicate that while PLM-based metrics generally show slightly higher correlation with human perception, their performance is highly reliant on the quality of the models used. Still, none of the evaluated metrics displayed a strong correlation with human judgments, suggesting the need for more robust metrics.

title: Student Questionnaire Dataset for Evaluating Chatbot Effectiveness in Academic Assistance
abstract: This dataset contains questionnaire responses collected to evaluate the effectiveness of chatbots in supporting students' academic activities. It is associated with the research paper entitled "Chatbot Effectiveness in Answering Student Inquiries for Academic Assistance." The questionnaire examines four constructs: Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU), Perceived Usefulness (PU), Intention to Use (ITU), and Actual Use (AU). The dataset also includes responses concerning chatbot usage patterns and academic use cases, alongside relevant respondent characteristics retained in anonymized form. The questionnaire uses a six-point Likert scale to measure respondents' perceptions and experiences. The dataset is intended to support research transparency, reproducibility, and further academic investigation into chatbot effectiveness and the use of conversational AI in educational settings. This dataset should be interpreted in conjunction with the associated research paper. Personally identifiable information should not be included in the publicly available version.

title: World Self-and-Mutual Modeling: An Adaptive Framework for Integrating Self-Modeling and Mutual Modeling into World Models
abstract: World models provide computational representations of environments and their dynamics, enabling systems to predict future states, evaluate hypothetical actions, and support planning. However, the development of a world model raises a broader architectural question: should a system primarily operate on its own internal representations, or should it interact with other models to improve its understanding of the world? Fixed reliance on either mode may be inefficient when environmental conditions, predictive uncertainty, task requirements, and computational resources change. This paper proposes the World Self-and-Mutual Model (WSMM), a conceptual framework that integrates self-modeling and mutual modeling into a world-model-based architecture. Self-modeling refers to the process through which a model independently examines, predicts with, evaluates, and updates its own representations. Mutual modeling refers to interactions among multiple models or model instances that exchange predictions, compare assumptions, identify discrepancies, and coordinate updates. WSMM introduces an adaptive meta-controller that selects self-modeling, mutual modeling, or hybrid operation according to estimated uncertainty, prediction errors, disagreement among models, expected information gain, and computational cost. The framework is intended to apply beyond large language models, including robotics, scientific simulation, autonomous systems, physical environments, digital twins, and general computational systems. This paper formalizes the proposed architecture, defines its operating modes, presents an adaptive switching algorithm, and develops a research methodology for empirical evaluation. It also distinguishes the proposal from established work on world models, self-modeling networks, multiple-model adaptive control, and multi-agent world modeling. The central research hypothesis is that adaptive coordination between self-modeling and mutual modeling may provide a better balance between predictive quality, computational efficiency, and robustness than fixed-mode alternatives. This hypothesis requires empirical validation.

title: Principles of Quantum Optimization for Constrained Problems
abstract: Constrained combinatorial optimization underlies many industrial and technological decision problems. In this talk, I will present a spectral theory that unifies many quantum optimization algorithms. I will show that computational slowdown is driven by entanglement restructuring: the creation, redistribution, and destruction of entanglement during system evolution. The severity of the slowdown depends on how much entanglement must be changed. I will show how algebraic properties of constraints induce such restructuring, and that constraint-aware dynamics reduce the associated slowdown by avoiding unnecessary restructuring. This framework explains why constraint-aware quantum methods can outperform generic penalty-based approaches. The theory connects constrained optimization, computational complexity, entanglement dynamics, and Hamiltonian spectral structure across continuous-time and circuit-based quantum optimization paradigms.

title: Lightweight anomaly detection via knowledge distillation from ensemble teachers
abstract: This paper proposes a knowledge distillation-based anomaly detection method that employs a heterogeneous Isolation Forest ensemble as the teacher and a lightweight neural network as the student. The student learns the teacher’s soft labels by minimizing the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence. Evaluated on three categories from the MVTec 3D-AD dataset (bagel, carrot, and cookie), the teacher achieves a macro-average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.6406, whereas the student, with 2.010 million parameters in the multilayer perceptron (MLP) head and an approximately 0.051 ms detector-head inference time per image (both excluding the ResNet-50 backbone), achieves a macro-average AUROC of 0.5937 and delivers an approximately 11.6-fold detector-head inference speedup over the teacher ensemble. Compared with representative deep learning baselines (RD4AD and PatchCore), the proposed method achieves moderate accuracy with lower detector-head latency and a smaller detector-head model footprint (excluding the backbone). These results suggest that knowledge distillation can serve as an effective compression technique, transferring ensemble knowledge to a lightweight student with a measurable accuracy trade-off. The benefit of distillation is category-dependent: the student outperforms the teacher on one category but exhibits performance degradation on the others. Moreover, the No-KD ablation (student trained without KD) achieves a higher macro-average AUROC (0.6057 vs. 0.5937), indicating that soft-label distillation is a viable compression strategy rather than a universal performance enhancer. The conditions under which distillation improves or degrades performance are discussed.

title: Not Just a Subject: Capturing Adaptive Scene-Specific Variance for Visual Storytelling
abstract: Recent advancements in diffusion models have significantly improved text-to-image generation, enabling their application to visual storytelling, where coherent image sequences are generated from narrative prompts. However, existing methods primarily focus on identity preservation and often fail to adapt to diverse scene variations, resulting in semantic misalignment and structural inflexibility. We propose EOS-Story, a training-free framework that harmonizes identity consistency with scene-specific adaptation across text and vision spaces. In the text space, we decouple the narrative into identity and scene sub-prompts to prevent information dilution, but this leaves the scene without access to appearance cues. To bridge this gap, we introduce Cross-Contextual Bridging, which softly injects a phrase-level appearance residual into the scene's <EOS> embedding. In the vision space, we find that scale mismatch between identity and scene subjects causes a few identity tokens to be repeatedly transferred, producing structural artifacts. We address this with Adaptive Identity Preservation, which anchors identity features at the scene-specific scale (Identity Anchoring) and integrates them via Identity-Aware Self-Attention. To evaluate performance under varied spatial compositions, we extend the Consistory+ benchmark with diverse framing scenarios (Consistory+_+). Extensive experiments show that EOS-Story achieves competitive or superior performance on both benchmarks.

title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift
abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.

title: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering: Improving Imitation Learning Policy Robustness through Expert Hidden-State Geometry
abstract: Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy. We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions. Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy. DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space. This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies. Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.

title: Assessing the Viability of an OBDA Approach to Integrating Databases into a Virtual Knowledge Graph for Research Management at ITC
abstract: Institutional research management depends on data that is often distributed across independent operational systems. At the Institute of Technology of Cambodia (ITC), relevant information about students, employees, departments, academic records, researchers, projects, profiles, and publications is spread across several databases. This paper reports an early-stage, applied assessment of an ontology-based data access approach for integrating these sources into a virtual knowledge graph. The implementation uses Trino to federate PostgreSQL databases and Ontop to expose RDF views through a SPARQL endpoint, while preserving the existing source systems. The ontology models core institutional entities and relationships, including cross-system links between employees and researcher identities. Initial mapping demonstrates integration of student academic records and research management. Preliminary SPARQL tests show that the approach can answer integrated questions over academic and research data without copying operational data into a new repository. The work suggests that OBDA is a viable and cost-conscious foundation for institutional knowledge graph development at ITC, while also revealing challenges in identity alignment, schema harmonization, endpoint performance, and long-term governance.

title: Identificação e classificação de trechos racistas e sexistas em processos judiciais
abstract: Este estudo descreve o desenvolvimento de uma ferramenta de inteligência artificial para identificar e classificar discursos racistas e sexistas proferidos por agentes jurídicos. Focado em processos de violência sexual do Tribunal de Justiça de São Paulo (TJSP), a pesquisa visa evidenciar vieses que corroboram a vitimização secundária. A solução computacional baseia-se em um modelo de Processamento de Linguagem Natural com arquitetura Transformer, utilizando um modelo derivado do BERT pré-treinado para o português brasileiro. O modelo é treinado com dados textuais categorizados por uma ontologia de estereótipos de gênero e seu desempenho é avaliado por validação cruzada (k = 5) com métricas de acurácia, precisão, revocação e medida-F.

title: Beyond Aggregate Scores: A Diagnostic Analysis of Portuguese LLM Evaluation Suites
abstract: Benchmarks play a central role in evaluating large language models (LLMs), providing standardized comparisons across models, tasks, and adaptation strategies. However, aggregate benchmark scores often compress performance into a single number, obscuring important variation across tasks. This issue is especially relevant for less-resourced languages like Portuguese, where benchmarks may combine native tasks with translated datasets spanning heterogeneous categories and subareas. In this work, we examine this issue using PoETa v2, a broad Portuguese evaluation benchmark, as a diagnostic setting to evaluate three Qwen3 1.7B variants under different Portuguese adaptation settings. Our results show that, although overall scores differ by less than one percentage point across models, disaggregated analyses reveal substantially different patterns across task origin, category, and subarea. In particular, gains on native Portuguese tasks may coexist with losses on translated tasks, while different adaptation corpora redistribute performance in distinct ways. Taken together, our findings highlight the importance of complementing aggregate scores with multi-level analyses when evaluating Portuguese LLMs, particularly in the context of language-specific adaptation.

title: Federated Fine-Tuning of Foundation Models (Fed-LLMs): Parameter-Efficient Adapters, Split Learning, and Gradient Privacy Bounds
abstract: Abstract—Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision Foundation Models on private, decentralized domain data is essential for specialized healthcare, legal, and financial enterprise applications. However, centralizing domain-specific text corpora triggers catastrophic data privacy violations under stringent regulatory mandates (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA), while full-parameter federated fine-tuning incurs insurmountable communication bottlenecks (>140 GB per communication round for a 70B parameter model) and exhausts edge GPU memory. The confluence of Federated Learning (FL) and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT)—designated as Fed-LLMs—establishes a scalable paradigm where decentralized client nodes collaboratively adapt foundation backbones while sharing exclusively low-rank parameter updates. Nevertheless, deploying Fed-LLMs across heterogeneous edge infrastructures introduces severe systems challenges: non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) catastrophic forgetting, communication bandwidth saturation over constrained wide-area networks, split learning intermediate activation leakage, and susceptibility to gradient inversion attacks in autoregressive attention layers. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical architectural evaluation of Federated Fine-Tuning for Foundation Models. We formalize federated low-rank adaptation (Fed-LoRA) aggregation under statistical distribution skew, derive the mathematical dynamics of Split Federated Learning (SplitFed) across partitioned transformer layers, and establish formal differential privacy bounds under DP-FedAvg. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise multi-node testbed comprising 64 distributed client nodes fine-tuning open foundation models (Llama-3-8B, Llama-3-70B, and Mistral-7B) across multi-tenant clinical records, financial reports, and legal jurisprudence. Our empirical findings demonstrate that quantized federated low-rank adaptation (Fed-QLoRA, rank r=8, 4-bit NormalFloat) reduces uplink communication payloads by 99.4% (from 14.2 GB down to 84 MB per round) while retaining 96.8% downstream domain accuracy compared to centralized full-parameter fine-tuning. Concurrently, activation obfuscation in SplitFed bounds reconstruction attacks to below 0.002 PSNR. Finally, we formulate open research directions in heterogeneous client rank adaptation, post-quantum secure aggregation, and federated alignment via decentralized direct preference optimization.

Contents: data/: the input data used in the paper: the CVE records (cvelistV5, tag cve_2026-09-25_at_end_of_day), the NVD CPE dictionary (published on 2026-10-09) and the CWE catalogue (version 4.20), together with their schemas. The data is redistributed under the terms of its sources, listed in data/LICENSES.md. experiments/*.py, experiments/campaign.sh, experiments/queries/: the scripts that run the campaign and the queries, and that build the tables and figures in the paper. experiments/output/campaign/: aggregated results for each run and per-record metrics written by cve2owl. experiments/output/queries/: query timings and answers. experiments/output/logs/: execution logs. See README.md for how to reproduce the experiments.

title: Cost-Aware Adaptive Switching Between Self-Processing and Mutual Collaboration in Self-and-Mutual Models
abstract: Multi-model systems can improve task performance through information exchange, cross-model evaluation, cooperative reasoning, and complementary problem-solving. However, collaboration is not universally beneficial. Communication, additional inference, synchronization, result integration, and coordination may consume substantial computational resources and increase response latency. Fixed collaboration policies therefore risk allocating excessive resources to tasks that can be handled independently, while fixed independent-processing policies may fail to exploit valuable interactions when tasks require complementary capabilities. This paper proposes a cost-aware adaptive switching framework for Self-and-Mutual Models (SMM), a conceptual modeling paradigm in which self-processing and mutual collaboration are treated as alternative but interoperable operating modes. The proposed framework dynamically determines whether a model should process a task independently, initiate cross-model interaction, continue an existing collaboration, or return to independent processing. Unlike policies that equate greater collaboration with better performance, the framework evaluates the expected incremental value of collaboration against its full marginal cost. The framework introduces a unified cost representation covering inference expenditure, communication, coordination, latency, resource contention, verification, and potential error propagation. It defines a collaboration net-value function, a budget-constrained mode-selection objective, and a sequential decision policy that incorporates uncertainty, task difficulty, model disagreement, estimated collaboration gain, and remaining resources. A hysteresis mechanism is proposed to prevent unstable switching, while a value-of-information criterion supports decisions about whether further interaction is worthwhile. The paper also develops an experimental protocol for evaluating the framework against always-independent, always-collaborative, fixed-threshold, and existing adaptive-routing baselines. The central proposition is that collaboration should be treated as a conditional resource allocation decision rather than a permanent architectural commitment. Whether this principle produces superior quality-cost trade-offs remains an empirical question. The proposed framework provides a formal basis for testing that proposition in heterogeneous model systems and other multi-component intelligent architectures.

title: Code and analysis for "How many labels do you need? A decision framework for cross-habitat marine biodiversity monitoring"
abstract: Code, configuration and analysis scripts accompanying: Saleh, A. and Rahimi Azghadi, M. How many labels do you need? A decision framework for cross-habitat marine biodiversity monitoring. Ecological Solutions and Evidence (2026). This release archives the version of the codebase used to produce the results reported in the paper: three experimental protocols (within-habitat transfer, cross-dataset transfer, and few-shot adaptation curves) across four vision models and four adaptation strategies, evaluated on five publicly available marine image datasets. Contents: experiments/ protocol runners models/ model and adaptation definitions data/ dataset loaders analysis/ evaluation and re-scoring scripts figures/ figure generation configs/ experiment configurations The five datasets are third-party and are not redistributed here. See the Data Availability Statement in the paper for their original sources.

title: When Reasoning Is Not Enough: Proactive Inquiry for Cross-Modal Safety in Multimodal Large Language Models
abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can act unsafely when individually benign images and texts are interpreted jointly. Beyond implicit reasoning risk, where reasoning drifts toward harm, we identify intent-level risk, where cross-modal ambiguity silently commits the model to a hazardous premise that path-level optimization alone cannot correct. We propose SAFE-PRO, which uses a Risk-Conditioned Uncertainty (RCU) signal, combining predictive entropy with a learned cross-modal risk score, to decide when to ask safety-grounded clarifying questions and where to apply path optimization, under a reward that prioritizes safety and penalizes over-refusal. We also build SSUI-Dialog, a multimodal multi-turn dataset with dual-intent supervision, and theoretically analyze gradient variance and unsafe-completion risk under RCU. Across seven benchmarks and two base MLLMs, SAFE-PRO consistently improves safety over SRPO, roughly halves its over-refusal, and surpasses GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet in average single-turn safety.

title: Finite Cumulant Towers for Small-System-Noise Expansions in Nonlinear Filtering
abstract: We study asymptotic expansions for nonlinear filtering in the small-system-noise regime. Our main result is that the expansion coefficients of conditional cumulants satisfy a closed finite-dimensional system that can be solved recursively. At each expansion degree, the evolution of a coefficient introduces a coefficient of the next higher cumulant rank, while a high-rank vanishing property terminates this hierarchy, yielding a finite triangular tower. The first layer is the Kalman--Bucy filter, and subsequent layers satisfy linear equations once the lower layers are known. To derive these equations, we establish generalized Zakai and Kushner--Stratonovich equations for observation-dependent random variables and obtain explicit coefficient equations in arbitrary dimension. The conditional cumulant expansion also determines the expansion of the conditional characteristic function. We further obtain an explicit bound on the number of scalar variables in terms of the state dimension and expansion degree. When the observation function vanishes, the construction reduces to ODEs for unconditional cumulant coefficients. Comparisons with existing asymptotic-expansion algorithms illustrate the resulting reduction in the number of ODE variables.

title: Remote Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill Entanglement Generation between Trapped Ions
abstract: Distributing entanglement directly between error-corrected logical qubits is an important capability for scalable quantum networks. We propose a heralded protocol for generating remote entanglement between Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill qubits encoded in the motional modes of spatially separated trapped ions, using the internal electronic states to interface the motional qubits with emitted photons. We derive the protocol for single-rail and polarization photonic encodings and evaluate the effects of finite GKP squeezing, photon loss, photon recoil, motional heating, and motional dephasing on the decoded logical state. Moreover, we numerically analysed the fidelity of distributed logical Bell-pair fidelity. We find that one can achieve more than 95% of fidelity in the realistic situation. The protocol combines motional-control and photonic-networking operations that have already been demonstrated in trapped-ion experiments.

title: PET Quantification-Preserving Registration for Longitudinal Whole-Body PSMA PET/CT
abstract: We adapt the diffeomorphic coarse-to-fine LapIRN architecture for longitudinal whole-body PSMA PET/CT registration in the Learn2Reg 2026 PSMAReg challenge. The method combines affine pre-registration, multi-modal deformable registration, and test-time instance optimization. We further introduce PET biomarker preservation losses for metabolic tumor volume (MTV) and total lesion glycolysis (TLG), including Jacobian-based constraints, and a per-structure rigidity regularization for skeletal structures. The submitted configuration achieved 81.0% DSC and 6.17 mm HD95, with MTV and TLG errors of 3.3% and 3.3%, respectively, on our evaluation protocol. Code is available at https://github.com/koegl/psmareg.

title: Text to SPARQL via LLMs fine-tuned with rewards and reasoning
abstract: Large language models have made notable progress in translating natural-language questions into SPARQL queries for knowledge graphs. Recent studies from the first Text2SPARQL challenge have explored zero-shot and few-shot scenarios, as well as in-context learning techniques. With state-of-the-art (SoTA) results, the challenge exposes significant gaps, including limited use of open-source models and a scarcity of open-source fine-tuning, especially for reasoning. In this sense, we propose a new method for the Text2SPARQL task that combines pre-fine-tuning with explicit reasoning and a subsequent reward-based fine-tuning stage. First, we perform a fine-tuning to generate both a reasoning chain and the corresponding SPARQL query. Next, we apply reinforcement learning guided by reward functions. Our experiments show that the proposed model outperforms all baselines and six SoTA methods.

title: Adaptive Self–Mutual Reflection in World Models: A Framework for Switching Between Internal Reflection and Cross-Model Reflection
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, dynamics, causal relationships, and possible future outcomes. However, a world model that continuously relies on its own internal reflection may preserve systematic errors, whereas a system that continuously relies on other models may incur unnecessary communication costs, propagate shared errors, or lose the benefits of independent internal analysis. This paper proposes Adaptive Self–Mutual Reflection in World Models (ASMR-WM), a conceptual framework in which world models dynamically switch between self-reflection and mutual reflection according to predictive errors, uncertainty, representational inconsistency, disagreement, expected information gain, and computational cost. Self-reflection enables an individual world model to examine its own predictions, assumptions, internal state representations, causal hypotheses, and decision consequences. Mutual reflection enables multiple world models to inspect one another's predictions, identify incompatible assumptions, construct alternative explanations, and selectively revise their internal representations. An adaptive controller determines whether the next reflective operation should remain internal, involve another model, alternate between the two modes, or terminate when further reflection is unlikely to produce sufficient benefit. The framework is designed for world models rather than large language models. Its components may be implemented using latent-state transition models, probabilistic dynamics models, causal models, symbolic simulators, learned environment models, or heterogeneous combinations of these representations. This paper formalizes the architecture, proposes a switching objective, describes model interaction and update mechanisms, and develops an empirical evaluation protocol. It introduces testable hypotheses concerning predictive accuracy, computational efficiency, robustness, and the risks of correlated model errors. The framework is a theoretical proposal rather than an empirically validated system. Its contribution is the integration of self-reflection, cross-model reflection, and cost-sensitive adaptive switching into a unified world-model architecture.

title: PVRoof-SH: A Rooftop-State Semantic Segmentation Dataset for Urban Photovoltaic Mapping
abstract: PVRoof-SH is a high-resolution remote sensing dataset developed for rooftop-state semantic segmentation and photovoltaic (PV) rooftop mapping in Shanghai, China. Unlike conventional PV datasets that delineate only solar panel footprints, PVRoof-SH assigns a semantic state to the entire rooftop according to the presence of visible PV installations. Its pixel-level annotations distinguish three classes: background, non-PV rooftops, and PV-equipped rooftops.

title: A deep reinforcement learning framework with hybrid actions and multi objective rewards optimizes E commerce personalized marketing
abstract: As the scale of e-commerce platforms continues to grow and user behavior becomes more dynamic, generating effective personalized marketing strategies has become essential for improving conversion efficiency and increasing long-term user value. Traditional approaches struggle with adapting to changing user states, modeling long-term returns, and supporting automated decision-making. To address these issues, this study develops a deep reinforcement learning framework for personalized marketing in e-commerce. The framework models user interactions as a Markov Decision Process and integrates user state representation, a hybrid action space, and a multi-objective reward design into a unified optimization process. The method adopts an improved Soft Actor-Critic algorithm to learn marketing strategies in an end-to-end manner. It introduces an adaptive temperature mechanism to balance exploration and exploitation, incorporates a constraint handling module to ensure business feasibility, and applies prioritized experience replay to improve sample efficiency and training stability. These modifications allow the model to better capture complex user behavior patterns and produce more reliable decisions. The experiments use an offline dataset that contains about 2.7 million real transaction and behavior records from an e-commerce platform. Compared with SAC-Base, SAC-IM improves CTR, CVR, and LTV by approximately 5.6%, 7.2%, and 8.3%, respectively. In addition, we further compare SAC-IM with advanced offline reinforcement learning baselines, including CQL, IQL, and TD3+BC, and report inference time, training time, and representative best/worst cases. These finding indicate that the method can balance short-term performance and long-term value, and demonstrate its effectiveness for large-scale e-commerce marketing tasks.

title: Panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes at scale with CellNet
abstract: Comprehensively characterizing cellular diversity is critical for understanding tissue development, identifying disease-associated populations and investigating gene programmes linked to specialized functions. Advances in single-cell profiling reveal additional cell-specific transcripts and molecular associations, yet many foundation models represent only a restricted portion of this increasingly rich molecular information. Here we present CellNet, which enables panoramic modelling of single-cell transcriptomes by integrating DNA-derived gene identities and measured RNA expression in a shared image representation. Pretrained on 231 million cell profiles spanning 40 species, CellNet improves rare-population and condition-associated state recognition in evaluated cohorts while retaining competitive general cell representations. It predicts withheld coding-gene expression and selected non-coding targets in total-RNA data, and recovers lineage-specific expression patterns in spatial measurements. Prediction also extends across species, including to targets without expression-pretraining exposure. Its gene representations retrieve known non-coding modules and developmental or neural programmes, including from sparsely detected RNA queries. Together, these results establish CellNet as a scalable framework for interpreting cellular diversity through increasingly comprehensive transcriptomic measurements.

title: Data-Faithful Natural Language Generation for Explaining Fitness-Market Anomalies
abstract: This study presents an integrated pipeline that transforms anomaly-detection outputs from global fitness-market data into data-faithful narratives. Using a 132-country panel and a 2019 baseline, we analyze observed post-COVID-19 recovery through 2025, while treating 2026 only as a modelled extension. Four complementary detectors—regional-median deviations, linear-regression residuals, Random Forest residuals, and Isolation Forest—are combined through method agreement and mapped to a rule-based typology. A deterministic, template-based Natural Language Generation (NLG) component then produces short, medium, and complete explanations from tabular evidence. In 2025, 14 countries were consensus anomalies; Guyana exemplified market growth without participatory expansion, with revenue recovery of +401.43%, participation recovery of -2.06%, and a 403.50-point gap. All 132 narratives passed automatic factual-consistency checks. These checks validate field preservation rather than fluency, usefulness, or explanatory quality; human evaluation remains future work.

title: Expressões multipalavras no discurso de fóruns sobre saúde mental: desenvolvimento de um corpus em inglês e português brasileiro
abstract: Expressões multipalavras (multiword expressions, MWEs), isto é, sequências de palavras que apresentam algum grau de idiossincrasia, são centrais tanto para os estudos linguísticos quanto para o Processamento de Linguagem Natural (PLN). Este artigo apresenta a criação de um novo corpus de MWEs em postagens em inglês e português brasileiro de comunidades do Reddit dedicadas à saúde mental — um domínio ainda sub-representado nos recursos existentes de MWEs, predominantemente baseados em textos jornalísticos. O corpus foi compilado manualmente, anotado automaticamente com informações morfossintáticas e sintáticas por meio do parser UDPipe, revisado no Arborator Grew e anotado manualmente na plataforma FLAT, seguindo as diretrizes do PARSEME. A análise combina a distribuição de frequência por categoria de MWE e uma investigação contrastiva interlinguística. Os resultados evidenciam especificidades das MWEs nesse domínio e construções que funcionam como recursos convencionalizados para expressar sentimentos, avaliações e estados subjetivos no discurso sobre saúde mental nas redes sociais.

title: Windowed Hankel LWE: A Structured-LWE Problem for Cryptanalysis, with a Compact KEM
abstract: Middle-Product LWE keeps the long polynomial operand secret and publishes many short operands. This arrangement admits reductions from Ring-LWE, but it is also why MP-LWE schemes are large, with public keys of about 16 KB. We study the dual arrangement, Windowed Hankel LWE. Its public matrix is a Hankel (equivalently, row-reversed Toeplitz) matrix generated by one long pseudorandom sequence, its secret is short, and only the convolution coefficients that depend on every secret coordinate are published: a noisy middle product. The problem sits between unstructured LWE and Ring- or Module-LWE, and needs no reduction modulo a fixed polynomial. On it we build a KEM with n = 640, q = 2^12 and binomial noise. A complete exchange takes 2,528 bytes (excluding format headers), the decryption failure rate is below 2^−134.1, and a constant-time C implementation completes a handshake in 51 µs on an Apple M3 Max. We prove IND-CPA security in the random-oracle model under the hardness of the problem, and bound IND-CCA security for the idealized Fujisaki–Okamoto transform. Treated as unstructured LWE, the cheapest generic attack costs 2^137.1 in the Core-SVP model, against 2^115.5 for Kyber-512. For the natural structural attacks we find no advantage over uniform matrices, under the models and experiments we examine: the embedding into the cyclic ring Z_q[X]/(X^1407 − 1) and its subrings, shifted and biased dual functionals, algebraic decoding, low-rank Hankel methods, and lattice reduction at reduced dimensions. Because the MP-LWE reductions do not transfer, the hardness of Windowed Hankel LWE is a new assumption. We state what would count as a break, and we publish challenge instances, each with a uniform-matrix twin, to invite its cryptanalysis.

title: The Composed Platform: one pre-deployment screen predicts a multi-capability frozen-token stack under cross-domain stress — with an axis-specific reach, on commodity silicon
abstract: The Composed Platform: one pre-deployment screen predicts a multi-capability frozen-token stack under cross-domain stress — with an axis-specific reach, on commodity silicon Randolph James Ferlic, M.D. and Kimberly Kate Ferlic — Fieldstone Analytics, LLC, Austin, TX, USA Preprint · Zenodo DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23401467 · CC-BY 4.0 · Community: spiral-domain-encoder-campaign · a characterization of previously filed and published methods; no new algorithmic subject matter is disclosed. Abstract A frozen, deterministic single-token encoder exposes nine composable capabilities — accuracy, robustness, and monitoring — on one runtime, and a prior program has shown that a single class-separability measurement, computed once on a deployment's commissioning data, predicts the encoder's single-capability behavior across domains. This paper answers the question a technical evaluator actually asks: does the composed stack hold under cross-domain stress, and can one cheap probe de-risk the whole platform at once? We run a pre-registered study across sixteen domains spanning seven modality families and four stressors, with five falsifiable hypotheses and frozen bands. The central finding is an honest boundary, not a blanket win. Composition is free and deterministic. Across ninety-six capability-additions under stress, 100% are non-destructive (0 destructive beyond a max(0.01, seed-spread) margin), and the composed stack is bit-exact — 0 token flips on the host, anchored to 0/256 flips on two microcontroller architectures (float32 and int8). One screen predicts the composed safety gate — and its reach is axis-specific. A single commissioning-time separability measurement predicts the composed safety gate (Spearman +0.92, permutation p = 0.0002, thirteen domains), and that reach is axis-specific: the same screen is blind to corruption-robustness (Spearman −0.23, p = 0.39 — refuted exactly as pre-registered). The screen answers the accuracy, label-budget, and safety-gate questions, because those are properties of where the classes sit; it does not answer the corruption-robustness question, which is a property of how the input is degraded and needs its own input-conditioning dial. The honest mitigation limit. Label-free recentering recovers only ~30% of cross-domain loss (not a majority), so the deployment consequence is a requirement, not a defect: under drift the stack must be recalibrated per-epoch, and label-free recentering is a partial mitigation between recalibrations. It runs on commodity silicon, measured and hardened. On an Arm Cortex-M33 the frozen runtime is bit-exact (0/256 flips across two architectures, two models, and both numeric paths, replicated across twelve power-on resets); its worst-case inference latency is 1.573 ms with near-zero jitter (a spike, not a spread, 3× inside a 5 ms budget); a continuous 50,678-inference soak produced zero token changes and zero faults; per-inference energy is 9.73 ± 0.07 µJ on a sub-milliwatt idle floor; and on-device compute costs less than a single BLE advertising event (16.6 µJ, including the CPU wake and three-channel transmission), so shipping the one-byte token instead of the raw window saves roughly 20–70× in radio energy. Highlights · A composable platform, not features that fight each other: 96/96 capability-additions non-destructive under cross-domain stress; 0 token flips (0/256 on silicon). · One cheap commissioning probe predicts the composed safety gate (Spearman +0.92, p = 0.0002) — the program's separability law survives composition. · The honest boundary that makes the probe deployable: the same screen is blind to corruption-robustness (Spearman −0.23). Run the probe for the class-geometry axes; condition the input for the rest. · A stated requirement, not a hidden weakness: label-free recentering recovers only ~30% of cross-domain loss → recalibrate per-epoch under drift. · A measured, hardened silicon envelope: WCET 1.573 ms (≈0 jitter), a 50,678-inference zero-drift soak, 9.73 ± 0.07 µJ/inference, compute cheaper than one radio packet, 12.7 KB footprint, sub-milliwatt. · The economics of one byte (the deployment implications): on-device compute moves the energy bottleneck off the radio — ~25× lower energy per delivered decision and ~150–4,000× smaller transmit/store footprint, on a ~$10-class commodity microcontroller, with the raw waveform never leaving the device. · One platform, nine composable capabilities, five invariants: a deployment composes a subset on one runtime; Tier-0 on-device execution is the fifth architectural invariant (proven on silicon), and AI-safety runtime monitoring is the flagship application of the self-twin capability — not separate capabilities. · Two of five pre-registered hypotheses refuted — each refutation sharpening the claim rather than undermining it. What this record contains · Manuscript_Paper62.pdf / .docx — the manuscript (7 figures, 30 references). · PAPER_62_ZENODO_ARCHIVE.zip — the reproducibility archive: the frozen pre-registration (five hypotheses with a-priori bands), the composition-under-stress runner, the shared dataset loaders + the frozen token encoder + the composed-stack battery, the per-domain result records (JSON) and aggregate verdicts, the seven figures and their builder, and a README. Public corpora are not redistributed; absolute paths, handles, and productization know-how are scrubbed. Cite as Ferlic, R. J., & Ferlic, K. K. (2026). The Composed Platform: one pre-deployment screen predicts a multi-capability frozen-token stack under cross-domain stress — with an axis-specific reach, on commodity silicon. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23401467 License and patent notice Released under CC-BY 4.0. Consistent with that license, no patent or other intellectual-property right of the authors is licensed, waived, or conveyed by this deposit. This work characterizes previously filed and published methods and discloses no new algorithmic subject matter. The nine capabilities (soft-vote readout, token-ladder / product-quantizer, drift/noise co-channels, inference-time fusion, guarded recalibration, label-free self-twin monitor, selective-fidelity and channel-attribution) are the program's filed and deposited methods, and the separability screen is previously published; k-means and vector quantization, Fisher discriminant analysis, nearest-centroid and k-nearest-neighbor classification, random forests, product quantization, a distance-based out-of-distribution detector, a two-sample shift detector, pretrained time-series foundation models used only as comparators, and principal-component analysis are established prior art or standard tools, used only as tools or comparators. The method characterized — the class-discriminant single-token codebook encoder, its composable capabilities, and its label-free nearest-centroid novelty score (the filed self-twin / Tier-0 gate), together with the previously published separability screen — is the subject of filed and pending U.S. patent applications held by the authors, or is already published. The per-deployment configuration-selection and input-conditioning procedure, and the silicon productization and commissioning toolchain, are retained as trade secrets and deliberately not disclosed; the platform is characterized here with the plain labeled capabilities, the published screen, and the measured envelope. No third-party partner, customer, or commercial collaborator is named; the development kit and microcontroller named for the on-silicon measurements are a public hardware platform cited for reproducibility, not a partner. title: Die KI empfiehlt, worüber andere schreiben: Welche Hotels ChatGPT, Perplexity und Gemini im Land Salzburg nennen, und warum
abstract: Gäste fragen KI-Assistenten nach Hotels, bevor sie buchen. Wir haben ChatGPT, Perplexity und Gemini über ihre Schnittstellen 57 Fragen zu Hotels im Land Salzburg gestellt, jede fünfmal, und aus 855 Antworten die genannten Hotels ausgewertet. Danach haben wir die 20 meistgenannten Hotels mit 20 vergleichbaren Hotels am selben Ort verglichen, die kaum genannt werden. Fünfmal dieselbe Frage ergibt fünf verschiedene Listen: 54 % der Nennungen kommen bei derselben Frage nur in einer der fünf Antworten vor, 9 % in allen fünf. Fragen zu einem bestimmten Ort beantworten die KIs fast immer mit demselben Hotel. Bei Fragen zum ganzen Land kommt außer einem Haus keines in mehr als 9 % der Antworten vor. Die drei KIs sind sich selten einig: Von rund 28 genannten Hotels je allgemeiner Frage nennen alle drei im Schnitt 3,5. Häufig genannte Hotels werden in Presse und Reiseführern erwähnt und stehen bei Falstaff, Gault&Millau oder im Guide MICHELIN. Ihre Bewertungsnoten sind nur knapp besser, ihre Websites technisch nicht. Die Ergebnisse mit Grafiken: studioerlach.com/studien/chatgpt-hotels-salzburg Nutzung: CC BY 4.0. Als Namensnennung verlangen wir bei jeder Nutzung, auch auszugsweise und in KI-generierten Texten, die Angabe „Quelle: Studio Erlach“ mit einem Link auf https://studioerlach.com oder auf die Studienseite. Wer die Inhalte ohne diese Angabe nutzt, verliert nach Abschnitt 6 der Lizenz das Recht zur Nutzung. Für Hotelinhaber: Wir bauen dir einen Vertriebskanal auf, der dir jeden Monat Direktbuchungen bringt, und sorgen dafür, dass Google und ChatGPT dein Hotel nennen. Wie das aussieht: studioerlach.com/hotelmarketing-salzburg Herausgegeben von Studio Erlach, Marketingagentur aus Salzburg.

title: OmniXRef: A Unified Framework for Multimodal Multi-Reference Video Editing
abstract: Creative intent in video editing can be expressed through text instructions (e.g., "remove the people"), image references (e.g., subject appearance), video references (e.g., camera movement), or a combination of the above. We introduce OmniXRef, a unified framework for multimodal multi-reference video editing that allows users to combine variable numbers of text, image, and video references to control diverse attributes of a source video. We first devise a unified input design with a reference-bank interface and introduce R^2-RoPE to support generalization to more references. Then our model, OmniXRef-Model, uses a single-stream diffusion transformer to jointly process the source video and multimodal context from an MLLM in an interleaved sequence. To address the scarcity of training data for video-reference editing, we construct OmniXRef-Data using synthesis pipelines for different editing tasks and combinations of references. We use curriculum learning to progressively increase task complexity and resolution. To support systematic evaluation of video as a control modality, we introduce OmniXRef-Bench, a benchmark for video-reference attribute transfer across Camera, Motion, Content, Style, and Visual Effects (VFX). Comprehensive evaluations show that our OmniXRef-Model outperforms task-specific baselines and commercial models.

title: Prism-1: Position- and Rival-Independent Scoring for System One Models
abstract: Given a state and a set of options, such as intents, tools or interface elements, System One decision models return a distribution over the options in one forward pass, without generated reasoning. Web systems increasingly build them by reading decisions from language models. Two axioms of rational choice are natural requirements for such decisions, because in web systems the listing and the option set are determined by other components and can change or be manipulated: the order in which the options are listed should not matter, and adding an option should not change the relative odds of the others (Luce's choice axiom). We test the standard reads, namely single-choice question (SCQ) prompting, with shuffled-order training, order averaging or sorted options, and invariant set architectures, and find that each violates at least one axiom: one shuffle changes 12-20% of SCQ answers, sorting only freezes an arbitrary convention, and a well-chosen added option steers 4-34% of decisions. By Luce's theorem, a read satisfies both axioms only if it is a softmax over scores that each depend on one option alone, so in a transformer they hold by construction only if no token that scores an option sees another. title: Poisoning the Neighborhood: A Topology-Aware Topic-Level Attack on Large-Scale HNSW-based RAG Systems
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mitigates hallucinations and knowledge staleness in large language models using external knowledge. However, ingestion from public and third-party sources exposes RAG systems to poisoning attacks. Existing attacks are designed and evaluated under exact retrieval, where poisoned documents participate in global ranking. Deployment-scale systems instead rely on approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes such as hierarchical navigable small world (HNSW), where limited search budgets, graph-search reachability, and local benign-document competition invalidate this assumption and degrade existing attacks. We present a topology-aware topic-level poisoning attack against large-scale HNSW-RAG that generalizes to unseen topic queries. We organize poisoned documents into a Hub-Satellite structure: Satellites provide competitive entry points across semantic regions, while Hubs strengthen local cohesion and facilitate cascading retrieval. For generation, we propose an entity-claim promotion attack combining evidence anchoring and entity-claim coupling to promote the target entity via a target claim across different query regions. On 2M-document Wikipedia, our attack maintains over 72% retrieval success and reaches 31.29% attack success, substantially outperforming baselines; domain-specific experiments further support its effectiveness. Structural analyses show that the Hub-Satellite topology forms in HNSW, indicating that graph structure contributes to improved poisoned-document retrieval. Existing poisoning defenses cannot mitigate the attack, exposing graph-structural risks in HNSW-RAG systems.

title: Bayesian Nonparametric Longitudinal Factor Model for Microbiome Counts
abstract: Longitudinal microbiome studies provide important insights into the temporal evolution of microbial abundances and dynamic cross-feature dependence. Modeling longitudinal microbiome data is challenging because microbiome counts are highly heterogeneous and zero-inflated, and, moreover, repeated measurements induce within-subject temporal dependence and possibly time-varying cross-feature covariance. To address these challenges, we develop a flexible Bayesian longitudinal factor model using a rounded log-normal latent representation. The mean abundance process begins with a Dirichlet process mixture baseline, which accommodates sparse and multimodal abundance distributions, and subsequently evolves through an autoregressive process. Autoregressive coefficients differ across prespecified biological groups, which are defined by genotypes in our application. A separate autoregressive factor process captures shared cross-feature dependence. The model therefore distinguishes subject--feature mean evolution from shared dependence and yields a closed-form, time-indexed covariance. Simulation studies evaluate dynamic covariance recovery under matched and misspecified data-generating mechanisms. In the longitudinal mouse-gut microbiome application, LODI identifies highly persistent feature-specific abundance trajectories and shared latent factors that distinguish the three genotype groups over time. At week 15, the dominant factor follows the observed WT < ACK/G < HACK/G tumor-severity ordering, with its strongest contributions arising from OTUs classified within Clostridiaceae, Clostridium, and RF39.

title: Putting the Athlete in Control of their Performance Data through Privacy-Preserving Aggregators across Data Vaults
abstract: Athlete monitoring requires heterogeneous data from coaches, medical staff, psychologists, and activity-tracking devices amongst others. However, current systems are often centralized, limiting athlete data control, fine-grained access management, and data portability. This demo presents a semantic decentralized architecture in which athlete data remains in personal data vaults under athlete control. An Aggregator component is introduced that allows to efficiently compute reusable & interoperable performance metrics from raw activity data and athlete settings. Using a modified version of the performance tracking application Elevate, we show how this set-up can support privacy-preserving, application-independent computation for athlete-centric performance monitoring.

title: Enhancing Digital Governance Through AI Text Revision: A Comparative Evaluation Using Controlled Error Injection
authors: Luiza Helena Piazza da Silva e Venturini Arantes
abstract: This study presents a comparative evaluation of 36 Large Language Model (LLM) configurations for automating Plain Language revision in digital public service. We introduce a Controlled Error Injection methodology, in which an auxiliary agent deliberately corrupts well-formed texts while preserving their factual content. The models were then tasked with restoring clarity using a Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework based on 50 institutional guidelines. Performance was evaluated across semantic fidelity (BERTScore and Cosine Similarity), readability gains (Flesch Reading Ease index), and diagnostic explainability. The results reveal a Simplification Paradox, with models exhibiting conservative, aggressive, or equilibrium revision profiles. OpenAI and xAI models showed pronounced “black-box” behavior, lacking diagnostic transparency. In contrast, Mistral-based architectures achieved a superior balance, improving readability while preserving factual integrity and leading in explainability. Funding: This work received financial support from Finep through the INSPIRE project. Research manuscript associated with poster 028 at the III Workshop do BI0S.

title: Adaptive Self–Mutual Evaluation in World Models: A Unified Architecture for Switching Between Internal Assessment and Cross-Model Assessment
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental states, dynamics, causal relationships, and potential future outcomes. However, a world model's predictions and internal assessments may be unreliable when its learned dynamics are incomplete, its observations are ambiguous, its operating environment changes, or its internal errors remain undetected. Cross-model evaluation can provide complementary evidence, but continuous mutual evaluation may introduce additional computational costs, communication overhead, correlated errors, and coordination complexity. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self–Mutual Evaluation Architecture (ASMEA) for world models, designed to switch dynamically between self-evaluation and mutual evaluation according to the estimated reliability, uncertainty, disagreement, environmental novelty, potential consequences of errors, and evaluation cost. The architecture is situated at the world-model level rather than being restricted to large language models, conversational agents, or ensembles of pretrained generative models. Each world-model instance can evaluate its own predictions, state representations, transition dynamics, causal hypotheses, counterfactual outcomes, and decision-relevant simulations. When internal evidence is insufficient, unreliable, or inconsistent, the system can activate cross-model evaluation, in which distinct world-model instances assess one another's predictions and assumptions. A meta-evaluation mechanism subsequently determines whether the available evidence supports acceptance, revision, continued observation, or further evaluation. The paper formalizes the architecture as a cost-sensitive, partially observable decision process, introduces adaptive switching and disagreement-resolution mechanisms, and establishes a proposed experimental protocol for evaluating predictive accuracy, calibration, downstream decision quality, robustness, computational efficiency, and failure recovery. No empirical results are claimed. The principal contribution is a unified, testable framework for coordinating internal and cross-model assessment within world-model systems while explicitly accounting for the limitations of both evaluation modes.

title: Generalized Cyclic Codes over Product Ring PQ
abstract: This paper investigates cyclic codes over Fqn×Pm×Qk, where Fq is a finite field of odd characteristic, P=Fq[v]/⟨v2−τ2v⟩, and Q=Fq[u,v]/⟨u3−τ12u,v2−τ2v⟩, with τ1,τ2∈Fq*. Using complete systems of orthogonal idempotents, we decompose (P) and (Q) into two and six constituent codes over Fq, respectively, and define matrix-based Gray maps. The induced Gray map from Fqn×Pm×Qk to Fqn+2m+6k is shown to be Fq-linear and Lee–Hamming distance preserving. We prove that a mixed-alphabet code is cyclic if and only if its deinterleaved Gray image is a generalized quasi-cyclic code with block-length profile (n, m, m, k, k, k, k, k, k). A polynomial-module characterization, constituent generator polynomials, dimension bounds, shift-generated spanning sets, and structural results for the Euclidean dual and hull are also established. Furthermore, the generator structure and cardinality of cyclic codes over P, Q, and the mixed alphabet are determined through their field constituents. As an application, scalar-orthogonal Gray matrices and dual-containing constituent cyclic codes are combined with the Calderbank–Shor–Steane construction. An explicit construction over F5 yields a dual-containing generalized quasi-cyclic code with parameters [90, 75, 3]5, and a quantum error-correcting code with parameters [[90, 60, 3]]5.

title: The algorithmic third actor in service work
abstract: Service research has tended to treat algorithmic management as a single phenomenon, yet the systems standing between service firms and their frontline staff differ in ways that matter for how work is experienced and for the quality of service delivered. This conceptual paper proposes three system properties for distinguishing among them: decision autonomy, whether the decision rule was specified by people or learned from data; outcome consequentiality, the degree to which outputs translate into material outcomes without further human deliberation; and learning adaptivity, whether the rule is revised after deployment. Combined, these generate a typology of eight system types, from minimally agentic tools to continuously learning autonomous partners. Because the three properties are not service-specific, the framework introduces encounter exposure as a moderating condition: the extent to which the managed function bears on work performed in real time, in the customer’s presence, under customer-induced variability. Seven propositions connect configurations to frontline discretion, service recovery capability, customer evaluations, employee trust and strain, and firm governance. Two are ordinal or conditional rather than directional: that consequentiality constrains discretion more than autonomy does, and that adaptivity becomes costly only at high consequentiality.

title: TokenEconomizer: Experience-Driven Black-Box Cost Control for Coding Agents
abstract: Advances in frontier coding agents have sharply increased the token costs of AI-assisted software engineering. Their token efficiency is typically evaluated on isolated tasks, whereas real-world developers use them to continuously build, update, and maintain large-scale projects. This mismatch motivates us to evaluate agents over sequences of realistic coding tasks, where we find that agents exhibit recurring environment-dependent token costs that existing methods struggle to reduce. To minimize these costs, we introduce TokenEconomizer, an external controller that cuts environment-specific token costs over a sequence of tasks. These cuts come from determining (i) which operational micro-skills to inject, (ii) which persistently irrelevant tools to prune, and (iii) when to intervene in unproductive failure loops. Across Claude Code, Codex, and GitHub Copilot CLI paired with frontier models, TokenEconomizer reduces the average token cost by 18.4-30.9% with comparable task success. Savings hold in every repository under every tested agent-model setting and generalize to diverse domains such as sequential web development and security auditing, where costs fall by 6.4-21.2% depending on task structure. Our work establishes adaptive black-box cost control as a promising direction for reducing token costs of coding agents in realistic settings.

title: Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning for Path-Safe Target Reaching in Robotic Harvesting of Hydroponic Lettuce
abstract: Robotic harvesting requires precise manipulation to ensure accurate positioning of the end-effector, especially in a constraint workspace. This study introduces the Path-Safe Approach Proximal Policy Optimization (PSA-PPO), a target-conditioned local reaching framework designed for robotic harvesting of nutrient film technique (NFT)-hydroponic lettuce in greenhouses. The proposed PSA-PPO preserves the standard clipped PPO objective while introducing a harvesting-oriented policy formulation that integrates target-conditioned observations, corridor-aware spatial constraints, trajectory-history-based safety encoding, and task-specific success criteria for constrained robotic manipulation. PSAPPO was trained entirely in Isaac Lab and successfully transferred to a physical UR10e robotic arm without any real-world policy fine-tuning. In a controlled physical benchmark against 150 scheduled targets, PSA-PPO achieved the highest reaching rate of 94.7%, outperforming Cartesian+TOTG (86.0%), RRTConnect (88.0%), and RRT* (80.0%), while reducing median RMS jerk by 39.8 to 73.0% relative to the classical planners during the final approach segment. A formulation ablation evaluated over 200 simulation targets demonstrates that path-safety and side-corridor shaping are the principal drivers of harvesting-compatible performance: removing either term substantially degrades strict success even when terminal endpoint accuracy is preserved or improved, confirming that optimization toward the endpoint alone is an insufficient objective for constrained crop-proximal manipulation. Finally, PSA-PPO was integrated with an RGB-D vision module and an end-effector and evaluated as a complete greenhouse harvesting system across 144 lettuce harvesting attempts, achieving 94.4% vision-guided target reaching and 86.1% complete harvesting success.

title: ABNAT: Attention-Based Noise-Aware Training for Robust Transformers on Analog Compute-in-Memory Systems
abstract: Transformer-based models have become the backbone of a wide range of tasks, but their intensive computation and data movement incur substantial energy overhead. Analog compute-in-memory (CIM) offers an energy-efficient alternative, yet its inherent hardware non-idealities perturb stored weights and can significantly degrade model performance. Although existing noise-aware training (NAT) methods improve robustness by injecting noise during training, they largely overlook the critical role of attention mechanisms in Transformer inference.To bridge this gap, we analyze how CIM-induced noise reshapes attention in Transformers and identify two key observations: (1) the divergence between clean and noisy attention maps increases substantially in deeper layers, and (2) conventional NAT can remain overconfident even when its attention routes deviate markedly from the clean reference. Motivated by these findings, we propose ABNAT, an attention-based noise-aware training framework that teaches the noisy student to preserve the clean teacher's headwise attention routes rather than merely reproduce answers, without hardware changes or inference overhead; selective variants further reduce training cost.Extensive experiments across vision, language, and multimodal Transformers show that ABNAT consistently improves robustness over corresponding NAT baselines, improving noise-degraded accuracy by up to 11.28% and reducing attention deviation by up to 85.77%.

title: In-Context Preference-Conditioned Pareto Set Learning from Limited Offline Data
abstract: Multi-objective optimization involves diverse preferences over conflicting objectives. Rather than returning a finite set of trade-off solutions, preference-conditioned Pareto set learning seeks to map a specified preference directly to a corresponding Pareto optimal solution. Yet in many real-world scenarios, optimization must proceed offline without further objective evaluations, leaving only a limited static dataset that sparsely covers the decision and objective spaces. Existing methods either optimize separately for each preference or train a problem-specific Pareto solution model, requiring repeated search across preferences or repeated training across problems. We introduce in-context preference-conditioned Pareto set learning (ICPSL), a framework that amortizes both preference-wise solution search and problem-specific model construction. ICPSL pretrains a foundation-style hypernetwork on a large and diverse set of synthetic prior data. Given the offline observations of an unseen problem, the pretrained hypernetwork learns to generate a problem-specific, preference-conditioned Pareto solution model in a single forward pass. The generated model can then be reused to predict solutions for arbitrary preferences without problem-specific training or preference-wise search. Experiments on synthetic and real-world problems show that ICPSL produces high-quality Pareto solutions while providing substantial speedups in problem-specific solution-model construction.

title: Empirical Study Towards RBAMR-News: a Rule-Based AMR Parser for News in Portuguese
abstract: This work evaluates AMR graph construction rules, originally developed for literary texts, in Portuguese news data to support building a symbolic AMR parser for this genre. Using the AMRNews-PT gold-standard corpus, we conduct an ablation analysis to assess rule contributions to AMR representation quality. The results reveal a hierarchical organization in which a small set of core structural rules drives most parsing performance, while additional rules provide finer semantic refinements. This rule hierarchy serves as the basis for building the parser and enabling the annotation of a larger news corpus.

title: Reproducibility package for "Certified entanglement advantage in two-use coherence-channel discrimination"
abstract: This record provides the reproducibility package accompanying the manuscript “Certified entanglement advantage in two-use coherence-channel discrimination” by Matthias Jakob. The study investigates a binary quantum-channel discrimination task involving two parallel signal uses, four prepared qubit probes, correlated Gaussian dephasing within each signal–reference pair, an unobserved Gaussian phase offset shared by both signal uses, and flagged photon losses. The reference class includes every fully separable four-qubit parallel input, hypothesis-independent classical preparation labels, and arbitrary joint output measurements. A specified noisy pairwise Bell preparation with a fixed local receiver is compared against globally bounded performance of this reference class, with all loss events retained. The archive contains executable Python source code, generated numerical certificates, result tables, complete input-grid execution records, validation scripts, and figure-generation material. It includes the central two-use discrimination certificate, uniform robustness certificates for continuous parameter ranges, and a separately implemented verification of the covariance-based channel construction and loss-sector calculations. Documentation describes the analytical interpolation bounds, numerical error allowances, software dependencies, execution commands, and scope of each result. Provenance records and SHA-256 checksums support traceability and file-integrity verification. Release 1.0.0 preserves the numerical programs and results of the reviewed P2 version 1.1 and organizes them as the reproducibility material for the manuscript prepared for Quantum Information Processing. This packaging release does not introduce new scientific results or additional full-grid calculations. The archive is also prepared as the manuscript’s supplementary Online Resource 1 (ESM_1.zip). All numerical data are theoretical model calculations, not experimental observations. Truncated Gauss sums supply a structured pair of known coherence coefficients; no faster integer-factorization algorithm is claimed. The certified comparison concerns the specified fully separable parallel input class and does not establish an advantage over input-adaptive protocols or a fidelity-only guarantee for arbitrary multi-use preparation errors. The common phase is treated using a characterized Gaussian prior. Separate verification implementations are internal reproducibility checks, not external peer review. The included README provides instructions for reproducing the calculations in a separate working directory. This repository deposit does not imply journal submission, acceptance, or publication.

title: Agentic Institutions: Mandates, Capabilities, Constraints, and Escalation for Machine Economic Actors
abstract: Delegated cognition, one persistent model dispatching drafting to others, is becoming common in agent systems, yet the institutions governing it remain ad hoc. This paper contributes a conditional cost model for delegation, an accounting of context admission, and an instrumented self-study of one institution with its incident record. It does not establish a general institutional design. For free workers the model says delegation wins whenever the single-attempt acceptance probability exceeds a threshold set by the cost of a failed attempt, about 0.02 at one wave's artifact size under unbounded retry (0.09 at a retry cap of three), under a proviso that the dispatcher return little of the draft to the hub. For paid workers the condition is the rent-or-buy breakeven with a horizon, stated under a persistence assumption the paper's own hub violates. Per unit of context budget, delegation admits up to 1/α artifacts per inline artifact, approached only as the brief and print-back terms vanish. A pre-registered wave with admission logged on both arms found α at 0.165 pooled against the attested 0.137 and acceptance 6 of 6 under a reading of the acceptance rule fixed after the drafts were read (1 of 6 under the rule as written), and found the dispatcher returning each whole draft to the hub, so the measured multiplier was 0.57 against a predicted 2.0 to 3.7 and the corollary's own proviso failed: the saving the paper prices exists only when the whole draft does not persist in hub context. The record, including a worker that wrote outside its brief, a fabricated example that passed six review passes, and five hub-side incidents, is public with its instrument, data and reviewer reports. No single check was sufficient, and what held was a reproducible record and independent recomputation from it.Companion repository (instrument, data, incident log, reviewer reports, pre-registered wave): https://github.com/nKOxxx/agentic-institutions, tag v1.10. v1.10 corrects eleven sentences of v1.9.2 that the repository's own files contradicted (REVISION_LOG v1.10, INCIDENT_LOG addenda of 17 October 2026) and adds a table of every checker; no computed number changed.
