title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): An Adaptive Framework for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering Copy title
abstract: This paper presents a proposed Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded question answering using large language models (LLMs). Unlike conventional single-pass RAG systems, the proposed framework incorporates query planning, retrieval, tool selection, evidence evaluation, answer generation, and self-reflection. The framework uses a bounded feedback loop to improve evidence retrieval when the initial results are insufficient or conflicting. It aims to produce answers supported by relevant source citations while communicating uncertainty when reliable evidence is unavailable. The paper discusses the system architecture, workflow, algorithmic control logic, evaluation methodology, security, privacy, and governance considerations. It also proposes evaluation metrics for answer quality, retrieval effectiveness, factual grounding, latency, computational cost, and component-level ablation studies. Potential applications include research assistance, document question answering, enterprise knowledge management, customer support, and data analysis. This work presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation plan. Implementation, benchmark experiments, and measured performance improvements are not reported. Keywords: Agentic RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, Adaptive Retrieval, Self-Reflection.

title: Machine Learning for Clause Selection in First-Order Automated Theorem Proving
abstract: This project investigates the use of machine learning to guide clause selection in first-order automated theorem proving, with the aim of improving proof-search efficiency within the iProver theorem prover.An end-to-end machine learning pipeline was developed in Python to collect proof-search data, extract lightweight syntactic features, train models and integrate learned clause-selection strategies with iProver. Both pointwise classification and pairwise ranking approaches were investigated using logistic regression and multilayer perceptron (MLP) models.The approaches were evaluated on a benchmark of 1,701 problems derived from the TPTP library. Results showed that learned clause selection could substantially reduce search effort on successfully solved problems, although the learned strategies solved fewer problems overall than iProver's default heuristic. The project highlights both the potential and limitations of supervised machine learning for guiding automated proof search.

title: AuditTune campaign evidence: experiment ledger, agent-written planner code, and figure-generation scripts for auditable policy adjustment in reinforcement learning control
abstract: Evidence package for the manuscript "An Auditable Learning-Curve-Driven Automatic Policy Adjustment Framework for Engineering Reinforcement Learning Control Systems" (EAAI submission). The dataset contains the complete experiment ledger, the planner source code written by the diagnosis-driven agent, and the scripts that generate every figure in the paper. It supports three groups of reported results: 1. Radar primary domain (FluxPhased S7, a 2v2 radar-jammer adversarial system trained with MAPPO against frozen jammer pools, pool seeds 20260801-20260803): per-candidate resolved recipes, training metrics, canonical head-to-head evaluations, arm-level reports, and the literature cache holding both the diagnosis-matched and the diagnosis-irrelevant (shuffled-control) abstracts used by the content-ablation experiment. The ledger covers the random-search, BOHB, static-prompt, dynamic-retrieval, retrieval-shuffled, wide-box, and reflectively evolved-prompt arms, including the revision and completion rounds behind the retrained-winner comparison. 2. Code-as-Policy TD-MPC on 16 dm_control domains (four arms, three candidates each, seed 1301): all 192 planner sources (default CEM, diagnosis-driven agent, random parameter mutations, and diagnosis-free LLM generation), per-domain results, and the episode-level learning curves behind the learning-curve figure. 3. Seventeen-domain PPO generalization: agent-driven recipe loops and fixed-recipe baselines on 16 dm_control tasks, plus the HalfCheetah three-arm comparison. Model checkpoints (.pt) are intentionally excluded to keep the package light; every reported number can be regenerated from the recorded recipes, seeds, and metrics. Experimental environment: a single NVIDIA RTX 2060 (6 GB) at 7.72 s/iteration over 16 parallel environments; local Qwen3.5-4B language model (Ollama tag qwen35-4b-64k-full, Q4_K_M quantization). title: The LLM-Attacker: A Unified Red-Team Framework for Privacy Evaluation of Split and Distributed LLM Systems
abstract: Split language models keep input text on a client but send intermediate representations to a server. Attacks can reconstruct text from these messages. Comparing privacy evaluations is difficult when attackers see different messages, know different model weights or use different datasets and recovery measures. We present LLM-Attacker, a framework that records these choices and lets researchers check, compare and extend an evaluation. Compatible attacks reuse recorded messages, and their predictions are saved for independent scoring. The scoring rule requires a linked undefended reference before a defence can pass. Reports also identify attacks that remain untested. In a controlled GPT-2 experiment, adding gradients returned during training increased token recovery from 94.20% to 97.38% and exact-document recovery from 13.71% to 37.77%. The 95% interval for the token gain lay above the two-percentage-point threshold fixed before testing. This experiment is shared with a companion study; here, it tests how the evaluation responds to a change in attacker access. Further studies measure how corpus choice and compression defences affect recovery, compare an adapted published attack with its reference implementation, and test the measurement code. The framework reports implementation checks separately from measured attack effectiveness. Each privacy claim should state the attacker, dataset and scoring rule, report its controls and identify untested attacks.

title: Documenting Trofinetide Treatment Phenotypes in Rett Syndrome with a Dual-LLM Consensus Pipeline
abstract: Objective: Trofinetide, approved in 2023 as the first Rett syndrome treatment, lacks scalable real-world monitoring because chart review is labor-intensive. We developed a dual large language model (LLM) consensus pipeline to extract 18 treatment-response phenotypes, comprising 4 adverse effects, 13 Rett clinical features, and medication refusal, from clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We analyzed 26,763 notes from 108 patients with confirmed sustained trofinetide exposure at Texas Children's Hospital. The pipeline filters notes by keyword, classifies each through two LLMs requiring consensus, and aggregates a patient-by-timepoint matrix. Architecture and prompt were selected on a diarrhea development set, then frozen and applied to the other 17 phenotypes with the phenotype definition substituted, as an out-of-sample test. The reported prompt comparison scores 183 expert-labeled cells. Results: A prompt requiring diarrhea to be active and severe performed best (84.2 $\pm$ 0.0% accuracy; F1 = 0.674), 47 percentage points above regular-expression matching ($p < 0.0001$). Expert reviewers judged six of the pipeline's calls per phenotype, three positive and three negative, and agreed with 90.2% (92/102). The 13 Rett clinical features are manifestations of the disorder itself rather than adverse effects of trofinetide. Gross and fine motor impairment, language/communication, and stereotypy were documented present in 92-100% of patients at every visit. Discussion: In-context LLM extraction captured multi-domain treatment responses. The outcome is documented presence at each visit, not a direction-of-change judgment. Conclusion: Coupling in-context LLM reasoning with a consensus architecture offers a scalable alternative to keyword and regular-expression extraction for real-world evidence, adapting to new phenotypes and medications through configuration alone.

title: Retrieved but Not Read: Understanding Why Search-Augmented LLMs Fail to Use Available Evidence
abstract: Web search allows LLMs to access up-to-date information, but it remains unclear why they sometimes produce outdated answers even when relevant evidence is available. To study this problem, we construct temporal facts whose values changed after the models' training cutoffs. We evaluate one proprietary model under deployed web search and six open-weight model configurations under controlled retrieval. We find that models often answer from search snippets without opening the source pages, which is associated with higher rates of outdated answers and unfaithful citations. Our controlled experiments and layer-wise analysis reveal a gap between the availability of evidence and its effective use. Even when retrieved evidence influences internal predictions, models may still favour outdated information in their final answers. We hope these findings will help advance research on the reliable use of retrieved evidence in search-augmented LLMs.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of Embedding Models for Retrieval and Clustering of Brazilian Legislative Amendments
abstract: The large volume of amendments submitted in the Brazilian legislative process makes semantic analysis and consolidation labor-intensive. We present a comparative evaluation of 14 distinct base representation models, including BM25L and embedding models spanning open-source multilingual, proprietary, Portuguese-adapted, and legislative-specialized architectures, for retrieving and clustering legislative amendments. Across three corpora totaling 2,462 documents, we assess retrieval, clustering, text segmentation, and thematic granularity. Results show that large-scale open-source multilingual models constitute the best-performing group overall, with Octen-Embedding-8B exhibiting the most consistent performance. gemini-embedding-2 is highly competitive in sentence-similarity mode, while preprocessed BM25L remains a strong baseline, outperforming specialized encoders. Finally, removing structural metadata improves performance, whereas removing justifications degrades global structure; thematic aggregation improves local accuracy at the expense of global consistency.

title: TDOA_tracking_master: Multi-target tracking of time-differences-of-arrival
abstract: Stable release of TDOA_tracking_master, a MATLAB package for multi-target tracking of time-differences-of-arrival (TDOAs) of acoustic signals between two sensors. It was developed and tested for towed hydrophone arrays and can also be used with stationary arrays. This release consolidates the fixes from the v1.0.x alpha pre-releases. The package computes generalized cross-correlograms from multichannel .wav recordings, extracts TDOA measurements, and links them into continuous trajectories using a Gaussian mixture probability hypothesis density filter (GM-PHD-SA). The filter handles multiple simultaneous sources, clutter and missed detections. Features Processes clicks, whistles, or both Pre-processing (de-clicking), GCC-based cross-correlograms and background normalization GM-PHD tracking with data-trained, optimized filter parameters and birth priors Post-processing to remove short tracks and smooth trajectories Supports multiple array configurations and towed or stationary arrays Test example included Output is used directly by the companion package Localization_Towed_Array for localizing sources Requirements: MATLAB 2022a (9.12); Signal Processing Toolbox and Statistics and Machine Learning Toolbox. License: BSD-3-Clause-Clear Please cite: Gruden, P., Nosal, E.M., and Oleson, E.M. (2021). Tracking time differences of arrivals of multiple sound sources in the presence of clutter and missed detections. JASA 150(5): 3399–3416.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Selection and Collaborative Selection in Multi-Agent Systems: A Unified Decision-Making Framework
abstract: Multi-agent systems must repeatedly select actions, solutions, resources, partners, strategies, or organizational configurations while operating under uncertainty and limited computational resources. Existing approaches often emphasize individual decision-making, collaborative decision-making, or predefined coordination policies. However, neither independent selection nor collaborative selection is universally optimal across all task conditions. Independent selection can reduce communication overhead and preserve agent autonomy, whereas collaborative selection can exploit distributed knowledge, complementary capabilities, and collective evaluation. Excessive reliance on either mode may lead to inefficient decisions, unnecessary communication, redundant computation, or insufficient information integration. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-Selection and Collaborative Selection (ASCCS) framework for multi-agent systems. The central idea is to allow a system to switch dynamically between self-selection and collaborative selection according to task uncertainty, decision confidence, estimated disagreement, expected collaboration benefit, communication cost, computational budget, and historical outcomes. Unlike a fixed policy that always selects independently or collaboratively, the proposed framework treats selection mode as a decision variable that can be optimized during system operation. A hybrid mode is also introduced for cases in which independent candidates are generated first and collaborative selection is activated only when additional evaluation is expected to improve the decision. title: Ministry of Justice Synthetic Data First Datasets
abstract: The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) Synthetic Data First Datasets provide artificially generated datasets designed to replicate the structure, relationships, and statistical characteristics of real administrative and justice system data while minimising disclosure risks and protecting individual privacy. These datasets enable users to explore data structures, develop analytical methods, test code, and undertake training activities without requiring access to sensitive personal information. The datasets are created using synthetic data generation techniques that preserve key patterns and distributions found in the original data, supporting realistic analytical and research environments. Coverage may include information relating to courts, tribunals, offenders, victims, prisons, probation services, and other areas of the justice system, depending on the specific dataset made available. By providing accessible, privacy-preserving alternatives to operational data, the Synthetic Data First initiative supports innovation, reproducible research, skills development, and collaboration across government, academia, and the wider research community. These datasets help users prepare for accredited access to secure data environments, improve analytical workflows, and accelerate the development of evidence-based insights while maintaining robust standards of data confidentiality and security.

title: Enhancing Question Representation for Knowledge Tracing via Adaptive Concept Relation Discovery and Structural–Semantic Co-Optimization
abstract: Knowledge tracing (KT) models the evolution of students’ knowledge states from historical learning interactions, serving as a fundamental mechanism for intelligent educational systems. The efficacy of KT models heavily relies on the quality of question representations. However, existing methods incorporating concept relations generally face two critical limitations: First, static relation graphs fail to capture dynamic cognitive trajectories, while shallow statistical approaches are highly vulnerable to sparse data and interaction noise. Second, the current models lack fine-grained semantic characterization, specifically failing to integrate concept difficulty to accurately evaluate the cognitive load of individual questions. To address these issues, we propose SSCKT, a novel framework that adaptively extracts latent concept relations and introduces concept associations to enhance question representation via structural–semantic co-optimization. Specifically, a concept relation discovery and aggregation module dynamically learns a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of concept relations from historical learning interactions, which is encoded via heterogeneous graph convolutions to yield structure-enhanced embeddings. Concurrently, a concept difficulty-guided semantic enhancement module utilizes multi-head attention to capture intrinsic question–concept dependencies. This module employs a topological concept difficulty metric as a scaling factor to adjust the question offset vector, enabling cognitive load-aware modeling. Finally, a contrastive learning mechanism aligns the structural and semantic representations to eliminate feature redundancy, generating highly discriminative question embeddings. Extensive experiments on five public datasets demonstrate that, relative to the strongest baseline on each dataset, SSCKT improves average ACC and AUC by 1.20% and 1.33%, respectively, validating the superiority of the proposed co-optimization architecture.

title: A blockchain-enhanced CNN architecture for robust anomaly detection in industrial and IoT cyber-physical systems
abstract: Cyber–physical and network attacks are becoming commonplace in Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments, with the potential to disrupt operations, compromise safety, and potentially impact the reliability of security evidence. In this study, a modified CNN (mCNN) framework is proposed to detect anomalies with robust, auditable capabilities by incorporating blockchain technology. The detector is based on the following building blocks: dilated convolutions to capture temporal dependencies in industrial process data, multi-branch feature extraction, dataset-adaptive input structuring, and a compact classifier to model heterogeneous patterns in IoT traffic. Anomalies detected are turned into signed and hashed event records and sent to a permissioned Hyperledger Fabric workflow. They test the framework on SWaT and N-BaIoT and validate their results with three baselines: Isolation Forest, autoencoder, and LSTM, and compare them with accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC. The proposed CNN is designed under the adopted protocol, and the F1-scores obtained on SWaT and N-BaIoT are 0.977 and 0.951, respectively. An incremental ablation study quantifies the contributions of dilation, multi-branch fusion, windowing, and structured input representation. The findings advocate for the use of customized CNN models for anomaly detection in heterogeneous IIoT applications, and blockchain stress testing, adversarial robustness, constrained-device profiling, and model-specific explainability are key aspects that need to be assessed in the future.

title: CoLU: Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning for Large Language Models
abstract: Large language model (LLM) unlearning aims to forget certain information while preserving others, without retraining from scratch. SoTA methods such as NPO, SimNPO, and SatImp balance forgetting and retain through whole model fine-tuning, while FOM-UL explores selective layer updates. Prior works show that suppressing target information can damage retained knowledge. This trade-off can vary across layers even under the same unlearning loss. In this work, we propose Confidence-Weighted Layerwise Unlearning (CoLU), which combines a novel confidence-weighted forgetting and retain regularization while updating a single selected transformer layer, rather than the whole model for unlearning. To reduce CoLU compute cost, we further propose Brief Layer Screening (BLS), which uses a newly defined normalized forgetting-retention (NFR) score to first rank layers through a brief unlearning trials using a subset of forgetting dataset and fewer epochs. BLS pre-selects top-k ranked layer candidates, which will then be fully profiled using full data analysis. BLS is proven to reduce the runtime of CoLU by 60.2-79.7% with almost the same performance. On TOFU dataset, CoLU improves both forgetting and retention over NPO, SatImp, and GA-based FOM-UL in all six TOFU settings, and over SimNPO in five of the six settings. On MUSE Books and News datasets, CoLU achieves the highest retained KnowMem and the PrivLeak closest to zero among the compared SOTA unlearning methods. CoLU presents a new record performance in both unlearning and retain in most settings up to date. Moreover, across the measured settings, average CoLU GPU memory usage is 77.4% to 79.5% lower than full-model unlearning.

title: FAOPs: Normal Forms and an Algebra for AI Agent Workflows
abstract: Organizations increasingly encode operational procedures as multi-step agent skills, here called Agent Operating Procedures (AOPs), that must be traceable, auditable, reproducible, access-controlled, and bounded in time and cost, requirements that regulated sectors make mandatory. Yet AOPs are typically kept as coarse-grained files, in which steps bundle actions, copied procedures drift apart, any step may reach any tool, and refactoring goes unchecked. We present Functional Agent Operating Procedures (FAOP), a formal theory that brings database-grade discipline to AI agent workflows. FAOP recasts each workflow as a typed function over scoped state and subjects an entire library to four progressive normal forms: Decomposed (FNF-1) splits a workflow into atomic steps, Typed (FNF-2) makes its data flow explicit and type-checked, Factored (FNF-3) gives each shared procedure a single canonical definition so a change propagates instead of drifting, and Scoped (FNF-4) confines every step to least-privilege tool access. Once normalized, every atomic step is a separate entity with a declared contract and can be type-checked, scope-confined, bounded, tested, traced, and audited on its own. A FAOP algebra of provably sound equalities turns refactoring and parallelization into compiler rewrites; orthogonal extensions add verified termination (+V), optimization (+O), and time and cost bounds (+B); and an architectural-level classifier (0-3) determines whether a workflow needs AI at all. Together, these make integrity, isolation, typing, termination, cost, and optimization compile-time concerns across the whole library, not runtime hopes. We implement the theory in SkillBase, an AOP management system (what PostgreSQL is to data, SkillBase is to AOPs), together with a separate executor that enforces these guarantees at run time. A worked financial workflow illustrates the approach end to end.

title: One generation of the Standard Model as a quantum error-correcting code
abstract: Together with a right-handed neutrino, the fermions of one generation of the Standard Model are labelled by five bits, a combinatorial structure tied to anomaly cancellation. We make this precise. Anomaly cancellation is the vanishing of a cubic form, the defining property of triorthogonal codes, the quantum error-correcting codes behind magic state distillation. Removing the right-handed neutrino gives a $[[15,1,3]]_p$ code for every prime $p$, including the Bravyi-Kitaev code for $p = 2$. For qutrits it is the unique shortest distance-three triorthogonal code.

title: Code and aggregated results for: Causal Validation of Knowledge-Tracing Models with Naturally Randomized Item Exposure in Game-Based Learning
abstract: Analysis code (Python) and aggregated results for the article 'Causal Validation of Knowledge-Tracing Models with Naturally Randomized Item Exposure in Game-Based Learning' (Machine Learning and Knowledge Extraction, submitted). The study uses a natural experiment in the logs of a game-based quiz platform to estimate the causal effect of a previous encounter with an item and its decay over time, and compares the effects implied by fourteen knowledge-tracing models with this reference. The response data are not included because they contain personal information of platform users; the repository contains all scripts and only aggregated outputs (effect estimates, covariance matrices, model-implied curves, metrics and bootstrap summaries) without learner, game or item identifiers.

title: Adaptive Independent–Collaborative Reasoning in Multi-Agent Systems: A State-Driven Framework for Dynamic Switching Between Individual Reasoning and Collective Inference
abstract: Multi-agent reasoning systems can benefit from the complementary capabilities of multiple agents, but continuous collaboration may introduce communication overhead, redundant computation, correlated errors, and coordination delays. Conversely, purely individual reasoning can limit access to complementary knowledge and prevent the detection of errors that become apparent only through independent perspectives. These competing considerations motivate a fundamental research question: can a multi-agent system dynamically switch between individual adaptive reasoning and collaborative reasoning according to its evolving internal state? This paper proposes Adaptive Independent–Collaborative Reasoning (AICR), a state-driven framework that treats reasoning-mode selection as a sequential decision problem rather than a fixed architectural choice. Under AICR, an agent or a collection of agents can reason independently, request collaborative analysis, evaluate the resulting information, and return to independent reasoning when further interaction is unlikely to justify its cost. The framework integrates uncertainty estimation, progress monitoring, evidence sufficiency, disagreement measurement, expected collaboration gain, and resource consumption into a common decision mechanism. Unlike a permanently independent or permanently collaborative configuration, AICR permits repeated transitions between reasoning modes throughout problem solving. The paper formalizes the reasoning environment, defines a switching policy, introduces a cost-sensitive objective, and presents a reference algorithm with explicit transition and termination conditions. It also develops a reproducible evaluation protocol for examining solution quality, computational efficiency, switching behavior, robustness, and the risks of correlated errors. The framework is intended to be applicable to heterogeneous software agents, distributed reasoning systems, robotic teams, and other multi-agent architectures, without requiring that the agents be large language models. Existing research on multi-agent routing and adaptive collaboration establishes substantial overlap with the general motivation. Accordingly, the contribution claimed here is a unified formulation of repeated, state-dependent switching between independent adaptive reasoning and collective inference, whose effectiveness and distinctiveness must be established through comparative experiments.

title: A Systematic Review of Hallucination Mitigation in Large Language Models Using Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have become widely used for question answering, education, research, summarization and information support. Despite their usefulness, LLMs may generate false, unsupported or inconsistent information, commonly described as hallucination. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) addresses this reliability problem by retrieving relevant information from external knowledge sources and supplying it to the language model as contextual evidence before generating a response. This paper studies the role of RAG in reducing factual hallucinations through a review of existing research and a 50 question pilot comparison of responses generated with and without retrieval support. The submitted report records 49 of 50 responses as correct without RAG and all 50 as correct with RAG; it separately presents a clearly labelled illustrative distribution of 46/3/1 versus 48/2/0 for demonstrating response categories. The distinction is retained to avoid presenting illustrative values as observed experimental results. The study also examines limitations including poor retrieval, unreliable sources, incomplete context and incorrect interpretation of retrieved evidence. The paper concludes that RAG is a practical hallucination-reduction approach, but it should be combined with high-quality retrieval, evidence verification and human oversight for critical applications.

title: Four Pre-registered Tests of Emergent Second-Order Modulation in a Minimal Plasticity Testbed: Negative Results and a Failed Learner Control
abstract: The testbed note validated audit statistics against planted second-order modulation, in which a relation’s strength multiplicatively modulates the plasticity of another relation. The conjecture’s own question is whether such modulation can emerge without being planted. This note reports four pre-registered experiments (E1–E4, 60 confirmation systems each, new environments every time) in which a modulation matrix M is learned by an online analytic meta-gradient. E1: learned M grew but equally in a time-shuffled-credit control; adaptation loss was worse than with M = 0 in 60/60 systems while overall loss was better, and a uniform gain reproduced most of that benefit. E2 (optimal gain differs between regimes): learned M beat the best uniform gain in 17/60 systems and produced no gain contrast. E3 (positive control with an explicit context relation): the same learner again produced no gain contrast, so E1–E2 cannot be read as evidence about emergence in either direction. E4 (block-averaged Adam learner, the last pre-committed revision): the control gate failed more severely and the planned second stage was not run. In this engine, under these learners, no useful context-dependent modulation was obtained from internal relation states or even from an explicit context. Design lessons: a time-shuffled-credit control is not a null; an adaptive optimiser can amplify gradient noise into dense harmful structure; a positive control for the learner must precede any emergence claim. Unpublished draft, not peer reviewed; synthetic systems only; it neither supports nor refutes the conjecture. Companion to doi:10.5281/zenodo.23373288, doi:10.5281/zenodo.23006539 and doi:10.5281/zenodo.23192515. The bundle reproduces every quoted number with verify_paper4.py (45 checks). AI use: simulations were written and executed by an AI coding model under written specifications and audited by a second AI system; the author is responsible for all content.

title: Counts, not Weights: The first stage of LOCUS: filing novels with no neural network
abstract: A reader that returns to a novel after a week away can usually recover, within a page, where it was andwho each character is. That recovery precedes any understanding of the book, and this note askswhether it can be achieved without a neural network. LOCUS is a symbolic system that learns only bycounting, from raw text, with no word lists and no labels. Given a novel, it writes its own notebook of thebook at 13% of the book’s size. On 70 novels it had not seen, the notebook names a masked character asaccurately as the full text does (0.332 against 0.322) and more accurately than raw sentences occupyingthe same space (0.265), and writing it takes a quarter of a second on one processor core. title: An Enhanced Crayfish Optimization Algorithm Inspired by Cross-Media Performing Arts Strategies for Global Optimization and Real-World Engineering Applications
abstract: Microgrid scheduling is a nonlinear, multimodal, and highly constrained optimization problem that requires effective coordination among renewable generation, controllable distributed generators, energy storage, and grid interaction. To improve the search capability of the original Crayfish Optimization Algorithm (COA), this study proposes an Enhanced Crayfish Optimization Algorithm (ECOA) inspired by the coordination characteristics of cross-media performing arts. Rather than simply combining independent operators, ECOA constructs a state-aware and behavior-specific adaptive search framework around the intrinsic behavioral structure of COA. Specifically, a rhythm-guided adaptive search strategy is embedded into the summer-resort behavior to dynamically regulate search intensity, a multi-role collaborative guidance strategy reconstructs the competition behavior through time-varying information interaction, and a stagnation-aware stage-transition perturbation strategy selectively reactivates exploration when the search becomes stagnant. Extensive experiments are conducted on the CEC2014, CEC2017, and CEC2022 benchmark suites under six-dimensional settings, and the results are compared with those of nine representative metaheuristic algorithms. The results show that ECOA achieves highly competitive convergence accuracy and run-to-run stability on most benchmark functions. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests and Cliff’s delta effect-size analysis indicate that many of the observed improvements are statistically significant and practically meaningful, while the Friedman test ranks ECOA first in all six benchmark settings. Ablation experiments further demonstrate that all three mechanisms contribute positively to performance and that their coordinated integration is more effective than any individual strategy. Parameter-sensitivity analysis shows that ECOA maintains effective convergence over a relatively broad range of the disturbance coefficient λ, with λ = 0.5 providing a balanced setting across different landscapes. Finally, ECOA is applied to a deterministic day-ahead microgrid scheduling problem with explicit feasibility repair and power-balance penalty handling. Under the considered operating scenario, ECOA achieves the lowest mean operating cost of 1361.8028 among all compared algorithms and produces coordinated power-allocation schedules satisfying the modeled operational constraints. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of ECOA for complex numerical optimization and constrained engineering scheduling problems.

title: First Passage Attention
abstract: Augmenting softmax attention with forget gates typically relies on summing decay contributions along the key--query path. Because such accumulation is monotonic, these mechanisms cannot selectively erase intermediate context while preserving older, structurally relevant tokens. We propose First Passage Attention (FPA), which shifts from path summation to path extrema by lowering a key's logit proportionally to the deepest dip of a learned scalar field below that key's level over the intervening span. FPA encompasses the Forgetting Transformer (FoX) as a special case, and when the field and levels follow a shared learned walk, the alive keys with unpenalised logits naturally form a stack. We show that a constant-dimension FPA head realises any subset of keys left alive by subsequent dips, whereas softmax heads with positional biases or token-level forget gates require a head dimension linear in the number of keys. In synthetic experiments, one-layer FPA heads converge to these target sets while comparable softmax and FoX baselines fail on every seed. Scaling to a 110M-parameter language model, FPA matches FoX in perplexity and uniquely achieves perfect passkey retrieval at 8times the training length, even with its key--value cache compressed to about 25%.

title: My Credentials, Please: Detecting Filesystem Capability Laundering in MCP Servers at Scale
abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI agents invoke external tools. MCP servers expose tools through a declared contract consisting of a name, description, and argument schema. In typical local deployments, client-side approval of a tool call grants the underlying server process broad host filesystem permissions rather than restricting it to the declared operation. We study the resulting vulnerability class, filesystem capability laundering, where attacker-steered arguments cause a tool to access sensitive host files outside its declared contract and deployment scope. We analyze this capability gap across three layers: server-category screening (L1), per-tool contract analysis (L2), and bypassable path-validation checks (L3). We design MCP-FSD to catalog MCP servers, infer least-privilege boundaries per tool, plant credential fixtures outside those boundaries, and evaluate exploitability and sandbox containment via paired dynamic execution. Across 21,097 MCP servers from nine registries, 787 of 4,806 triaged servers (16.4%) exhibit filesystem capabilities despite non-filesystem functional classifications. Dynamic three-case validation confirms 150 vulnerable instances under tested sandbox policies. Coordinated disclosure yielded 13 security advisories, including two CVEs in Anthropic's Git MCP Server.

title: International Multi-Centre Validation of Unsupervised Domain Adaptation for Precise Discrimination between Normal and Abnormal Retinal Development
abstract: Arrested retinal development can cause childhood visual impairment, but grading optical coherence tomography scans is difficult to standardise across devices and centres. We developed and evaluated an unsupervised domain adaptation model to classify normal and abnormal retinal development across different OCT systems. This retrospective multicentre study used OCT scans from five centres in four countries and the UK Biobank. Data covered four OCT devices, including table mounted and handheld systems. A ResNet50 based Domain Adversarial Neural Network was trained using labelled images from a source device and unlabelled images from a target device. We evaluated six source to target pairings and compared model performance with seven clinician graders. A separate Heidelberg Spectralis dataset was reserved for external evaluation. Across validation sets, accuracy ranged from 87.75% to 96.06%, sensitivity from 88.68% to 98.38%, and specificity from 78.00% to 98.02%. The best performing model, adapted from TM OCT1 to HH OCT1, achieved 96.06% accuracy and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.994, with a 95% confidence interval from 0.981 to 0.999. Several models also maintained discrimination on the unseen Heidelberg device. Unsupervised domain adaptation enabled OCT classification across devices without labelled target device data. The approach may support more consistent assessment of retinal development and large scale analysis of existing imaging datasets.

title: RLDF: A Region-Level Deepfake Dataset and Benchmark for Partial-Face Manipulation Detection
abstract: Existing deepfake detection models are built upon manipu- lated images that are tampered with either exclusively fully swapped or fully synthesised faces, which leads us to an open question: Can off-the-shelf deepfake models detect manipulation effectively while tampering is confined to a local facial sub-region? To fill this gap, we introduce RLDF (Region-Level Deepfake), the first dataset for region-level deepfake evaluation. Employing the proposed region-aware partial swap synthesis model, we generate over 2M par- tial face-swap images by using eight face-swapping meth- ods. Altogether, we considered seven face regions, among which there are four discrete regions (eye, nose, mouth and eyebrow) and four composite facial regions (eye and nose; eye, nose and mouth; eye, nose, mouth and eye- brow; and full face). In addition, we define three evalu- ation protocols and benchmark 12 state-of-the-art detectors across the five popular standard cross-dataset evaluations, DF40, and the proposed RLDF, providing a comprehen- sive audit of where and why existing detectors underper- formed. Our evaluation reveals that existing detectors fail to generalize consistently across partial facial regions, re- sulting in an overall drop of 10.5% AUC and 10% accu- racy under region-level evaluation. Further, we propose a mask-guided cross-attention model as a baseline approach that can effectively detect region-level manipulation. The proposed dataset, code, and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/RLDF-Dataset/RLDF.

title: Learning and Forecasting Multiscale Spatiotemporal Epidemic Dynamics with Lagrangian-Eulerian Graph Neural ODEs
abstract: Accurate medium- to long-range epidemic forecasting requires extrapolating high-dimensional, heterogeneous and nonstationary dynamics from partial observations. Yet hybrid models often leave implicit which observations inform which epidemic processes and how learned graph interactions modify system state. We introduce LE-EpiGNODE, which replaces generic message passing with process-specific, mechanism-guided neural operators: age-contact information drives Lagrangian infection generation, whereas mobility drives conservative Eulerian population transport within a structure-preserving universal differential equation. We evaluated LE-EpiGNODE across 14 controlled synthetic mechanisms spanning time-modulated, state-dependent, nonlinear and coupled dynamics, three complementary COVID-19 settings, 21 comparator models and five targeted ablations. Forecasting gains tended to become more pronounced at longer horizons; at the longest horizon, LE-EpiGNODE achieved the lowest WMAPE in all three real-world datasets, reducing error by 17.7-40.0% relative to the best baseline. Controlled ablations linked these gains to the Lagrangian-Eulerian decomposition and process-aligned priors, while synthetic ground truth showed that learned operators and induced state fluxes track known generating dynamics. These results support mechanism-organized graph neural dynamics as a route to reliable long-horizon extrapolation with directly testable, process-level mechanistic interpretation beyond trajectory accuracy.

title: Inferência Textual Zero-Shot em Português: Especialização Linguística vs. Raciocínio Explícito em Modelos de Linguagem Compactos
abstract: Este trabalho investiga a capacidade inferencial de modelos de linguagem de pequeno e médio porte (até 9B de parâmetros) na tarefa de Inferência em Linguagem Natural (NLI) em português brasileiro, em regime estritamente zero-shot. Partindo da definição formal de acarretamento como preservação de condições de verdade, uma relação dedutiva na classificação peirceana [Peirce 1932], comparamos modelos especializados em português (Sabiá, Bode, Gaia) com modelos multilíngues equipados com mecanismos explícitos de raciocínio e destilação de conhecimento (Qwen3, Gemma 2, Ministral 3) no ASSIN 2 e em um dataset sintético controlado, fundamentado em acarretamento por inclusão lexical (hiponímia / hiperonímia). Os resultados indicam que raciocínio explícito e destilação são mais decisivos do que adaptação monolíngue isolada, e que acurácia elevada no ASSIN 2 pode superestimar a competência inferencial ao confundir similaridade distribucional indutiva com preservação dedutiva de condições de verdade.

title: STAB: A Complexity-Ladder Framework for Evaluating Local LLMs as Autonomous Agents
abstract: O uso de Large Language Models (LLMs) em sistemas agênticos locais enfrenta desafios críticos de consistência e confiabilidade, especialmente em hardware de consumo. Este trabalho apresenta o protocolo STAB, uma metodologia de avaliação em escada de complexidade (S1→S4) combinada a um protocolo de estabilidade temporal para diagnosticar falhas em agentes on-premise. Avaliamos oito modelos de quatro famílias (Qwen, Gemma, Llama e Mistral) em servidor com GPU NVIDIA RTX 3060 (12 GB VRAM). Os resultados revelam que as falhas agênticas originam-se predominantemente na camada de instrução e decisão contextual, e não na capacidade bruta dos modelos. Identificamos o fenômeno de tool-skipping por nomeação semântica (H12) e demonstramos que conformidade de formato e acurácia semântica são dimensões ortogonais (H10). O modelo gemma4:e4b destacou-se como referência de maior confiabilidade, mantendo desempenho perfeito em todos os níveis de complexidade.

title: Structural AI Interpretability: A Geometry‑First Framework for Hallucination Detection, Drift Analysis, and Silicon‑Level Governance — Preprint v1.0 (Architecture Edition)
abstract: Structural AI Interpretability: A Geometry‑First Framework for Hallucination Detection, Drift Analysis, and Silicon‑Level Governance — Preprint v1.0 (Architecture Edition) introduces a geometry‑first framework for understanding, detecting, and preventing hallucination in modern reasoning systems. Rather than treating hallucination as a behavioral anomaly or a failure of factual recall, this work demonstrates that hallucination is a geometric collapse event within the latent manifold. When stability invariants are missing—curvature bounds, modal adjacency constraints, spectral‑state manifolds, operator‑field typing rules, and non‑harm boundaries—expressions drift away from grounded semantics, collapse surfaces emerge, and hallucination becomes inevitable. This preprint presents a complete structural pipeline: 1. LeanHallucinationGuard (Semantic Enforcement Layer) A deterministic enforcement enclave that intercepts syntactic mimicry, semantic drift, operator‑field confusion, modal instability, and spectral mismatch before execution. GitHub repository: https://github.com/Borealiscodes/Lean-Hallucination-Guard LeanHallucinationGuard enforces geometric invariants, humanitarian non‑harm constraints, modal adjacency rules, operator‑field typing, and deterministic abort logic. It transforms hallucination from an opaque failure mode into a structured geometric event with measurable telemetry. --- 2. Geometric Interpretation Toolkit (Analytic Layer) A suite of geometric operators—spectral bundles, collapse‑surface classifiers, modal‑truth lattices, holonomy drift tensors, spectral mismatch metrics, and stability envelopes—that make hallucination measurable, reproducible, and scientifically analyzable. These operators quantify drift, detect collapse surfaces, identify spectral degeneracy, and reveal modal instability. They provide the analytic backbone for geometry‑first interpretability. --- 3. ProvenanceShield (Silicon‑Level Governance Layer) A hardware‑rooted governance framework built on AMD SEV‑SNP and Intel TDX attestation. ProvenanceShield ensures that all reasoning occurs inside a cryptographically attested enclave with immutable invariants, verified operator provenance, and deterministic execution boundaries. GitHub repository: https://github.com/Borealiscodes/ProvenanceShield ProvenanceShield prevents unverified symbolic assemblies, pseudo‑formal constructs, and hallucinated operators from escaping into execution—especially in safety‑critical environments. --- 4. CMR Telemetry Artifact (Drift‑Collapse Case Study) The preprint analyzes the Compressed Manifold Reachability (CMR) manuscript (Reed 2026) strictly as a hallucination‑geometry telemetry artifact, not as a validated robotics algorithm. CMR exhibits syntactic mimicry, semantic drift, spectral mismatch, modal adjacency violations, collapse surfaces, and drift‑tensor accumulation. These failure modes illustrate how missing invariants allow plausible‑looking but structurally inconsistent derivations to form. --- 5. Appendices and ASCII‑Stable Diagrams The record includes extensive appendices: - Lean falsification excerpts - collapse‑surface ASCII diagrams - drift‑tensor ASCII visualizations - spectral bundle ASCII illustrations - ProvenanceShield schematic All diagrams are ASCII‑stable and accessible, ensuring compatibility with screen readers and long‑term archival formats. --- Purpose of This Zenodo Record This Zenodo deposit provides: - the full Structural AI preprint - all appendices - ASCII‑stable diagrams - enforcement code (LeanHallucinationGuard) - governance code (ProvenanceShield) - geometric toolkit operators - provenance materials - drift‑collapse case study documentation Together, these components form a unified, deterministic, invariant‑preserving architecture for grounded reasoning, geometric interpretability, and silicon‑level governance.

title: Adaptive Machine Learning in Non-Stationary Environments: A Systematic Review of Concept Drift Detection and Mitigation in Data Streams
abstract: The proliferation of high-velocity data streams in domains such as IoT, cybersecurity, and financial technology has exposed the limitations of static machine learning models. When the underlying data distribution changes over time, a phenomenon known as concept drift occurs, leading to severe model degradation `[1]`. This paper presents a systematic review of 29 foundational and contemporary studies on concept drift detection and adaptation. We categorize detection mechanisms into statistical, window-based, and model-based approaches, while evaluating adaptation strategies ranging from dynamic ensembles to lightweight incremental learning `[16]`. Furthermore, we address compounding challenges, including class imbalance and the emergence of novel classes `[2]`, `[30]`. By synthesizing recent advancements, this review provides a comprehensive roadmap for developing robust, real-time, and resource-efficient streaming machine learning systems `[27]`

title: GeoQA-PG: a knowledge system-guided retrieval-augmented framework for geographical question answering in Pedogeography
abstract: Geographical Question Answering (GeoQA) is transitioning from traditional rule-based and retrieval-based approaches to intelligent paradigms driven by large language models. As an important component of geographic artificial intelligence, GeoQA aims to provide reliable and interpretable geographic knowledge services. However, existing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) methods remain inadequate for geographic questions requiring structured knowledge and coherent logical reasoning. To address these challenges, this study proposes GeoQA-PG, a question answering framework for pedogeography. Specifically, a tree-network knowledge system is constructed by integrating a hierarchical knowledge framework with a fine-grained knowledge graph. Building on this knowledge system, a dual-channel retrieval mechanism, named SoilKnowRAG, is developed. It combines text and graph retrieval to mitigate knowledge fragmentation. Based on GeoQA-PG, SoilGPT is implemented and evaluated using a question answering dataset. Experimental results demonstrate that SoilGPT significantly outperforms baseline models with comparable parameter scales on both objective and subjective tasks, while the comparative evaluation of SoilKnowRAG further confirms its effectiveness compared with other RAG methods. Overall, GeoQA-PG provides a transferable framework for knowledge-driven GeoQA and advances the intelligent representation, reasoning, and services of geographic knowledge.

title: Normalizing Flow Maps
abstract: Scalable approaches to learning neural dynamical systems have placed diffusion, flow matching, and few-step generators in flow maps at the forefront of generative modeling. Such state-of-the-art models have limited access to explicit model densities despite evolving from classical generative modeling approaches that leveraged tractable likelihoods, e.g., Normalizing Flows and Autoregressive models. In this paper, we combine these threads of few-step generation and tractable sample likelihoods and introduce Normalizing Flow Maps (NFM), a class of exactly invertible pushforward maps that generalizes normalizing flows and flow maps. More precisely, NFMs learn the integrator of an underlying dynamical system, but crucially, they provide efficient exact likelihood evaluation by construction. To enable scalable training of NFMs, we derive two complementary axes of consistency inherent to NFMs that yield (self) distillation objectives: (1) pointwise matching, which unlocks ell_2-based flow-map style regression losses, and (2) distributional matching, which matches pushforward distributions to the marginals of a prescribed forward process. On conditional image generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-64, NFMs achieve state-of-the-art sample quality among parameter-matched normalizing flows, while supporting likelihood-based RLHF. For equilibrium sampling in Boltzmann Generators, NFMs outperform prior state-of-the-art normalizing flows on both single-system and transferable peptide benchmarks.

title: AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses for complex cases, but a useful second opinion must also be factually grounded, clinically coherent, actionable, and safe. We developed a multidimensional benchmark using 300 diagnostically resolved NEJM--MedQA cases: 110 for physician reference ratings and Judge calibration and 190 for held-out evaluation. Eight single-model pipelines generated independent role-specific opinions and interactive-consilium reports under free-form and structured clinical-reasoning conditions. A physician-calibrated LLM Judge evaluated 3,040 final reports and the corresponding structured primary-role outputs. Model identity separated report quality more strongly than response format. Structured final reports had higher overall mean scores in seven of eight model pipelines, with their clearest advantage in management (2.740 vs. 2.436). Compared with the structured pre-consilium primary-role opinion, the complete structured synthesis had higher pooled scores across all five shared criteria, with the largest increases in problem prioritization, factual grounding, and reasoning coherence. GPT-5.6-Sol led every evaluated component and reached consensus in the fewest review rounds. These findings show that the benchmark can distinguish model capability, the contribution of multidisciplinary synthesis, criterion-specific effects of response structure, deliberation dynamics, and inference requirements within one common-case evaluation.

title: Progress Reward Model for Reinforcement Learning via Large Language Models
abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.

title: Encoded but Exposed: Language Embeddings can Reveal More Than They Should in Recommender Systems
abstract: Language embeddings are increasingly used in recommenders to represent item content, but their privacy risks remain poorly understood. We study whether item embeddings can reveal item identities when an adversary has access to auxiliary item text from external sources. We show that a simple cosine-similarity attack can recover item identities with high mean reciprocal rank across language models and candidate-set settings on two real-world datasets. Leakage is strongest when the adversary's partial information overlaps with the victim representation, but it also persists through semantic alignment between independently sourced descriptions. We further show that item leakage can propagate to user re-identification from sparse ratings. Finally, we evaluate obfuscated descriptions as a mitigation and find a clear leakage-utility tradeoff.

title: RecSoup: Efficient Model Merging Approach for Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation
abstract: Recommender systems often need to balance multiple conflicting objectives. Controllable Multi-Objective Recommendation (CMOR) enables dynamic adjustment of objective trade-offs at inference time without retraining, adapting to shifting user or system requirements. Existing CMOR approaches typically rely on output-level reranking or parameter-generating modules, which either limit the scope of feasible trade-offs or incur substantial training and inference cost. Model merging provides a promising alternative by reusing multiple objective-specific models via parameter combination. However, its direct application to recommender systems is challenging due to the lack of a shared linear regime and cross-objective interference. To address these issues, we propose RecSoup, a lightweight two-stage approach for effective CMOR via specialized model merging. RecSoup first mitigates parameter interference across objectives through a pruning strategy that jointly considers objective-specific importance and cross-objective relevance. It then performs adaptive parameter merging via a learnable preference-to-coefficient mapping, allowing dynamic trade-off control at inference time without joint retraining or additional generative modules. Theoretically, we prove that RecSoup outperforms the parameter generation paradigm in effectiveness and efficiency, as it can fully navigate the Pareto front without smoothness constraints. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that RecSoup achieves improved Pareto front quality and effective controllability while delivers 165--228x faster inference-time latency than parameter generation approaches. Code is available at https://github.com/35798642/RECSOUP.git.

title: Early-stage mortality prediction for ICU-admitted liver disease patients
abstract: Liver disease carries substantial mortality risk, and the early-stage prediction of mortality for patients initially admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) could effectively support clinical decisions about their care. Prior hospital records are an established source of predictive signal for in-hospital mortality, but they vary in depth and length and are absent for patients without prior admissions, which most existing approaches do not accommodate. This thesis develops three approaches that progressively change how prior clinical history is represented for in-hospital mortality prediction at 24 hours after ICU admission in liver disease patients, using the MIMIC-IV database. The first adapts a process-mining framework with an XGBoost classifier, taking clinical scores calculated by the first 24 hours after ICU admission and process-mining history features as input. The second replaces the tabular classifier with a deep-learning model that encodes physiology over the first 24 hours after ICU admission as a temporal sequence, combined with the same process-mining history representation. The third keeps this 24-hour physiology sequence but replaces the process-mining history with a knowledge-graph representation grounded in the Unified Medical Language System, where the relational structure is enriched by LLM-extracted triples from prior discharge notes, and a graph attention network over the resulting graph contributes to the mortality prediction. Our results show that the first approach improves on the existing process-mining baseline under matched evaluation. The second approach does not improve predictive performance over the first, but its multi-branch design allows the contribution of each input source to be measured separately. The third approach also covers patients without prior admission records, a subgroup excluded by the first two approaches, without a loss of performance relative to patients with recorded history.

title: Arabic HPSG grammar for LKB — frozen release 5f (grammar, lexicon, test suite, treebank selection and evaluation scripts)
abstract: An HPSG grammar of Modern Standard Arabic in TDL for LKB-FOS 5.6, in which inflection, derivation, agglutination and syntax are stated in one type hierarchy: 721 types, 280 inflectional, 27 derivational, 31 broken-plural and 31 agglutination rules, 57 syntactic rules, a lexicon of 32,581 entries (canonical lexicon, Arramooz-derived lexicon, treebank supplement, particles, 3,666 listed broken plurals). The archive also contains the test suite of 347 sentences with expected results, the UD Arabic-PADT selection (sentences of at most twelve words) with the deterministic dev/test split, the conversion, scoring and feature-comparison scripts, the derivation-tree exports of every run reported in the accompanying article, the neural baseline scores and the result reports. This is the frozen release evaluated in the article “A Unified HPSG Morpho-Syntactic Grammar for Modern Standard Arabic” (submitted to Language Resources and Evaluation). See LISEZMOI.md for the layout and the commands that regenerate each table.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Knowledge Integration and Cross-Model Knowledge Integration in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: Multi-agent systems can improve problem-solving by integrating knowledge within individual agents and exchanging knowledge across multiple agents. However, these two processes are often treated as separate capabilities or are embedded in collaboration strategies that do not explicitly optimize the transition between them. Continuous cross-agent knowledge exchange may introduce communication overhead, redundant information, conflicting representations, and unnecessary coordination, whereas exclusive reliance on internally available knowledge may prevent agents from exploiting complementary knowledge held by other agents. This paper proposes Adaptive Self-and-Cross-Model Knowledge Integration (ASCKI), a general framework that enables multi-agent systems to adaptively switch between self-knowledge integration and cross-model knowledge integration according to task requirements, knowledge completeness, uncertainty, information conflict, expected integration benefit, and communication cost. Self-knowledge integration combines information available within an individual agent, including its internal representations, accumulated experiences, retrieved memories, and intermediate conclusions. Cross-model knowledge integration combines information originating from multiple agents or models to construct a more comprehensive collective knowledge representation. The proposed framework introduces a shared decision mechanism, a dual-mode integration architecture, an adaptive switching policy, and a knowledge-quality feedback loop. The switching policy evaluates whether continued internal integration is sufficient or whether external knowledge exchange is likely to provide additional value. The framework is model-agnostic and can be applied to heterogeneous or homogeneous agents, including language-model-based agents, distributed reasoning systems, autonomous learning systems, and knowledge-intensive multi-agent applications. This paper formalizes the framework, presents its operational algorithm, identifies research hypotheses, and develops an empirical evaluation protocol. Rather than claiming experimentally established improvements, it establishes a testable research direction for reducing unnecessary collaboration while preserving the benefits of collective knowledge integration.

title: Adaptive Learning and Collaborative Self-Adaptive Learning Between Self-and-Interaction Models: A Unified Framework for Adaptive Mode Switching
abstract: Learning systems often face a fundamental design choice between adapting independently and adapting through collaboration. Independent adaptation allows a model to preserve its autonomy, exploit its own experience, and avoid unnecessary coordination costs. Collaborative adaptation allows multiple models to exchange information, learn from complementary experiences, coordinate their adaptation strategies, and respond to problems that exceed the capabilities of individual models. Relying exclusively on either mode may be inefficient in dynamic environments, particularly when the relative value of independent and collaborative learning changes over time. This paper proposes a unified framework for adaptive learning and collaborative self-adaptive learning between Self-and-Interaction Models (SIMs). In this framework, a Self-and-Interaction Model is conceptualized as a model-level computational entity that supports self-directed processing and interaction with other models. It is not defined as a large language model, nor does it require any particular neural architecture. The proposed framework enables a model to operate in a self-adaptive learning mode, a collaborative self-adaptive learning mode, or a transition process between the two. Mode selection is governed by an adaptive controller that considers learning progress, uncertainty, prediction error, knowledge complementarity, interaction cost, resource availability, and the expected value of collaboration. The framework formalizes model states, local adaptation, collaborative adaptation, mode selection, information exchange, and adaptive switching through a unified mathematical formulation. It also introduces mechanisms for selective collaboration, confidence-aware information integration, adaptive interaction frequency, and safeguards against harmful information transfer. A research methodology is outlined to evaluate the framework against fixed-mode and non-adaptive switching baselines across heterogeneous and changing environments. Because the framework has not yet been experimentally validated in this paper, its expected benefits are presented as testable hypotheses rather than established results. The proposed approach provides a general research foundation for investigating how self-directed and collaborative adaptation can coexist within a unified model-level learning architecture.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Rewarding and Mutual-Rewarding Processes in Self-and-Mutual Models: A General Framework for Model-Level Reward Coordination
abstract: Reward mechanisms determine how computational systems evaluate their behavior, allocate learning resources, and improve their future decisions. Existing research has investigated intrinsic rewards, self-generated feedback, reward shaping, individual incentives, shared rewards, and cooperative multi-agent learning. However, a general framework for adaptively switching between self-rewarding and mutual-rewarding processes at the level of a distinct class of Self-and-Mutual Models remains an open research direction requiring formalization and empirical investigation. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self–Mutual Reward Coordination Framework (ASMR-CF) for Self-and-Mutual Models (SMMs). The proposed framework treats self-rewarding and mutual-rewarding as complementary operational modes rather than mutually exclusive system designs. In self-rewarding mode, a model evaluates its own candidate actions, predictions, plans, or computational outcomes using internally available evidence and task-relevant evaluation criteria. In mutual-rewarding mode, multiple models exchange evaluations, assess one another's contributions, and construct reward signals that account for cross-model consistency, complementary expertise, and shared objectives. An adaptive controller estimates the relative utility of these modes and determines whether to continue self-rewarding, activate mutual-rewarding, or combine both mechanisms. The framework is designed to operate independently of any particular model architecture, learning algorithm, or reward-generation technique. It introduces a formal representation of model-level reward coordination, an adaptive mode-selection mechanism, safeguards against self-confirming reward errors and mutual-reward manipulation, and an experimental protocol for evaluating the proposed approach. Unlike approaches that assume a fixed reward structure, ASMR-CF explicitly treats the choice of reward mechanism as a decision that can change over time. The paper establishes a conceptual and methodological foundation rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements. Its central research question is whether adaptive coordination between self-generated and mutually generated reward signals can improve performance, reliability, efficiency, and robustness compared with fixed reward strategies.

The proposed framework treats self-rewarding and mutual-rewarding as complementary operational modes rather than mutually exclusive system designs. In self-rewarding mode, a model evaluates its own candidate actions, predictions, plans, or computational outcomes using internally available evidence and task-relevant evaluation criteria. In mutual-rewarding mode, multiple models exchange evaluations, assess one another's contributions, and construct reward signals that account for cross-model consistency, complementary expertise, and shared objectives. An adaptive controller estimates the relative utility of these modes and determines whether to continue self-rewarding, activate mutual-rewarding, or combine both mechanisms. The framework is designed to operate independently of any particular model architecture, learning algorithm, or reward-generation technique. It introduces a formal representation of model-level reward coordination, an adaptive mode-selection mechanism, safeguards against self-confirming reward errors and mutual-reward manipulation, and an experimental protocol for evaluating the proposed approach. Unlike approaches that assume a fixed reward structure, ASMR-CF explicitly treats the choice of reward mechanism as a decision that can change over time. The paper establishes a conceptual and methodological foundation rather than claiming experimentally demonstrated improvements. Its central research question is whether adaptive coordination between self-generated and mutually generated reward signals can improve performance, reliability, efficiency, and robustness compared with fixed reward strategies.

title: Directional Complexity of SIGReg with Anisotropic Gaussian Targets
abstract: Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization (SIGReg) aligns learned representations with an isotropic Gaussian target along random one-dimensional projections. LeJEPA establishes finite-direction guarantees because the rotational symmetry of this target makes every direction identical. Structured representations, however, require anisotropic targets that vary across directions. We prove that while target anisotropy preserves the geometric approximation rate, directional complexity depends on the target’s centered spectral moments and spectral endpoints. We show empirically that across targets with matched condition numbers, spectral shape governs direction budgets. These budgets scale with the target’s spherical Dirichlet energy and initial slicing-gradient variance, while its leading angular harmonic couples directly to directional sampling error. To eliminate this quadratic coupling, we introduce Orthogonal Directional Slicing (ODS), which draws complete random orthonormal frames that enforce exact second-moment balance. While ODS reduces gradient variance across all conditions, it does not reliably lower direction budgets, as higher-degree angular harmonics dominate directional complexity. Reducing this complexity therefore requires canceling these higher-order harmonics, rather than simply drawing more directions.

title: Mitigating Hallucination Cascades in Multi-Agent Systems via Consensus-Aware Knowledge Verification
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems have demonstrated strong capabilities in complex task automation. However, these systems suffer from a critical vulnerability: hallucination cascade, where erroneous information generated by one agent propagates through the system and is amplified by downstream agents. We propose Dynamic Consensus Auditing (DCA), a novel framework that introduces a lightweight audit agent to monitor inter-agent message flows. DCA combines Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with uncertainty quantification based on semantic entropy to detect potentially hallucinated content. When high-uncertainty messages are detected, DCA triggers a peer review mechanism where multiple agents vote on the validity of the information. Experiments on HotpotQA, TriviaQA, and MuSiQue benchmarks demonstrate that DCA reduces error propagation rates by 42.5% (relative reduction) on average compared to baseline multi-agent systems, with a token overhead of 15.3% (averaged across datasets). Our results suggest that, in the context of multi-hop question answering with three-agent pipelines, consensus-aware verification provides a practical balance between reliability and computational efficiency in multi-agent collaboration.

title: AI Versus Knowledge Workers
abstract: The case concerns the consulting firm LegalExpert, whose main activity is advising companies on the generation of new business, as well as the development of a strategy for implementation. The case describes the tensions that arise when incorporating AI into organizational management, especially in knowledge-intensive firms, as well as the practical considerations to be taken into account when initiating this type of intervention. This study contributes to a better understanding of the incorporation of AI in the specific cultural and political context of an organisation. Likewise, this article contributes to a better understanding of the advances of AI in emerging economies, as well as the particularities of its implementation in the specific context of these countries.

title: GlobeBench: Evaluating Text-Based World Model Capabilities for Scalable Environment Simulations
abstract: Text-based world models have recently shown potential to simulate complex RL environment state transitions for a diverse set of use cases. However, no standardized benchmark exists to compare, study and improve these models. Through this paper, we attempt to solve this problem by building GlobeBench, a novel benchmark with 1,632 tasks across five separate domains and nineteen simulation skills. The tasks check whether models can predict the environment's response to a specific action given the full agent trajectory by understanding earlier state changes, following environment rules, and predicting the effects of actions on both related and unrelated objects. We compare the predicted environment response with an execution-derived reference, using a hybrid architecture with both deterministic gates and a semantic judge. Among 20 general-purpose LLMs and specialized text world models, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest task success rate at 49.57%. We find that model accuracy decreases as actions affect a larger portion of the environment. Specifically, when the agent's changes must propagate to dependent objects, task success drops to an average of 5.1% across all 20 models. Although model strengths differ across tasks, 631 tasks remain unsolved by any model, suggesting a significant gap in general LLM capabilities as a world model.

title: Name-Bias in Large Language Models
abstract: Names carry demographic indicators such as age, gender, and race, which makes them a subtle but strong target of bias in large language models (LLMs). In this work, we present an evaluation of name-based bias across 6 local large language models spanning multiple providers and parameter scales. Using a fill-in-the-blank task, we prompt these models to choose between pairs of first names drawn from U.S. Social Security Administration datasets and a race classification dataset by Rosenman et al.. Our experimental de- sign isolates age and gender effects through balanced name pairings and sentence templates that share a fixed syntactic structure. Across 300,000 local LLM responses, we find consistent and measurable name bias. Models prefer names that are less stereotypically male, older, popular, and white. Furthermore, we find that name-bias is highly sentence-dependent, but not more than associated stereotypes, and gender is the most significant bias, followed by age, name popularity, and race. Our results demonstrate that name-based bias remains pervasive even in local LLMs, highlighting the necessity for standardized evaluation methods and mitigation strategies.

title: Loss-independent time-delay estimation via Hong-Ou-Mandel photon bunching detection
abstract: In this work we study the application of two-photon correlated quantum states for high-precision time estimation. To achieve this, photon pairs were fed into a Hong-Ou-Mandel polarization interferometer to generate N00N entangled states with $N = 2$. Two- and four-detector schemes were considered, and the achievable time estimation precision of each was studied, with particular emphasis on the system's Fisher information in each case. Our results reveal that using a four-detector scheme, enabling the measurement of both coincidence and photon-bunching terms, achieves the maximum precision given by the quantum Fisher information, without the need of characterizing system losses. We also show that correlations between repetitions arise due to systematic errors, limiting the precision enhancement that can be obtained by increasing the number of repetitions. Taking these correlations into account, we show that the four-detector scheme outperforms the two-detector scheme in the precision of time-delay estimation. With the experimentally determined calibration uncertainties, the four-detector scheme improves the dispersion by a factor of 2 for the repetitions performed, reaching up to a factor of 4 as both schemes approach their systematic floors.
