title: Hierarchical universal open structure dataset for atomistic modeling
abstract: Atomic-scale simulations have been transformed by machine-learning models that predict the properties of atomistic structures with the accuracy of quantum calculations, but at a small fraction of the cost. These models have increased dramatically in generality, thanks to the availability of synthetic datasets of ever-increasing size and scope. The proliferation of datasets, with properties often computed using different levels of electronic-structure approximation, is problematic, as there is often overlap between different datasets, and strong correlations between structures obtained with short molecular dynamics trajectories or geometry optimization. To address these problems, we introduce a protocol to stratify a dataset into a hierarchy of nested subsets, subsampling from the coarsest to the finest resolution based on an "ecumetric" built to reflect the latent space representation of several popular universal machine-learning interatomic potentials. We then use this approach to combine most of the open structural datasets currently available, consolidating them into MAD-COSMO, a well-organized collection of almost 1.7 billion structures, whose 2^{24} most diverse members form the MAD-CORE stratified coreset, which can be easily used for all sorts of tasks, from exploratory experiments to the training of foundation models at scale. We envision that this collection will guide and help coordinate future efforts, focusing them on the most relevant and/or undersampled regions of chemical and structural space, and that it will be further extended to incorporate the outcomes of the collective work of this community.

title: Robust Covariance Estimation for Entry-wise Contaminated and Partially Observed Data via Expectation Maximization Algorithm
abstract: Robust covariance estimation under entry-wise contamination and missing data is challenging in various signal processing applications. Under the Student-$t$ model, observation-level reweighting induces a uniform attenuation across samples, which can lead to cumulative information loss even when most coordinates remain informative. The alternative Student-$t^*$ model enables coordinate-wise robustness, but its E-step is not available in closed form. We extend inference for the Student-$t^*$ model to incomplete observations through a stochastic approximation EM (SAEM) algorithm operating on a reduced latent space: stochastic updates of the coordinate-wise scales are combined with Rao-Blackwellized Gaussian conditional moments, which avoids explicit sampling of latent Gaussian variables while preserving a likelihood-based framework. Experiments on synthetic and real sensor data show a lower Fisher-Rao error than Gaussian, Student-$t$, imputation-based and detect-then-estimate estimators at moderate to high outlier rates under diffuse contamination.

title: Policy-Aligned Predictive Verification for Adaptive VLA Action-Chunk Execution
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA's internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with pi_0 and pi_0.5 across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success-query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy's proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.

title: Curupira: Arquiteturas Híbridas Transformer-BiLSTM para Detecção de Discurso Ofensivo em Português Brasileiro
authors: Patricia Medyna Lauritzen de Lucena Drumond
abstract: Este trabalho apresenta o Curupira, estudo empírico controlado de arquiteturas neurais para detecção de discurso ofensivo em português brasileiro sob protocolo metodológico rigoroso: split treino/validação/teste honesto, cinco sementes aleatórias, controle explícito de capacidade paramétrica e teste de significância via bootstrap pareado. Oito configurações são avaliadas no OLID-BR, cobrindo quatro ordens de magnitude em parâmetros. Os resultados devem ser interpretados para este conjunto de dados e regime de treinamento, e indicam cinco achados principais: (i) o desempenho se concentra próximo de Macro-F1 = 0,70, com o BERTimbau (110M de parâmetros) superando um híbrido Transformer→BiLSTM leve (350K) em 4,3 pontos; (ii) a atenção global produz ganho estatisticamente significativo sobre uma BiLSTM equiparada em capacidade; (iii) aumentar a capacidade neural não melhora o desempenho no cenário avaliado; (iv) a ordem de composição importa, com Transformer→BiLSTM superando BiLSTM→Transformer em 6,3 pontos; (v) codificação posicional senoidal sobre embeddings congelados degrada substancialmente o desempenho, reduzindo o Macro-F1 de 0,66 para 0,26.

title: Adaptive Self-Search and Collaborative Search in Self-and-Mutual Models: A Unified Framework for State-Dependent Search Switching
abstract: Search is a fundamental process through which computational systems explore possibilities, discover information, identify solutions, and improve their internal representations of a problem. Existing approaches include independent search, population-based search, multi-agent collaborative search, and adaptive combinations of different search strategies. However, these approaches do not necessarily provide a unified, model-level framework in which autonomous search and collaborative search are treated as two complementary operating modes of a broader model architecture. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-Search and Collaborative Search Framework for Self-and-Mutual Models (ASCS-SMM). The framework conceptualizes Self-and-Mutual Models as a model-level architecture that supports both independent exploration and interaction among models. Self-search enables a model to explore a search space using its own internal state, experience, hypotheses, and available computational resources. Collaborative search enables multiple models to exchange information, compare candidate solutions, divide search tasks, and jointly explore regions that may be difficult to investigate independently. A state-dependent switching mechanism determines when the system should continue self-search, initiate collaborative search, maintain collaboration, or return to independent exploration. The proposed framework integrates search-state estimation, uncertainty assessment, progress monitoring, resource allocation, diversity preservation, collaboration utility estimation, and switching-cost management. It is intended to be applicable to optimization, scientific discovery, planning, knowledge exploration, and other computational systems without requiring a specific model architecture or learning paradigm. This paper develops the conceptual foundations, formal definitions, mathematical formulation, operating procedure, evaluation hypotheses, and experimental design of the framework. As a conceptual proposal, its effectiveness and novelty relative to the complete existing literature remain to be established through systematic review and empirical evaluation.

title: Fundamentals of Digital Signatures
abstract: This chapter presents the core principles of digital signatures and explains why they are fundamental to secure digital systems and blockchains. We learn how digital signatures provide data integrity, authenticity, non-repudiation, and how these properties reinforce each other. The chapter explains the working mechanisms of major signature schemes, including RSA and ECDSA, with attention to correctness, security assumptions, and computational efficiency. It then shows how digital signatures operate in blockchain systems, covering the UTXO model, account-based design, and recent advances such as SegWit, Taproot, deterministic signing, and signature aggregation. We can examine key properties required in blockchain settings, including privacy, scalability, and resistance to forgery. The chapter concludes with a comparative overview of representative schemes such as multisignatures, blind signatures, ring signatures, threshold signatures, and EdDSA.

title: What It Is, Not What It Says: Securing Agentic Browsing Interactions with Web Semantics
abstract: AI agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, yet they consume webpages as screenshots or text, exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content. Browsers enforce semantics under which what an element can do depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents flatten these semantics, so injected text can persuade the LLM to exercise the user's authority for content that has none. As LLMs remain easy to persuade, the agent's interface to the web must itself ensure the integrity of what the agent reads, interprets, and does. We propose Intact, which runs on an unmodified browser. Intact builds GenTree, a bespoke representation that captures provenance and web semantics. Intact passes the page via GenTree to the LLM one element at a time, so the LLM decides on each element without any other element's text. Its harness executes each step only within the capabilities of the step's element and asks the user before acting on third-party content. On 1,270 real webpages, GenTree attributes 2.3x as many elements to third parties as the browser, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. On 1,091 of these webpages with injected attacks, only 12.8% of attacks get through Intact's planner, each at most as a consent request, against 73.1% for a conventional planner. evidence.title: What It Is, Not What It Says: Securing Agentic Browsing Interactions with Web Semantics
evidence.abstract: AI agents increasingly browse the web on users' behalf, yet they consume webpages as screenshots or text, exposing their LLMs to unvetted third-party content. Browsers enforce semantics under which what an element can do depends on what it is and where it comes from, not on what it says. Agents flatten these semantics, so injected text can persuade the LLM to exercise the user's authority for content that has none. As LLMs remain easy to persuade, the agent's interface to the web must itself ensure the integrity of what the agent reads, interprets, and does. We propose Intact, which runs on an unmodified browser. Intact builds GenTree, a bespoke representation that captures provenance and web semantics. Intact passes the page via GenTree to the LLM one element at a time, so the LLM decides on each element without any other element's text. Its harness executes each step only within the capabilities of the step's element and asks the user before acting on third-party content. On 1,270 real webpages, GenTree attributes 2.3x as many elements to third parties as the browser, which misattributes 58.7% of them to the first party. title: Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking
abstract: Neural watermarking systems are typically trained as tightly coupled embedder-detector pairs and implicitly assume static deployment. In real-world deployments, embedders and detectors are frequently updated and selectively decoupled for security and versioning purposes, which can break detection in previously embedded content and, more critically, increase false-positive rates on embedders that a given detector is intentionally not intended to recognize. In this paper the concept of backward compatibility in zero-bit audio watermarking is formalized. A training framework is proposed that pairs a new detector with a sequence of frozen legacy embedders (its legacy chain), using a performance-weighted sampling strategy so that the detector retains accuracy across all earlier versions. This coupling, while necessary for backward compatibility, is shown to induce an embedder-collapse effect that catastrophically degrades the true negative rate (TNR) against out-of-chain embedders. To counteract this, a Angular Diversity Loss (ADL) is introduced that explicitly forces each new embedder to occupy a distinct region of the output space. The combined approach restores near-perfect TNR with no measurable cost to detection accuracy or perceptual audio quality.

title: Rethinking Successive Rejects Algorithms
abstract: In the best-arm identification problem, an algorithm adaptively selects arms to find the arm of the largest mean reward. Successive Rejects (SR) is a simple fixed-budget best-arm identification algorithm that eliminates one candidate arm at each phase. At first glance, SR seems to have limited adaptivity, since it follows predetermined phase lengths. However, for Gaussian arms with common variance, SR's worst-instance error exponent normalized by the popular complexity measure $H_1(P)$ is optimal up to a constant factor, which partly explains why SR's performance is competitive compared with state-of-the-art adaptive sampling algorithms. In this paper, we extend the framework of SR by optimizing its predefined schedule of phase lengths. We formulate phase-schedule design as an optimization problem for the normalized error exponent. Then, we introduce a version of SR with the optimized schedule, which we call $H_1$-balanced Successive Rejects ($H_1$-SR). This schedule is optimal within the class of SR-type algorithms with deterministic equal-count schedules. For Gaussian arms with common variance, $H_1$-SR achieves at least $11/12$ of the optimal normalized rate over all adaptive algorithms for every $K\ge2$, and this approximation ratio converges to one as $1-O(1/\log K)$ as $K\to\infty$. This is a significant improvement over original SR, whose corresponding fraction of the optimal normalized rate converges to $1/4$. Finally, experiments on ten synthetic instances and two dataset-derived Gaussian benchmarks compare the optimized schedule with original SR at finite horizons. They show substantial gains on many instances while also exposing a regime in which more aggressive early elimination is costly.

title: ManiFusion: Unlocking the High-Throughput Generation via Superposition in Manifold Space
abstract: Diffusion models achieve high-quality image generation but remain computationally expensive due to iterative denoising across many timesteps. Existing acceleration methods mainly reduce per-sample latency, but gains along this axis are becoming saturated. We instead explore an orthogonal throughput-oriented direction by processing multiple samples within a single denoising evaluation. To this end, we propose ManiFusion, a backbone-agnostic framework for multi-sample generation through fused-space computation. ManiFusion jointly processes multiple samples by fusing them before the denoising backbone and separating them afterward through unfusion. We provide a geometric perspective on how multiple samples can share a fused representation while retaining the information needed to guide their individual generation trajectories. To better align fusion allocation with denoising stages, ManiFusion uses Trajectory-Fusion Scheduling (TFS), which dynamically adjusts fusion factors throughout sampling. ManiFusion generalizes across diffusion families, including both U-Net and transformer backbones in pixel and latent spaces. We further show that ManiFusion composes with existing acceleration methods and reaches throughput regimes unattainable by prior approaches with minimal quality degradation.

title: DLOSAC: Joint Spatial-Geometric Image Estimation via Delaunay-Guided Local Optimization RANSAC
abstract: Reliable image geometric estimation from noisy matching points is typically addressed using RANSAC, often combined with local optimization to refine inliers and model parameters. However, existing paradigms are predominantly residual-centric; even heuristic attempts to enforce spatial uniformity suffer from a sequential, two-stage nature that inherently decouples distribution optimization from geometric refinement, preventing an effective trade-off. In this paper, we propose DLOSAC, a local optimization framework that jointly incorporates both geometric consistency and spatial distribution information. We begin by constructing a Delaunay triangulation over candidate inliers to explicitly encode neighborhood topology. The geometric module introduces an edge-based consistency metric to evaluate geometric errors, while the spatial module derives distribution descriptors from triangle areas and edge attributes to quantify the clustering of inliers. Finally, we combine edge-based geometric constraints, spatial distribution regularization, and traditional point-level geometric constraints to improve the quality of geometric parameters. Extensive experiments on six publicly available real-world datasets, covering three types of geometric estimation tasks, achieve state-of-the-art performance.

title: Fine-grained prosody control in speech synthesis
abstract: Human speech tells us more than written text. Through prosody, we can add information either about ourselves and how we are feeling, or about the lexical content and how it should be understood. Text-to-speech (TTS) models have achieved highly controllable lexical content, evidenced by highly intelligible output. The same level of prosody control has not yet been achieved. We can choose what is being said, down to the phoneme, but not exactly how it is said in terms of the pitch, loudness, timing, and voice quality. This is crucial for creating speech that is appropriate in a given context and fulfils end-user needs. Current approaches commonly rely on utterance-level style embeddings or natural language descriptions, or training on massive amounts of data for greater prosody variation. They do not allow direct prosody adjustments to reflect the context or personal preference of the TTS user. Some TTS systems explicitly model a subset of the acoustic correlates of prosody. In theory, these predictors allow fine-grained control, but this is left implicit and rarely tested in-depth. The models appear easy to control, but is it straightforward to use this control mechanism and add prosodic information about the content or speaker? In this thesis, we investigate the FastPitch model as an exemplar of the current approach to fine-grained control. We examine its controllability in the context of replicating prosody from a reference recording by explicitly extracting acoustic correlates of prosody and transforming them into targets for the model. This approach to prosody control is called voice puppetry. Using reference speech for control is intuitive, but brings additional considerations. Is it possible to achieve fine-grained control across domains and speaker differences, as well as acoustic features? We first explore whether FastPitch is responsive to changing the predicted acoustic features independently. Results show that the model responds to target changes in two out of three acoustic features, although the targeted values are not produced perfectly in the output. Additional experiments indicate that different reference speakers lead to different controllability success. If the acoustic features cannot be calculated reliably, it affects target calculation and consequent prosody generation. In the data used, pervasive creakiness has a bigger impact on (pitch) controllability than speaker gender and accent. The reference utterances in these experiments have prosodic patterns which add topical emphasis to one word in a sentence. Despite imperfect reproductions of the prosody, results show that the additional information is understood by listeners. The second set of experiments focuses on affective prosody. For these, the reference utterances come from multiple emotion-labelled speech datasets and cover a much larger variety of prosody contours. Through analysis of this data, we highlight the limitations of using z-normalisation in the calculation of speaker-normalised pitch values, as well as the limitations of the training data for generating more extreme acoustic values. We propose two methodology updates which help mitigate these issues but also lead to decreased audio quality and intelligibility. We test the emotion transfer from the reference recordings without overly relying on the emotion labels, retrospectively supported by participant comments on the unsuitability of some reference recording labels. When participants are asked to compare model output to the reference prosody, they mostly rate the emotions as 'expressed very similarly'. Finally, we investigate how the controllability success of our voice puppetry approach compares to two alternatives: Daft-Exprt, a similar model to FastPitch but with a built-in reference encoder, and SeedVC, a zero-shot voice conversion model. Both implicitly model prosody from reference recordings, compared to voice puppetry's explicit extraction of acoustic features. Compared to Daft-Exprt and SeedVC, voice puppetry output produces a more faithful prosody contour, especially the pitch trace. Despite the greater objective faithfulness of voice puppetry output, participants in the listening test judge it to have the lowest affect similarity to the reference. Listening test results also suggest that while the voice puppetry quality is noticeably lower, it does produce output with greater similarity to the training speaker. Fine-grained prosody control remains an open research problem. On the modelling side, the acoustic targets are not produced perfectly in model output. On the speaker side, simple transformations such as shifting and scaling are insufficient to translate prosody from one speaker to another. Given some non-parallel data of a reference speaker and a training speaker, it is difficult to define a prosody transformation which retains the training speaker identity, does not lead to a loss in audio quality, and fully encapsulates the prosodic intent. Through our experiments, we identify a series of challenges which complicate fine-grained prosody control in neural speech synthesis, which future models aiming to offer fine-grained control will need to address.

title: THE ANTECEDENT REVERSAL PRINCIPLE (ARP)
abstract: The Antecedent Reversal Principle (ARP) is proposed as a candidate domain-independent analytical principle derived from a canonical conversational case, THE PRIORITY PARADOX (TPP). In the primary case, one participant states that another will no longer receive priority, while the second participant redirects the inquiry toward whether priority had ever been granted. The central abstraction is not temporal contradiction. Rather, the analytical target moves from a claimed state or outcome toward an underlying condition, premise, dependency, enabling state, or grounding relation on which that outcome is taken to depend.Time is therefore treated as one possible relational medium rather than as the mechanism itself. The formal core is represented by a relation C\rightarrow O, where C is an underlying condition, M is an enabling or transformational medium, and O is an observed, claimed, or evaluated outcome. ARP introduces an analytical target-reversal operator R such that \mathcal{R}(O)=C; this notation does not assert causal reversal.Three analytical layers are used: philosophical-epistemological, systemic-mechanistic, and formal-operational. Thirty structured test cases are organized across these layers, with TPP retained as the canonical primary case and with both supporting and disconfirming cases required.The manuscript deliberately distinguishes a formal schema from empirical universality. It therefore treats ARP as a candidate generalized principle whose universal status must be established, restricted, or rejected through operational definition, cross-domain testing, out-of-sample prediction, comparison with alternative explanations, counterexample analysis, and independent replication. Mathematical notation is used only where variables and operations have an explicit interpretation: no equation is treated as evidence by itself.

title: FAIR²-FoodHealth: a provenance-rich knowledge graph linking empirical food composition, nutrients, health-variable definitions and cardiometabolic guidance
abstract: Background: Food, nutrition and health data differ in terminology, identifiers, units and access conditions, so joining them by name or code can silently attach evidence to the wrong concept. Methods: FAIR²-FoodHealth publishes tidy CSV tables and an RDF knowledge graph generated deterministically from them, preserving source-native terms and values. Links to FoodOn, ChEBI, the NCI Thesaurus, LOINC and the Mondo Disease Ontology are qualified SKOS mappings with method, confidence, review status and licence; and hypertension, obesity and type 2 diabetes are linked to the nutrients on which cited dietary guidance focuses, with locators and populations. An empirical layer from USDA FoodData Central contributes 52 food records from two releases with 398 per-100 g values copied unchanged, and 20 computationally drafted source-nutrient decisions, including explicit rejections of total sugars as added sugars and of food energy content as energy intake. Results: Version 0.4.0 comprises 24 tables (666 records) and 15,028 triples; the tables, SHACL shapes, a complete CSV-to-RDF round trip, pinned queries for eleven competency questions and 45 tests (34 injected defects) all pass. Qualified mapping yields 196 value-to-guideline paths for 28 Foundation Foods records; a naive shared-word join yields 434, of which 238 attach added-sugar or energy-intake guidance to the wrong quantity. Exact description matching linked 18 of 24 same-food records without error, whereas token similarity proposed 3 wrong links. Conclusions: Food scientists can use the tidy CSV tables directly for federated analytics, data-quality checks and cross-release compositional comparisons in which every link is a recorded decision rather than a silent name match. Digital-health developers and AI engineers can deploy the RDF graph and qualified mappings to ground retrieval-augmented nutrition assistants in cited, provenance-rich evidence instead of fragile string matching. All mapping and matching decisions are computational drafts awaiting independent expert-panel review; the checks establish structural integrity, not nutritional or clinical validity, and FAIR² compliance is not claimed.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Autonomous Exploration and Collaborative Exploration in Multi-Agent Systems: A Utility-Driven Framework for Dynamic Exploration Coordination
abstract: Multi-agent systems can explore complex environments through autonomous exploration, in which individual agents independently select actions and collect information, or collaborative exploration, in which agents coordinate their activities and exchange information to improve collective discovery. Although both modes offer important advantages, neither is universally optimal. Autonomous exploration can preserve behavioral diversity, reduce communication overhead, and support decentralized operation, whereas collaborative exploration can improve information integration, reduce redundant searches, and facilitate coordinated discovery. A fixed exploration policy may therefore create avoidable inefficiencies when environmental conditions, information uncertainty, agent capabilities, or communication costs change over time. This paper proposes Adaptive Autonomous–Collaborative Exploration (AACE), a utility-driven framework that dynamically switches multi-agent systems between autonomous and collaborative exploration. Rather than treating exploration as a permanently independent or permanently cooperative process, AACE evaluates the estimated marginal value of collaboration relative to its computational, communication, coordination, and redundancy costs. The proposed framework integrates uncertainty estimation, expected information gain, exploration progress, inter-agent information overlap, communication cost, and switching stability into a unified mode-selection mechanism. It supports decentralized implementation, agent-specific decisions, and heterogeneous exploration capabilities. The framework is formulated as a sequential decision problem in which the exploration mode is selected according to estimated long-term utility. A hysteresis-based switching mechanism is introduced to reduce unnecessary oscillations between modes, while a minimum-duration constraint and a periodic reassessment mechanism can improve operational stability. The paper presents the algorithmic architecture, mathematical formulation, implementation procedure, evaluation protocol, research hypotheses, and limitations. It proposes comparisons against always-autonomous, always-collaborative, fixed-period switching, and alternative adaptive baselines. No empirical superiority is claimed because the framework has not yet been experimentally evaluated. The central research proposition is that utility-driven switching can improve the trade-off between information acquisition, exploration efficiency, and coordination overhead under conditions in which the relative value of autonomy and collaboration varies over time.

title: Confidential Computing: Hardware-Enforced Enclaves (TEEs) in Multi-Tenant Cloud and AI Workloads: Architectural Foundations, Attestation, and Performance Bounds
abstract: Abstract—Modern enterprise computing relies predominantly on multi-tenant public cloud infrastructures and outsourced AI model accelerators. While data-at-rest is robustly protected via cryptographic storage encryption (AES-XTS-256) and data-in-transit is secured via Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3), data-in-use remains vulnerable in volatile memory (DRAM, caches, register files). Root-privileged cloud hypervisors, malicious cloud service provider (CSP) insiders, and physical memory interposers can snoop plain-text secrets, proprietary AI weights, and private customer telemetry. Confidential Computing establishes an emerging architectural paradigm that secures data-in-use through hardware-enforced Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs). By executing workloads within cryptographically isolated enclaves governed by hardware memory encryption engines, TEEs remove the cloud host OS, hypervisor, and system firmware from the Trusted Computing Base (TCB). However, deploying complex enterprise microservices and distributed deep neural network training within hardware enclaves introduces critical challenges: memory encryption and integrity verification latency, inter-enclave memory capacity constraints, PCIe-bus side-channel vulnerabilities, and complex remote attestation handshakes. This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical architectural evaluation of hardware-enforced TEEs across contemporary multi-tenant cloud and AI workloads. Our findings demonstrate that hardware-accelerated memory encryption induces an acceptable 3.8% to 6.2% computational latency overhead on standard workloads, while PCIe encryption for confidential GPUs introduces up to an 11.4% throughput reduction during high-bandwidth tensor parallel communication. Finally, we formulate open challenges in post-quantum remote attestation, architectural side-channel mitigation, and composable heterogeneous multi-TEE fabrics.

evidence.title: Confidential Computing: Hardware-Enforced Enclaves (TEEs) in Multi-Tenant Cloud and AI Workloads: Architectural Foundations, Attestation, and Performance Bounds
evidence.abstract: Abstract—Modern enterprise computing relies predominantly on multi-tenant public cloud infrastructures and outsourced AI model accelerators. title: Adaptive Self-Verification and Cross-Verification in World-Level Self-and-Inter Models: A Unified Architecture for Reliability-Aware Model Validation
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environments, their states, dynamics, and potential future outcomes. However, the reliability of a world model cannot be guaranteed solely by its ability to generate plausible predictions. Verification must also determine whether its internal representations, predicted transitions, and inferred relationships remain consistent with available evidence and with other relevant models. Conventional verification strategies may rely primarily on internal consistency checks or external evaluation, while fixed verification policies can incur unnecessary computational costs or fail to respond adequately to changing uncertainty. This paper proposes an Adaptive Self-and-Inter Verification Architecture for World Models (ASIV-WM). The architecture conceptualizes world-level self-and-inter models as a coordinated modeling system in which self-verification and cross-verification are alternative but complementary verification modes. Self-verification evaluates a model using its own internal constraints, historical observations, predicted transitions, and consistency relationships. Cross-verification evaluates its representations and predictions against other models, independently derived evidence, alternative transition hypotheses, or shared environmental observations. A verification controller adaptively selects, combines, or switches between these modes according to uncertainty, prediction error, disagreement, risk, evidence availability, verification cost, and estimated verifier reliability. The proposed architecture is model-centric rather than language-model-centric. It can be implemented using state-transition models, probabilistic dynamics models, constraint systems, simulation models, causal representations, or other structured world-modeling mechanisms. The paper formalizes the architecture, defines its principal components, introduces a verification-mode selection objective, describes conflict resolution and escalation procedures, and develops an experimental methodology for evaluating reliability, computational efficiency, and robustness under distribution shifts. The framework is presented as a research proposal rather than an experimentally validated system. Its principal contribution is the explicit integration of adaptive verification-mode control into a world-level self-and-inter modeling architecture, with the goal of moving beyond fixed self-verification and permanently active cross-verification.

title: Code, locked analysis plans and aggregate results for: The Added Value of Knowledge Graphs for Post-Referral Hospitalization Prediction: A Multi-Cohort Benchmark Using Health Insurance Claims
abstract: This archive accompanies the study "The Added Value of Knowledge Graphs for Post-Referral Hospitalization Prediction: A Multi-Cohort Benchmark Using Health Insurance Claims". The study builds a referral-aware temporal knowledge graph from Indonesian national health insurance (BPJS Kesehatan) sample claims and measures how much its knowledge layer (ICD hierarchy and Charlson groups, code co-occurrence, referral flows, diagnosis-to-clinic relations) adds to six models (logistic regression, LightGBM, GRU, Transformer, GraphSAGE, HGT) that predict hospital admission within 90 days of a primary-care referral. Frozen models were evaluated on internal and temporal test sets and seven external cohorts, with a randomized knowledge graph and GRAM as controls. Contents: all code; the protocol and the three analysis plans; the lock and test-opening records with SHA-256 fingerprints (2026-10-09 to 2026-10-15); and aggregate results (metrics, contrasts with bootstrap intervals, calibration, ablations, GRAM attention weights). The script verify_fingerprints.py recomputes the recorded fingerprints (expected: 49 of 49 match). This archive was deposited after the locks and test openings; it documents the locked materials and is not a preregistration. The BPJS Kesehatan sample data cannot be redistributed by the authors and can be requested from BPJS Kesehatan. The archive contains no participant-level data. Code and file names are in Indonesian; README.md includes a glossary.

title: Multimodal Filesystem Memory For Long-Horizon Embodied Agents
abstract: Agents operating over long horizons need an effective memory that allows them to reuse their experience throughout long interactions. If the entire history of an interaction is retained, it becomes difficult to find the relevant experience, while compressing it into summaries may result in the loss of visual and spatial details that are required later on. We present MFM, a multimodal filesystem memory architecture that keeps complementary types of agent memory. Episodic memory stores the observations, actions, and outcomes, and spatial memory associates experiences with locations. Semantic and procedural memory build up general knowledge and reusable methods of acting, and working memory holds the current plans. MFM makes use of searchable textual records to connect these different representations to the underlying multimodal episodes. The agents are able to find previous experiences by means of contextual cues and to examine the original observations in order to recover details that are missing from their textual descriptions. Through consolidation, the agents convert experience into higher-level knowledge and procedures while still keeping references to the original episodes. In the case of long-horizon Minecraft and computer-use tasks, MFM leads to improved performance with three base models. With GPT-6-Astra, MFM completes Mine Diamond from Scratch and reaches 16 out of 24 milestones on the Ender Dragon task, as against 12.7 for the best baseline. On CUABench-KiCad it attains a mean reward of 0.440, as compared to 0.400 for the best baseline and 0.267 in the case of no persistent memory.

title: Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition in Videos
abstract: Understanding characteristics and activities of individuals in complex multi-person environments is crucial for real-world applications. However, existing datasets often simplify this problem to grounded group activity recognition, single-person activity recognition, or close-set activity recognition, thus limiting the generalizability of models trained on these datasets. In this work, we introduce the task of Grounded Human-Attributed Description and Activity Recognition (GHADAR), which involves describing the characteristics and activity descriptions of \textbf{every} person in a video, provided the location of the person in the video, which is more practical for real-world applications. To facilitate this, we introduce a new dataset derived from AVA-Actions by generating open-set captions for the person description and activity. In addition, we propose a novel method to effectively utilize the information contained in grounding during training by constraining the cross-attention masks during training in VLMs to improve performance for this task. Our experiments show that our method outperforms SOTA VLMs on this task. Finally, we demonstrate the limitations of existing evaluation metrics, which are overly reliant on human-annotations and exact text-text matching. As an added video-based evaluation, we propose a holistic VLM-based evaluation schema that compares concepts {\em directly} between the video and the generated predictions. Thus, in this work, we develop a complete framework for GHADAR, including a dataset, a novel method and an evaluation schema, thereby establishing a strong foundation for future research in this domain.

title: Missed Detections and False Alarms in a CNN Technosignature Detector on Breakthrough Listen Data
abstract: Radio technosignature searches rely on machine learning detectors to shrink the candidate pool before a human looks at it. They are validated on held-out data from the training distribution, which excludes the cases where they are most likely to fail: a technosignature has unknown morphology, and terrestrial interference is unbounded in variety. I trained a standard competition detector once, froze it, and probed it with 15,000 injections across ten morphologies and five amplitudes, placed into real Green Bank backgrounds. Two directions were tested: genuine signals with morphologies other than a straight narrowband line, and interference resembling the training data. Recall did not follow the predicted ordering, and it fell as signals brightened, even for a needle of the kind the detector was trained on (from 0.590 to 0.090). One interference morphology reached a false positive rate of 0.627, comparable to the detector's own baseline recall of 0.5525 on genuine signals. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) showed attention along the injected path in one missed family by a pre-specified test, and visually in a second. A pre-specified, time-averaged ON-OFF filter removed false alarms and genuine detections at the same rate. The detector reads only the ON panels. Since the only evidence distinguishing a genuine candidate from terrestrial interference lies in the discarded OFF panels, it cannot tell if a signal originates from the target star; it can only tell if it resembles the training data. This explains the false alarm directly; the missed signals reflect what the detector learned to recognise, which reading the OFF panels would not by itself change.

title: Mixture of Multi-Sequence Feature Difference for Contrast-Enhanced MRI Synthesis
abstract: Contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (CE-MRI) is crucial for accurately diagnosing and segmenting brain tumors. However, the acquisition of CE-MRI requires injecting contrast agents, which poses potential health risks and increases scan costs. Here, we propose a CE-MRI synthesis method from non-contrast sequences, reducing both risk and cost. Unlike existing methods that rely on channel-wise concatenation to fuse multi-sequence information for synthesis, we introduce a Mixture of Feature Difference (MoFD) module. The proposed module uses a dynamic weighting strategy to adaptively select and aggregate informative features from both individual source sequences and explicit differences among them. Quantitative and qualitative evaluations demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms baselines in terms of image fidelity and perceptual quality on the UCSF-PDGM and UPenn-GBM datasets. Our method successfully reconstructs tumor regions and achieves segmentation performance comparable to that obtained with real CE-MRI. Our ablation studies show that although adversarial learning improves perceptual quality, a regression-based variant of our method achieves higher structural fidelity.

title: On the Complexity of Symmetric Boolean Functions in Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages
abstract: Multiparty Private Simultaneous Messages (PSM), also known as Decomposable Randomized Encoding (DRE) or information-theoretic garbling, is a model for non-interactive secure computation. Each party encodes its input using shared randomness and sends a message to an evaluator who does not know that randomness. The evaluator must recover the function output without learning anything else about the inputs. Perfect privacy requires identical transcript distributions on inputs with the same output. We also study the weaker notion of support privacy, which requires only that these distributions have the same support. We study the communication complexity of symmetric Boolean functions when each of the $n$ parties holds one input bit. Lower bounds. We prove a superlinear lower bound for support-private PSM protocols computing $OR_n$. Our technique gives $Ω(n\log n)$ lower bounds for $MAJ_n$ and $EMAJ_n$ (with even $n$), and an $Ω(n\log q)$ lower bound for $MOD_q$ when $q\leq(1-c)n$ for a fixed constant $c>0$. Upper bounds. We construct perfectly private PSM protocols of total communication $\widetilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ for every symmetric Boolean function, improving on the known quadratic bound. For $MAJ_n$, known branching-program constructions yield an upper bound of $O(n\log^3 n\log\log n)$. For $EMAJ_n$ and $MOD_q$ with prime $q$, the lower bounds are tight up to constant factors in the stated regimes. Under support privacy, we obtain $\widetilde{O}(n)$ communication for every symmetric Boolean function. Earlier lower-bound techniques of Ball et al. (ITCS 2020) yield only trivial linear bounds for symmetric Boolean functions. Concurrent and independent work by Holmgren and Wu proves a $ω(n)$ lower bound for $OR_n$ using the same combinatorial core. Both works used AI assistance.

title: Rewriting Induction for Higher-Order Constrained Rewriting
abstract: Ensuring that software behaves as intended is a central challenge in software development. Formal verification provides mathematically rigorous methods for reasoning about program behavior. One such method is term rewriting, in which the elementary computational steps defining a program are specified by rewrite rules and program behavior is captured by the rewrite relation. The rewrite relation can be seen as a language-independent operational semantics, suitable for program analysis. However, a limitation of traditional term rewriting systems is that primitive data structures, such as integers, must be encoded inductively. This does not correspond to how such data structures are treated in real programming languages. A solution is provided by Logically Constrained Term Rewriting Systems (LCTRSs), where primitive data structures can be treated semantically, providing a more faithful basis for reasoning about program behavior. In this thesis, we use the higher-order extension of LCTRSs, called Logically Constrained Simply-typed Term Rewriting Systems (LCSTRSs), to study program equivalence, based on the intuition that two programs are equivalent if they exhibit the same input-output behavior. We develop several proof systems to establish program equivalence in practice. Although program equivalence is undecidable in general, we introduce heuristics that enable automation in simple cases.

title: Assessing Simulation-Based Dataset Generation for Object Detection
abstract: Dataset generation is a critical component in training robust perception models for tasks such as object detection and road segmentation, where large-scale annotated data are required. In this work, we present a comparative study of two simulation platforms, CARLA and aiSim, focusing on their effectiveness for synthetic dataset creation. The research evaluates how effectively neural networks trained on synthetic data from each platform can generalize to real-world conditions, with particular emphasis on real-world object detection performance. While both simulators provide automated annotation pipelines, they differ in usability, flexibility, and scalability when constructing labeled datasets. The study specifically focuses on training neural networks using synthetic data from each simulator and evaluating their performance on real-world footage, thereby assessing the domain transfer capability of the generated datasets. This approach allows for a direct comparison of how simulation realism and scenario diversity impact generalization to real-life conditions. The findings provide insights into the limitations of current simulation tools in bridging the gap between synthetic and real-world data and identify the factors that most strongly influence successful transfer learning.

title: Skew-product semigroup actions with applications to post-quantum-oriented key exchange
abstract: We study semigroup actions induced by the left skew product of functions and use them to define a session-dependent key-exchange framework. Correctness is governed by a local compatibility condition on the derived acting functions and therefore does not require commutativity of the skew-product semigroup. This leads naturally to a distinction between the algebraic mechanism ensuring a common session value and the computational hardness of the corresponding effective action. To make this distinction explicit, we first analyze a finite-field Ore realization and show that, although it satisfies the required algebraic compatibility, its effective action collapses and can be inverted by linear algebra over the fixed field. We then replace this weak effective action by a valuation-lifted realization built from a prime-order cyclic action, instantiated through oriented supersingular elliptic curves. The resulting construction incorporates an interactive multiplicative session derivation based on the joint state hαβ *a. Finally, we formulate the Shared-Action Problem for recovery of the common algebraic session value, show that in the valuation-lifted realization it can be solved using parallelization, and reduce session-key security to Shared-Action hardness in the authenticated-links, classical random-oracle model.

title: SSAT: A reproducible toolkit for task-conditioned spatial sensitivity auditing of vision models
abstract: SSAT (Spatial Sensitivity Audit Toolkit) is an open-source Python package for reproducible, dataset-scale auditing of how image and video classification models respond to interventions on user-defined spatial or semantic regions. It reports effect sizes alongside evidence grades from matched controls and cross-operator checks, records preprocessing-aware geometry that exposes area confounds, and keeps full model outputs with provenance for inference-free reanalysis of stored interventions. Synthetic, ImageNet-1k, and NTU RGB+D studies demonstrate shortcut recovery, geometry diagnostics, and protocol reuse across CNN and transformer classifiers and modalities; further analyses quantify grade sensitivity to thresholds and control counts, and audit cost scaling.

title: Exploring The Empirical Privacy Landscape of Synthetic Data
abstract: Methods for training language models on sensitive data differ in how they balance capability gains against the risk of leaking private information. In this paper, we present a controlled comparison of data-level and training-level interventions for navigating the capability-privacy tradeoff on synthetic medical records with canaries to probe for leakage. Direct finetuning performs best on capability metrics but leads to the most privacy leakage, while DP-SGD reduces leakage at substantial cost to capabilities. Generating synthetic data from these records offers a more favorable balance, particularly when guided by a uniqueness-aware instruction to replace private details. Relative to naive paraphrasing, privacy-aware rewriting improves privacy protection across a variety of different rewriting models. We also find that more capable rewriting models generally reduce the risks of downstream privacy leakage, although held-out fit does not improve monotonically and increased test-time compute yields inconsistent gains. Overall, these results highlight privacy-aware rewriting as a promising direction for achieving a more favorable trade-off between capabilities and empirical privacy compared to other training-level methods, and our evaluation framework supports comparisons of future models and methods.

title: Multi-Target Few-Shot Prompting with Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Few-shot prompting is useful when instructions and rewards are hard to specify. One such application is editing by example, where a demonstrated formatting change or API migration may need to be applied across multiple sites. However, such edits often depend on both left and right context, making generation with causal autoregressive models awkward. We therefore introduce multi-target few-shot prompting with diffusion language models, where examples guide the infilling of multiple masked regions within a shared canvas. To address the known challenge of reliably following demonstrations in few-shot prompting, we further leverage selective masking of the canvas to derive a likelihood-ratio reward that favors example-supported infills. Across few-shot prompting benchmarks and software refactoring case studies, we find that demonstrations improve infilling accuracy, with example guidance yielding further gains in several settings.

title: Decoding Naturalistic Speech from fMRI with Temporal Modeling and Multimodal Alignment
abstract: Reconstructing what a person perceives from their brain activity is a stringent test of whether neural recordings carry meaningful information. Naturalistic speech offers a rich testbed for this challenge: it unfolds over multiple timescales, but fMRI's noisy, temporally smeared measurements make this structure hard to recover. We introduce NOEMA, a temporal convolutional decoder that aligns windows of consecutive fMRI measurements with multimodal stimulus embeddings. These embeddings combine complementary text, audio, and speech representations of the same stimulus segment, enabling its retrieval directly from brain activity. On two naturalistic speech datasets, Cephalonauts One and LeBel, NOEMA retrieves the correct segment among 2,000 candidates within the top 10 for more than 42% of held-out queries. This substantially outperforms baseline decoders, an advantage that persists when the candidate pool is extended with thousands of distractors absent from training. Controlled ablations establish the contributions of temporal modeling and complementary stimulus representations.

title: Bridging the Markerless Tracking Validation Gap: Intraoperative X-ray Workflow Integration
abstract: Markerless intraoperative tracking of spinal anatomy via RGB-D sensors is a promising alternative to invasive bone-anchored fiducials, yet no existing clinical dataset provides independent subsurface ground truth for validating these methods. We address this gap with a clinically viable pipeline that derives per-vertebra 6-DoF pose from routine intraoperative C-arm fluoroscopy, co-registered to the RGB-D camera frame through a multimodal fiducial array detectable in both imaging modalities. Critically, the pipeline requires no additional radiation, instrumentation, or deviation from standard surgical workflows, relying solely on the fluoroscopic images already acquired during routine level checks. A calibrated transform chain links the vertebral pose recovered via multi-view 2D-3D CT-to-fluoroscopy registration to the RGB-D coordinate frame, enabling direct comparison of any markerless registration estimate against a subsurface reference. Ex vivo validation against optically tracked ovine vertebrae confirms end-to-end accuracy of 2.06 +- 0.29 mm and 3.35 +- 0.93 degrees, sufficient to serve as independent ground truth for methods with substantially larger errors. We demonstrate the pipeline's utility by evaluating two markerless registration strategies on clinical data spanning 11 vertebrae across 1,500 frames from three surgical sequences: the first such evaluation against an independent subsurface reference in a clinical setting. The proposed framework provides reusable infrastructure for benchmarking emerging markerless tracking methods on real surgical data.

title: Do Agents Need a New Kind of Paper? SPRA: Structured Paper Representation for Agents
abstract: Scientific agents must connect research problems, methods, and findings dispersed through narrative articles. We introduce SPRA (Structured Paper Representation for Agents), a paper-level representation of persistent research objects and typed relations. Its empirical-AI profile organizes Problems, Contributions, Components, ExperimentSetups, Measures, and Findings for querying, traversal, and reuse. Selected paper-level citation relations record dependencies, component use, and comparisons with prior work; source locations support verification. We instantiate SPRA across more than one million AI papers, with 19.95 million research units and 24.07 million internal relations. Evaluations access SPRA through Schema-RAG with task evidence fixed before inference. Across seven subfields, SPRA improves source-conditioned scientific QA by 0.381/5 over passage retrieval while remaining close to Full Compact (0.078/5 lower on average). In directed cross-paper reasoning, qualification improves by 0.184/5 over passage retrieval; Top-5 synthesis shows mixed quality effects. Across all paired RQ2 tasks, including Top-5, input+output tokens decrease by 28.5% relative to passage retrieval and 95.3% relative to Full Compact. In idea generation, a 0.067-point lower Overall score than Full Compact accompanies 93.7% fewer input+output tokens. Together, these results support SPRA as a usable representation of scientific content and a foundation for research workflows that connect, inspect, and reuse paper-level research objects. The SPRA resource is accessible through the SciVerse scholarly-data platform.

title: Yapay Zekâ Aracılı Alışverişte Pazarlamanın Dönüşümü: Tüketici Karar Sürecinden Marka Stratejilerine
abstract: Yapay zekâ, pazarlamada uzun süre işletmelerin tüketicileri analiz etmesini, kişiselleştirilmiş teklifler geliştirmesini ve pazarlama faaliyetlerini otomatikleştirmesini sağlayan bir teknoloji olarak ele alınmıştır. Üretken yapay zekâ ve daha özerk sistemlerin gelişimi ise yapay zekâyı tüketici tarafında bilgi arama, alternatif oluşturma, değerlendirme, seçim ve belirli koşullarda işlem gerçekleştirme süreçlerine katılan bir karar aracısına dönüştürmektedir. Bu çalışma, yapay zekâ aracılı alışverişin tüketici karar sürecini ve marka stratejilerini nasıl dönüştürdüğünü bütünleştirici bir pazarlama perspektifiyle incelemektedir. Literatürün kavramsal sentezinden hareketle, teknik özerklik ile tüketicinin yapay zekâya devrettiği karar yetkisi birbirinden ayrılmakta ve yapay zekâ destekli alışverişten otonom/agentic alışverişe uzanan beş düzeyli bir karar yetkisi sürekliliği önerilmektedir. Bu yaklaşımda agentic commerce, yapay zekâ aracılı alışverişin tamamıyla eş anlamlı değil, yüksek karar ve işlem yetkisi devrini temsil eden uç biçim olarak konumlandırılmaktadır. Çalışma, karar yetkisi devrinin bilişsel kolaylık ve karar verimliliği sağlayabilmesine karşılık tüketici özerkliği, algılanan kontrol, güven ve mahremiyet açısından gerilimler yaratabileceğini ortaya koymaktadır. Ayrıca yapay zekâ aracılı etkileşimlerin müşteri yolculuğunun gerçek yapısı ile işletmeler tarafından gözlemlenen yapısı arasındaki mesafeyi artırabileceği tartışılmaktadır. Marka stratejileri açısından ise klasik marka değerinin önemini koruduğu, ancak markaların yapay zekâ tarafından bulunabilir, değerlendirilebilir ve seçilebilir olmasının yeni bir stratejik katman oluşturduğu ileri sürülmektedir. Bu ilişkiler, tüketici–yapay zekâ–marka arasındaki çift yönlü geri beslemeleri ve bağlamsal koşulları içeren Karar Yetkisi–Marka Stratejisi Çerçevesi altında bütünleştirilmektedir. Önerilen çerçeve kavramsal bir sentez niteliğinde olup farklı tüketici, ürün, sistem ve pazar koşullarında ampirik olarak sınanması gerekmektedir.

title: Causal Invariant Bio-Inference: Breaking the Observational Barrier in Rhizosphere Dynamics via Physically-Constrained Edge-GNN Structural Causal Models
abstract: Observational machine learning models (e.g., Transformers, CNNs, Random Forests) fit joint probability distributions P(Y|X) and inherently break down out-of-distribution when spurious correlations fail under environmental volatility. In rhizosphere dynamics, unobserved confounders and micro-climatic shifts frequently lead to catastrophic prediction failures. To break this observational barrier, we introduce Causal Invariant Bio-Inference for RADIUS 0 / MediEEZI, combining Judea Pearl’s do-calculus interventional framework P(Y|do(X=x*)) with structural causal models (SCMs) and decentralized Edge Graph Neural Networks (Edge-GNNs). By embedding a stoichiometric and biochemical constraint matrix (C_bio derived from KEGG/MetaCyc pathways) directly into the adjacency optimization, we restrict the causal search space to thermodynamically allowed interactions and enforce strict directed acyclic graph (DAG) topology via matrix exponential constraints. This physically-constrained architecture enables provably convergent, continuous in-situ causal bio-inference across soil-plant-microbiome interactions, closed-loop environmental control life support systems (ECLS), and non-invasive health monitoring without requiring destructive sampling.

title: Peer Review Report For: Towards Reliable Prosody Detection in Teaching Practical Phonetics: A Sustainable Digital Approach [version 3; peer review: 1 approved, 2 approved with reservations]
abstract: This research focuses on providing quality education to specialists in the field of linguistic studies, phonology, theoretical and practical phonetics by creating an innovative automated service which can ease the linguists endeavour to transcribe and examine suprasegmental features of human speech prosody. The authors attempted to design a docker-based architecture for prosody labelling. The pre-processing stage compiled 47 manually marked recordings, ten of which were annotated at clip level. The data-processing stage produced a corpus of 882 denoised, labelled clips via librosa , noisereduce , and Label Studio. The model selection stage compared 4909 scikit-learn configurations and 120 CNN configurations. The strongest classical approach (Random Forest) achieved an accuracy of 0.373, whereas the best CNN scored 0.455 against a majority-class baseline of 0.316. Per-class analysis showed that the classical models performed poorly across most intonation categories, assigning 94% of predictions to the two most frequent classes. These results indicate early-stage prototype performance rather than a validated evaluation and are not yet sufficient to support reliable automatic intonation marking. Having recognised the prototype limitations, the researchers have scheduled a roadmap for improving the tool. evidence.abstract: This research focuses on providing quality education to specialists in the field of linguistic studies, phonology, theoretical and practical phonetics by creating an innovative automated service which can ease the linguists endeavour to transcribe and examine suprasegmental features of human speech prosody. The authors attempted to design a docker-based architecture for prosody labelling. The pre-processing stage compiled 47 manually marked recordings, ten of which were annotated at clip level. The data-processing stage produced a corpus of 882 denoised, labelled clips via librosa , noisereduce , and Label Studio. title: Protocol-Constrained Adversarial Evasion Against Transformer-Based Network Intrusion Detection
abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS) approaches that are transformer based demonstrate good performance in classification but are susceptible to protocol-oriented adversarial attacks. We present Appendix Protocol-Constrained Adversarial Evasion (PCAE), producing perturbations within protocol feasibility constraints to do so in a manner that does not corrupt the packets or leave us discovered. Our proposed model is an improving mechanism based on the threat model, the Conformal Prediction-Augmented Adaptive Defense (CPAAD), which is a multi-head self-attention encoder with distribution-free uncertainty quantification based on split conformal prediction. Assessed in enterprise (CICIDS2017 and CICIDS2018), IoT (N-BaIoT), and Industrial Control System /SCADA (SWaT) settings with FGSM, PGD and C&W attacks, CPAAD has a 90 or higher marginal coverage and a 61.4 level decrease in adversarial success compared to unprotected baselines and beats seven competing defenses by all metrics.

title: Mutual learning of self-supervised ViTs for image classification with limited labeled data
abstract: With the rapid advancement of self-supervised learning in computer vision, pretrained models have shown remarkable transferability across a wide range of downstream tasks by effectively leveraging large-scale unlabeled data. However, prevailing approaches predominantly adopt supervised fine-tuning strategies on individual models, often overlooking the potential complementarity between different pretrained models during adaptation. This limitation constrains the further improvement of model performance. To address this, the authors propose a bidirectional mutual learning framework that enables two distinct self-supervised models to be jointly fine-tuned on a target task. By exchanging predictions during training, the models share knowledge and collaboratively enhance their representations. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate that their method consistently outperforms conventional full-parameter fine-tuning and low-rank adaptation (LoRA) in classification performance. Notably, the superior results achieved on the Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) data set highlight the potential of their method in medical imaging analysis.

title: Measuring Mechanistic Uncertainty in Large Language Models via Causal Robustness
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in critical domains, where their susceptibility to hallucinations makes reliable and interpretable uncertainty quantification essential. We introduce the concept of mechanistic uncertainty, which characterizes uncertainty through the stability of the internal mechanisms supporting a model's response. We propose the causal robustness margin, defined as the minimum internal intervention required to deviate the model's output, and operationalize it using Jacobian Lens (Jlens) concept steering vectors. Across three open-source models and five question-answering datasets, we show incorrect and uncertain responses exhibit smaller margins, indicating greater sensitivity to internal interventions, and the causal robustness margin complements conventional output-based uncertainty methods. Finally, in a controlled knowledge injection experiment, correctly learned facts show increased margins after training, suggesting that causal robustness provides a mechanistically grounded signal of uncertainty.

title: ShiftQAT: Quantization-Aware Training for the Numerical Contract of a Fixed-Function Edge CNN Accelerator
abstract: Fixed-function CNN accelerators make edge inference fast and energy-efficient, but they execute only networks that obey a precise numerical contract. On the MAX7800x family, this contract requires power-of-two, per-tensor, symmetric scales, 8-bit activations and biases, integer-only arithmetic, and one statically configured shift per layer. We present ShiftQAT, the quantization-aware training (QAT) flow we developed for this family, which produces networks satisfying the contract by construction. It is the default training path of ai8x-training, the family's open-source training toolchain. ShiftQAT resolves residual, concatenation, and weight-sharing dependencies so that activation scales propagate statically and each layer's requantization reduces to one offline-configured shift. It also trains weights and biases on a joint power-of-two grid that fits the 8-bit bias budget. Among the compared methods, only ShiftQAT satisfies all of the contract's scaling constraints, including signed 8-bit activation storage. Even so, on ImageNet it matches the W8A8 accuracy drop of less constrained QAT methods and stays within 2.9 percentage points of FP32 at W4A8. On MAX78002 silicon, ShiftQAT-trained MobileNetV2 and ResNet-18 classify ImageNet images in 14.6 and 8.4 ms at 5.1 and 2.8 mJ per inference.

title: Where, How, and When: Query-Guided Grounding for Video Understanding
abstract: Understanding video content requires reasoning at multiple levels of granularity, from identifying objects to interpreting their interactions and localizing when specific actions occur. This thesis studies three query-guided grounding tasks that answer where key objects are (object-level grounding), how they interact (relationship-level grounding), and when specific moments occur (moment-level grounding). For object-level grounding, we present QDETRv, a query-guided extension of the Detection Transformer for one-shot localization of unseen objects in videos, which combines query-context fusion, a memory module for temporal consistency, and unsupervised pretraining on synthetic object trajectories. We further propose the Temporal Object-Aware Vision Transformer (TOViT) for few-shot video object detection, which builds on a language-aligned open-set vision encoder and propagates high-confidence object features across frames. For relationship-level grounding, we introduce few-shot referring relationships in videos: given a (subject, predicate, object) query and a few support videos sharing the predicate, the entities are localized by optimizing a T-partite random field using a meta-learned relation network with query-conditioned translational embeddings, Global Semantic Aggregation, Local Localization Aggregation, and belief-propagation-based message passing. For moment-level grounding, we propose the Moment Alignment Transformer (MATR) for video-to-video moment retrieval, which uses dual-stage Dynamic Time Warping for pre- and post-fusion alignment, learnable queries for boundary prediction, and self-supervised pretraining with temporal augmentations; MATR also extends to text-to-video moment retrieval with performance comparable to, or better than, the state of the art. These contributions advance query-guided video understanding across spatial, relational, and temporal grounding.

title: Can Autonomous Vehicles Keep Their Cool? A Survey of Thermal Side-Channel and Perception Attacks
abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) couple safety-critical perception to thermally constrained compute. Interfaces built for night perception and package thermal reliability were never engineered as confidentiality boundaries, and closing one such path leaves the other intact. Physical adversaries can spoof thermal infrared (IR) sensors used for night driving, while unprivileged software co-tenants can fingerprint perception workloads from thermal, dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), and thermal event interrupt (TEI) telemetry required for package safety. These paths differ in mechanism and privilege; both exploit interfaces that AV stacks cannot disable without compromising Safety of the Intended Functionality (SOTIF). Classical microarchitectural and cyber-physical systems (CPS) surveys address cache timing, adversarial machine learning, and camera or LiDAR spoofing; no prior survey jointly frames physical thermal IR attacks and unprivileged silicon thermal telemetry as one residual-risk class. This survey systematizes thirteen representative works into thermal perception integrity, telemetry leakage, and model-information extraction, comparing them by privilege, timescale, co-tenancy, deployability, and AV relevance. We distinguish attack family from adversary class and map defenses to residual risk while thermal management remains operational. A commodity proxy supports the software co-tenant branch only; physical IR evidence comes from cited literature. We identify open problems in on-target automotive evaluation, fusion trust under IR spoofing, chiplet thermal coupling, capability-based telemetry, and standards-ready threat analysis, aiming to motivate co-design across sensors, operating systems, silicon, and automotive standards.

title: Sector-Specific Financial Sentiment Lexicons for Portuguese: Evidence from Brazilian Stock News
abstract: This paper investigates whether sector-specific financial sentiment lexicons improve the analysis of Brazilian stock-market news in Portuguese. We use 19,460 news items about 38 firms in the financial, electric, and manufacturing sectors, published between 2020 and 2025. Starting from OpLexicon, we build sector-specific lexicons through unsupervised expansion based on PMI and conditional word-polarity association. The lexicons are evaluated by lexical heterogeneity and through LSTM price forecasting. Results show sectoral variation and moderate classification performance, but limited predictive gains. Sentiment improves forecasting only in manufacturing, while other sectors do not benefit from its inclusion. The findings indicate that sector-specific lexicons are useful resources, although their predictive value are context dependent.

title: Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): An Adaptive Framework for Evidence-Grounded Question Answering
abstract: This paper presents a proposed Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) framework for adaptive, evidence-grounded question answering using large language models (LLMs). Unlike conventional single-pass RAG systems, the proposed framework incorporates query planning, retrieval, tool selection, evidence evaluation, answer generation, and self-reflection. The framework uses a bounded feedback loop to improve evidence retrieval when the initial results are insufficient or conflicting. It aims to produce answers supported by relevant source citations while communicating uncertainty when reliable evidence is unavailable. The paper discusses the system architecture, workflow, algorithmic control logic, evaluation methodology, security, privacy, and governance considerations. It also proposes evaluation metrics for answer quality, retrieval effectiveness, factual grounding, latency, computational cost, and component-level ablation studies. Potential applications include research assistance, document question answering, enterprise knowledge management, customer support, and data analysis. This work presents a conceptual framework and proposed evaluation plan. Implementation, benchmark experiments, and measured performance improvements are not reported. Keywords: Agentic RAG, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, AI Agents, Evidence-Grounded Question Answering, Adaptive Retrieval, Self-Reflection.

title: Quantitative Glandular Tissue Component Assessment on Breast Ultrasound Using an Anatomically Constrained Deep Learning Framework
abstract: Background/Objectives: Glandular tissue component (GTC) has been incorporated into BI-RADS v2025 as part of breast tissue composition assessment, but visual grading remains subjective and does not provide continuous quantification. We developed and evaluated an ROI-guided, anatomically constrained deep learning framework for quantitative GTC assessment on breast ultrasound. Reader performance was compared between unaided and AI-assisted sessions. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 421 ultrasound images from 114 women for model development and 150 women for clinical evaluation. The framework segmented fibroglandular tissue (FGT) and glandular tissue to calculate continuous GTC percentage and assign the corresponding image-derived P1–P4 category. Four model configurations were compared during model development using patient-level five-fold cross-validation. Standalone AI performance was evaluated against expert consensus. Two senior and two junior radiologists assessed the clinical cohort without and with AI assistance, separated by a 4-week washout period. Results: During model development, the anatomical constraint markedly improved anatomical consistency while quantitative error and segmentation performance remained comparable. In the clinical cohort, continuous GTC percentage showed an MAE of 3.88 percentage points and strong correlation with the reference percentage (Spearman ρ = 0.957, p < 0.001). evidence.abstract: Background/Objectives: Glandular tissue component (GTC) has been incorporated into BI-RADS v2025 as part of breast tissue composition assessment, but visual grading remains subjective and does not provide continuous quantification. Reader performance was compared between unaided and AI-assisted sessions. Methods: This retrospective single-center study included 421 ultrasound images from 114 women for model development and 150 women for clinical evaluation. The framework segmented fibroglandular tissue (FGT) and glandular tissue to calculate continuous GTC percentage and assign the corresponding image-derived P1–P4 category. Exact P1–P4 agreement was 78.0%, adjacent agreement was 99.3%, and weighted κ was 0.888. However, 26 of 36 reference P4 cases (72.2%) were underestimated. Exact agreement was significantly higher for all four readers in the second, AI-assisted session than in the first, unaided session (all p < 0.001). title: From Trajectories to Experience: A Survey of Experience-Driven LLM Agents
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents can plan, use tools, and recover from errors within a task, yet many carry little from one task to the next and repeat mistakes they have already resolved. The root cause is a lack of experience accumulation: trajectories record what failed and how the agent recovered, but this information is seldom turned into guidance for later tasks. Research on this capability spans reflection, agent memory, workflow learning, and skill acquisition, but these lines describe similar content in different terms and lack a common account of experience itself, leaving basic questions open: what counts as experience, how it should be accumulated, used, and revised, and how to tell whether it improves later behavior. This survey addresses these questions with a unified framework. We define agent experience as action-guiding information grounded in task trajectories and retained to guide later episodes where it applies, whether as a trajectory precedent, a semantic lesson, or a reusable procedure. We focus on explicitly accessible experience, including its use as a training signal for internalization into model parameters. We describe each unit of experience by its guidance, applicability conditions, execution evidence, and reliability evaluation, so that memory entries, workflows, and skills become directly comparable, and follow experience through four lifecycle functions---formation, organization, utilization, and maintenance---that determine how it is accumulated, used, and revised. To judge reported gains, we distinguish three improvement claims---fixed experience reuse, feedback-driven sustained improvement, and improvement of the learning mechanism---by the evidence each requires. Current studies most clearly support fixed experience reuse, chiefly on tasks with tests or reference answers; evidence for the other two claims remains partial. Our analysis yields recommendations for seven application settings and a central design principle: keep guidance connected to its applicability conditions and to the evidence that supports or challenges it. Finally, we outline eight open problems, from learning with human expert records to testing whether gains accumulate, toward agents whose improvement is cumulative, transferable, and correctable.
