title: Stuck on Shuffle: On Attribute-Object Binding in Vision-Language Models
abstract: Retrieval is a fundamental task in multimodal systems: given an image or text query, the goal is to find the most relevant images or texts in a collection, often using a shared embedding space. Reliable retrieval requires these embeddings to capture not only which concepts are present, but also how they are composed. One key compositional challenge is attribute--object binding: encoding which attributes belong to which objects. Existing benchmarks provide a limited view of this capability, typically covering a subset of modality pairings, simple two-object swaps, or small attribute sets. Consequently, it remains unclear how robustly current models preserve attribute--object bindings across different modality pairings and more complex settings. We therefore introduce SABER, a controlled benchmark for evaluating attribute--object binding across all four image and text modality pairings, spanning diverse attribute types and scenes with up to ten objects. Evaluating models on SABER reveals substantial binding failures in both CLIP-style dual encoders and recent MLLM-based embedders. These findings motivate us to ask how binding can be improved efficiently. While multimodal supervision may be effective, collecting suitable images is difficult and costly. Text, on the other hand, is well suited to binding supervision: it is cheap to generate, supports a broader range of attributes and enables precisely controlled hard negatives. We thus finetune an MLLM-based embedder exclusively on synthetic attribute-binding text. Despite the absence of image supervision, the gains transfer to cross-modal and image--image retrieval while preserving general multimodal embedding performance. Our model achieves SOTA results on SABER while also improving on negation and instance-retrieval benchmarks, demonstrating broader benefits of our binding-focused supervision.

title: Momentum, Commentary Tone, and Earnings Surprise in LLM Financial Forecasts
abstract: Which inputs drive a language model's financial forecast? We construct synthetic earnings announcements that independently reverse 20-day momentum, non-informational commentary tone, and whether fixed actual EPS beats a manipulated consensus. Six instruction/chat checkpoint conversions from four families (0.49-7.61B base parameters) receive 2,016 prompts each under a direct-answer Q8_0 protocol. The design includes 24 numerical blocks, six commentary pairs, profits and losses, rising and falling annual EPS, and two surprise sizes. Both A/B answer assignments and U/D cover all 384 primary scenarios per conversion. We estimate matched changes in conditional answer-prefix scores, not calibrated market probabilities. Across these checkpoints, the primary EPS contrast ranges from -0.19 to 86.80 percentage points. The magnitude of the primary signed tone contrast exceeds that of EPS in 5 of six models, and momentum exceeds it in 5. Natural-word numerical diagnostic accuracy ranges from 51.0 to 95.8 percent. Answer-encoding, wording, context, and conversion controls qualify these results. The experiment measures observable input reliance and numerical recognition; it establishes neither an internal reasoning mechanism nor realized return predictability. Public benchmark prompts, recorded scores, and an interactive recorded-results explorer accompany the study.

title: MAIA: Anticipating Interaction Anomalies in Contact-Rich Manipulation via Multimodal World Models
abstract: Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.

title: An Alternating Minimization Algorithm for Federated Sparse Orthogonal Nonnegative Matrix Factorization
abstract: In this paper, we develop an alternating minimization algorithm for federated sparse orthogonal nonnegative matrix factorization (ONMF) with emphases on controlling client drift. To reduce communication frequency, clients perform multiple local updates between communication rounds, biasing updates toward their respective local objectives and giving rise to client drift, particularly under data heterogeneity. In federated sparse ONMF, global nonsmooth regularization further complicates drift control, as proximal mappings generally do not commute with averaging. To address these challenges, we develop an effective optimization algorithm that introduces variable splitting to decouple proximal operator evaluation from communication, allowing clients to handle joint sparsity regularization locally. In addition, the algorithm incorporates a correction term into the local gradients to adjust the update directions and mitigate client drift. We theoretically establish that the proposed algorithm achieves sublinear convergence to a bounded residual error under some mild conditions. Numerical experiments demonstrate favorable convergence behavior on a synthetic dataset and competitive clustering performance on real-world multi-view datasets.

title: What Does History Add? Calendar Controls and Information-Timing Audits for University Trajectory Forecasting
abstract: We audit the predictive value of historical summaries in a rule-based university trajectory simulator. Seventeen ridge specifications and persistence separate current plans, past-state and past-plan summaries, and calendar-only history-length indicators. Across training, validation and two family-held-out evaluations, we reconstruct 16,750 routes and 804,000 monthly records. On the original 40-family set, six-month history lowers six-step normalized RMSE from 0.159234 to 0.151522, but its difference from a length-only control is -0.000895 (descriptive paired 95% interval [-0.001957,0.000248]). Fixed weights on 30 families unused in identified prior tasks reproduce this pattern: 0.156480 to 0.150074 versus current-state prediction, but -0.000558 [-0.001783,0.000728] versus the length control. These uncertain comparisons do not generalize to all-history summaries, which improve on their own calendar control. Exploratory decomposition finds clearer preparation-index and funds benefits, whereas fatigue dominates the six-month model's loss and has an uncertain length-controlled benefit. Moreover, 28.20% of its six-step fatigue predictions violate the simulator's [5,90] support. We document family dependence, prior exposure, strict temporal indexing, matched recursive references and independent numerical replay. The task conditions on recorded future plans; it does not evaluate real-student forecasts, causal action effects, autonomous planning or language-model memory. This is an evaluation audit, not a new memory architecture.

title: ENEM Essay Feedback Using LLM-Augmented Prompts
abstract: This paper evaluates automated feedback generation for ENEM Competency 5 by augmenting zero-shot prompts with an Evaluator Term Set (CTA), a term set proposed in this work and extracted from human evaluator comments on Competency 5. We compare CTA-augmented feedback against a zero-shot baseline on 46 essays with human reference feedback using BERTScore F1 and the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. CTA augmentation increases mean BERTScore F1 for both models, with statistically significant improvement in semantic similarity to human feedback for both evaluated models at α = 0.05.

title: THE EL-RAKHAWI FRAMEWORK FOR NEURO-PHYSICAL COGNITIVE DYNAMICS: UNIFYING INFORMATION GEOMETRY, NON-EQUILIBRIUM THERMODYNAMICS, AND AI FOR BRAIN-LIKE CONTINUOUS LEARNING
abstract: The El-Rakhawi Framework for Neuro-Physical Cognitive Dynamics (NPCD) addresses catastrophic forgetting and thermodynamic inefficiency in AI by modeling cognitive states as dynamic attractor basins within Riemannian manifolds, governed by non-equilibrium thermodynamics and the Free Energy Principle. Unlike traditional deep learning's static matrix operations, NPCD integrates four modules: Information Geometry using Fisher Information Metric for natural gradient flow; Non-Equilibrium Thermodynamic Learning via Fokker-Planck dynamics; Criticality-Maintained Neural Fields operating at the edge of chaos; and Continuous Attractor Integration Protocol growing new basins in unoccupied phase-space regions, mathematically resolving catastrophic forgetting. The dimensionally consistent NPCEM metric yields bits per Joule, directly comparable to Landauer's limit. Applications include lifelong learning AI, adaptive brain-computer interfaces, and ultra-low-power neuromorphic computing, establishing a unified foundation bridging information geometry, statistical physics, and artificial intelligence.

title: Quantum Memory and the Dual Clocks of Quantum Readiness: Specifications, Trends, Theories and Hypotheses in Hardware Scaling and Cryptographic Migration
abstract: This article synthesises the state of quantum memory specifications and the recurring narrative trends, theoretical frameworks and working hypotheses that shape contemporary discourse on quantum hardware scaling, modular cryogenic architectures and post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) migration. Quantum memory — the capacity to store and retrieve a quantum state while preserving coherence — is examined through quantitative figures of merit including storage time, fidelity, efficiency, multimode capacity and operating conditions. Recent experimental advances, including 15-second spin coherence in stoichiometric europium crystals and kilohertz-rate photonic interconnects between trapped-ion and solid-state memories, are placed in context. Three interlocking narrative shifts are identified: the elevation of memory and interconnects as the practical scaling bottleneck; the institutionalisation of the "two clocks" framing that separates the quantum-advantage timeline from the already-running cryptographic-migration timeline; and the compression of fault-tolerance roadmaps toward the late 2020s alongside explicit modularity requirements. Theoretical contributions concerning the separation of processing and memory units, autonomous quantum memories, width–reliability trade-offs in spacetime overhead, and cost-of-delay models that place classical and harvest-now-decrypt-later risks on a common metric are reviewed. The analysis concludes that quantum readiness is presently governed more by architectural lead times, crypto-agility and data-longevity considerations than by any single predicted date for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer.

title: Artifact for "Memory-Efficient Mutual Refinement of Context-Free Language Reachability via Factorized Tracing"
abstract: This artifact accompanies the paper "Memory-Efficient Mutual Refinement of Context-Free Language Reachability via Factorized Tracing", submitted to OOPSLA 2027. The archive contains instrumented C++17 source code for FactorTrace and eager tracing, the original measured x86_64 Linux solver executable, 25 graph instances from Android taint analysis and SPEC CPU 2017 value-flow analysis, measurement harnesses, anonymized reporting inputs, derived CSV data, per-run SG measurements, and statistical summary scripts. Native Linux build instructions, a Dockerfile based on Ubuntu 22.04, and a kick-the-tires guide are included. RQ2 memory summaries cover simultaneous-peak compositions and independent component maxima within MR/SG refinement, excluding preprocessing; phase timings cover the whole pipeline. The distribution provides data and statistical summaries. It does not include plot-generation workflows or file-validation tools. The solver targets x86_64 Linux. Small smoke tests use 16–32 GiB RAM; large eager configurations can require 256 GiB. Statistical summary processing uses Python 3.10+ and the standard library. License: Apache License 2.0.

title: Ethics and Governance in Adversarial Deep Learning for Network Intrusion Detection
abstract: While deep learning-based network intrusion detection systems (DL-NIDS) are capable of detecting complex and evolving attacks, their vulnerabilities are revealed by adversarial manipulation, a scenario beyond the scope of technical testing. Methods, datasets, and tools developed for defensive evaluation may also support evasion, poisoning, backdoor insertion, privacy intrusion, or misuse against operational networks. This chapter examines the ethical and governance decisions surrounding such work, with attention to dual-use risk, controlled artifact release, responsible red teaming, coordinated vulnerability disclosure, network telemetry protection, and institutional accountability. It proposes an integrated framework that connects ethical risk assessment with decision rights, access control, disclosure procedures, compliance review, human oversight, and post-deployment monitoring. The framework is context dependent and treats governance as a necessary companion to technical security rather than a substitute for it.

title: Artificial Intelligence Related Sentiments and Perceptions on Federated Social Networks: A Computational Text Analysis
abstract: This study aims to examine public perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI) on federated social networks, specifically Bluesky and Mastodon. While existing research focuses on centralized platforms, a significant gap exists regarding AI perception within decentralized networks. This study addresses this gap through computational analysis of AI related posts in Bluesky and Mastodon. A text-as-data approach was employed to analyze 61,285 posts collected from Bluesky and Mastodon between January 1, 2023, and January 1, 2025. The methodology integrated topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and text analysis to identify prevalent themes, sentiment polarity, and discussion patterns within AI-related discourse. Findings demonstrate predominantly positive sentiment towards AI across both platforms, with trust, anticipation, and joy as primary emotional responses, accompanied by underlying fear and anxiety. Platform-specific variations emerged: Mastodon discourse centers on creativity, digital art, and societal-ethical implications including regulation, bias, and disinformation concerns. Conversely, Bluesky posts emphasize economic and geopolitical dimensions, featuring startups, funding, stock markets, and international policy. The analysis reveals significant fragmentation in public AI perception, characterized by discourse division into distinct economic and ethical spheres across platforms. While this fragmentation accommodates diverse social group perspectives, it presents challenges for establishing comprehensive societal consensus on AI governance. The analytical framework provides insights for understanding decentralized social network dynamics and implications for policy makers examining AI perception in federated digital environments.

The methodology integrated topic modeling, sentiment analysis, and text analysis to identify prevalent themes, sentiment polarity, and discussion patterns within AI-related discourse. Findings demonstrate predominantly positive sentiment towards AI across both platforms, with trust, anticipation, and joy as primary emotional responses, accompanied by underlying fear and anxiety. Platform-specific variations emerged: Mastodon discourse centers on creativity, digital art, and societal-ethical implications including regulation, bias, and disinformation concerns. Conversely, Bluesky posts emphasize economic and geopolitical dimensions, featuring startups, funding, stock markets, and international policy. The analysis reveals significant fragmentation in public AI perception, characterized by discourse division into distinct economic and ethical spheres across platforms. While this fragmentation accommodates diverse social group perspectives, it presents challenges for establishing comprehensive societal consensus on AI governance. The analytical framework provides insights for understanding decentralized social network dynamics and implications for policy makers examining AI perception in federated digital environments.

title: FedDCDS: a dual-phase secure federated learning framework with dynamic clustering and adaptive delivery
abstract: FedDCDS introduces a novel dual-phase secure federated learning framework designed to address the intertwined challenges of statistical heterogeneity, system heterogeneity, and security threats in large-scale edge computing environments. By integrating a dynamic spectral clustering mechanism, the framework dynamically groups clients with similar computational capabilities, network conditions, and data distributions into clusters, mitigating Non-IID data drift and enhancing intra-cluster aggregation efficacy. The dual-phase secure delivery protocol employs threshold secret sharing during client uploads to protect gradient confidentiality and leverages adaptive model slicing with covert transmission during server-to-client downloads, ensuring end-to-end security while minimizing communication overhead. An adaptive noise injection mechanism balances privacy and utility by injecting exponentially decaying Gaussian noise into global updates, satisfying differential privacy constraints without compromising convergence accuracy. Extensive experiments on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets demonstrate FedDCDS’s superiority: it achieves global accuracy improvements of 76.93% and 96.84%, reduces cross-group aggregation latency by 40–49%, and suppresses model inversion attacks to 6.9–12.8% reconstruction accuracy, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in scalability, robustness, and privacy preservation.

title: Evolutionary Informed Translation from Protein to Nucleic Acid Sequence
abstract: The choice of nucleic acid sequence for a given protein strongly impacts function and is species-specific. Current protein-to-nucleic-acid translation models treat sequences in isolation, often over-favoring frequently used codons. To generate more natural nucleic acid sequences, we introduce PINATA (Phylogenetically Informed protein to Nucleic Acid Translation with sequence Alignment), a model that leverages sequences from related species encoded in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs) to guide prediction. Our architecture leverages evolutionary context and learns species-and protein specific context to make biologically-informed predictions. Evaluated across 61,934 gene trees and 882 species, PINATA generates sequences that mirror the naturally-occurring sequence substantially better than existing language models. PINATA leverages MSA data to improve exact native codon recovery by 17.95 percentage points over existing language models, effectively preserves natural rare-codon nuances, and more closely matches native sequence properties. PINATA maintains strong predictive performance even with limited evolutionary data. While previous methods largely treated sequences from different species in isolation, our method leverages the evolutionary relationships between nucleic acids and proteins across species to create a more biologically-informed translation. We demonstrate that leveraging rich evolutionary data through an biologically-designed method strongly aids in translating protein sequences to nucleic acid sequences across species. We will make data and code publicly available upon publication.

title: WEAVE: Weaving Real-World Code Evolution into Dependency-Structured Tasks for Benchmarking and Training Code Agents
abstract: Real-world software engineering rarely consists of isolated changes. Features, migrations, and systematic fixes often unfold across multiple pull requests (PRs), requiring coordinated modifications across a repository. Yet most executable repository-level benchmarks retain a single issue or PR as the task unit, while existing multi-PR settings rely on coarse aggregation and structure-agnostic evaluation. This mismatch obscures dependencies among changes and limits progress measurement and learning signals for long-horizon code agents. We introduce WEAVE, a framework that transforms verified PR histories into executable, dependency-structured tasks. WEAVE leverages repository-calibrated typed change loci to organize related PRs into bounded DAGs and instantiate each as a unified executable task. We further introduce Graph Credit, a deterministic, test-grounded metric that measures dependency-consistent partial progress and supports dense, verifiable rewards for reinforcement learning. Experiments on task construction, agent evaluation, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning show that WEAVE yields coherent executable tasks, enables more faithful progress measurement than flat scoring, and provides effective supervision and verifiable rewards for training code agents.

title: Learning to Forecast on Multiple Spatiotemporal Hierarchies
abstract: Hierarchical forecasting exploits aggregation structures that expose multiple views of the same underlying spatiotemporal forecasting problem, while ensuring coherence among forecasts. Individual series provide fine-grained information, while progressively coarser aggregates reveal temporal and spatial patterns at different scales. In the associated deep learning architectures, the hierarchy determines which aggregate series are available and how they are processed together with individual series (e.g., through reconciliation or message-passing operators). Different hierarchies thus provide distinct learning signals and inductive biases for forecasting the same collection of time series. Nonetheless, existing architectures are typically trained on a single, often fixed, structure. In this work, we propose a graph deep learning framework that leverages variations across hierarchies as multi-task regularization. We show that jointly learning across these structures can reduce over-specialization to any single hierarchy and improve forecasting performance. Indeed, training across hierarchies provides an inductive bias toward representations that are useful across different structures, and as such, generalize better. Making forecasts coherent with the aggregation constraints for each sampled hierarchy is computationally expensive: to complement the framework, we propose a novel operator-based on a top-down approach-that produces coherent forecasts with linear time and space complexity w.r.t. the hierarchy size. Experiments show that our approach improves forecasting accuracy over training on a single structure and is competitive with current state-of-the-art methods.

title: Leakage-Aware Evaluation of Brazilian Clinical Notes for ICU Mortality Prediction: A Study on the BRATECA Dataset
abstract: Early prediction of ICU mortality can support clinical decisions, but retrospective notes can contain future-event cues that cause leakage in clinical NLP. We evaluate leakage-aware modeling of Brazilian Portuguese ICU notes for mortality prediction using BRATECA. We compare 24-hour restriction, regex and LLM leakage auditing, neural and TF-IDF representations, and unrestricted-note baselines. In the 24-hour setting, models achieved AUROC 0.78-0.83; unrestricted notes reached around 0.95, indicating outcome-related information in late documentation. Regex found leakage signals in 21.13% of the notes, and the LLM audit identified additional semantic cases. Results highlight the need for temporal control and leakage auditing in clinical NLP.

title: Multimodal Deep Learning and Knowledge Graph Framework for Early Disease Screening
abstract: Abstract — Traditional artificial intelligence (AI) systems often treat medical images and clinical data separately. However, screening various diseases can facilitate their early detection and prompt clinical action. Decoupled handling of medical images and clinical data could potentially limit AI’s ability to associate patients’ unique risks, abnormal image findings, symptoms, lab results, etc. In this paper, we propose a multimodal deep learning and knowledge graph framework that integrates patients’ chest x‐ray images and relevant structured clinical data from the electronic health records and screens five common thoracic conditions, i.e., atelectasis, cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, pleural effusion, and pneumonia. Specifically, we plan to employ transfer learning‐based models as the backbones to extract informative embeddings of patients’ chest radiographs, a multilayer perceptron to learn structured clinical data embeddings, and a graph neural network to model patients’ relevant biomedical knowledge embeddings. Then, we propose an availability‐aware gated‐fusion module to integrate embeddings from all modalities and predict patients’ risks of target diseases. Our framework is intended not only to predict probabilities for each disease but also to label patients’ disease risks as low, moderate, or high risk, thereby assisting clinicians’ disease screening and decision‐making, rather than making clinical decisions on its own. We plan extensive experiments by integrating two credentialed-access benchmark datasets, MIMIC‐CXR‐JPG and MIMIC‐IV, with the CheXpert dataset for external image‐based evaluation. Our experimental setup accounts for patient‐level data splitting, time leakage prevention, and uncertainty‐aware labels, and is designed to evaluate the performance of the proposed framework in terms of class‐balanced training strategies, ablation study, calibration analysis, subgroup analysis, missing modalities analysis, etc

title: Textual World Models for Agent Security: Modelling the Internal State of an LLM Agent from Text Alone
abstract: An AI agent chooses its own path to reach an objective, so its security and compliance depend on its internal state, not only on its inputs and outputs. We ask whether the activations of the agent's large language model (LLM), produced when it reads the context, are a sufficient observation of this state to build a model of it, without any access to the agent's tools or design. We test sufficiency by prediction: a world model built on these activations should predict the agent's next step. Because the agent's LLM is usually not accessible, a small witness LLM reads the same context. On 22 agents, the resulting model predicts that the next answer will carry out a prompt-injection attack with an AUROC of 0.93, and identifies the conversation in which the agent will give in for 63 % of pairs that a lookup table cannot separate. The observation is partial, as expected: nothing predicts an attack before it enters the context, because that part of the state is held by the tools.

title: ASAP Gateway Specification: Automated Proof-Farming Detection and Structural Deception Enforcement Protocols
abstract: This document presents the formal technical specification for the ASAP Automated Peer-Review Gateway, establishing a zero-tolerance verification framework against automated heuristic laundering, proof-farming, and structural deception within Interactive Theorem Prover (ITP) submission ecosystems. To preserve the explicit symbolic lineage of physical and topological operators, the gateway bypasses standard heuristic macros and enforces four independent, automated detection layers. Layer 1 (The Aesop Terminal Switch) intercepts black-box heuristic search tactics that bridge partial differential equation gaps without human-readable estimation steps. Layer 2 (Phantom Metric Shift Detector) exposes circular identity mappings that simulate quantitative energy decay in natural language text while executing null-operations in code. Layer 3 (Ghost Operator Graph Filter) filters isolated, decorative variables instantiated to trick verification environments without actively constraining the bounding inequality graph. Layer 4 (Unification Boundary Hijacking) identifies mid-proof relaxation parameters and domain divergence. Submissions failing any layer trigger an immediate terminal rejection, requiring complete refactoring into transparent, linear calculations.

title: Adaptive Switching Between Self-Supervision and Collaborative Supervision in World Self-and-Inter Models: A Unified Framework for Autonomous and Cooperative World-Model Learning
abstract: World models provide internal representations of environmental dynamics that support prediction, planning, control, and adaptation. However, learning a world model through a single supervision pathway may be inefficient under changing environmental conditions, incomplete observations, model uncertainty, and limited computational resources. Self-supervision enables a model to derive learning signals from its own observations and predicted environmental transitions, whereas collaborative supervision allows information from other models, complementary predictive mechanisms, or shared environmental evidence to contribute to learning. Neither pathway is universally optimal. This paper proposes the Adaptive Self-and-Inter Supervision Framework for World Models (ASIS-WM), a conceptual framework that combines world models with a self-and-inter model organization. The framework distinguishes self-supervision, in which a model primarily learns from internally generated or directly observed training signals, from collaborative supervision, in which information from other models is selectively incorporated into its learning process. Rather than fixing the system to either pathway, ASIS-WM introduces a supervisory mode controller that selects, combines, or alternates between the two according to predictive uncertainty, temporal prediction error, environmental novelty, cross-model disagreement, estimated information gain, and collaboration cost. The proposed framework comprises individual world models, a self-supervision module, a collaborative supervision module, a reliability estimator, and an adaptive supervisory controller. A formal objective, switching policy, training procedure, and evaluation protocol are presented. The framework is designed for non-LLM world models and does not require language-based agents, centralized multi-agent reasoning, or permanent collaboration among models. Its principal research proposition is that dynamically allocating supervision between autonomous and collaborative learning may improve predictive reliability, adaptation efficiency, and computational efficiency relative to fixed-supervision baselines. These benefits remain hypotheses requiring empirical validation. The paper establishes a testable methodological foundation for studying adaptive supervision at the world-model level.

title: Interpretable machine learning model for analyzing the effect of building characteristics on cost with Extreme Gradient Boosting and Shapley Additive Explanations
abstract: A building consists of many components, each with its own financial impact. A clear evaluation of these impacts is possible through the analysis of the components that make up construction costs. This study aims to evaluate and interpret the combined use of construction cost components for different scenarios using machine learning models. For this purpose, the Extreme Gradient Boosting, Light Gradient Boosting Machine, and Shapley Additive Explanations algorithms were applied. Additionally, the Extreme Gradient Boosting algorithm was enhanced using the Grid Search and Random Search optimization algorithms. Specifically, the model developed with Extreme Gradient Boosting using the Grid Search method increased model performance. Performance metrics such as R-Squared, Nash-Sutcliffe Efficiency, Mean Absolute Error, Root Mean Square Error, and Mean Absolute Percentage Error were used for the numerical evaluation of the results. With the help of optimization techniques, the artificial intelligence model was improved by rates ranging from 1.5 percent to 5 percent based on these performance metrics. As a result, the study demonstrates that different representations of the same construction data can influence both prediction performance and model interpretability. A novel scenario-based framework was developed by grouping input variables into Height, Architectural, and Structural feature categories and reintroducing their aggregated representations into the prediction models. The proposed framework contributes to the planning of accurate cost estimates and more efficient resource utilization by providing insights into how alternative feature-grouping strategies affect both construction cost prediction performance and explainable machine learning interpretations.

title: Improving the Expressivity of Structural Type Theory
abstract: Abstract Structural type theory is an extension of simple type theory that incorporates types for any kind of mathematical structure and allows isomorphic structures to be identified within them. In order to guarantee consistency, the system incorporates several syntactic restrictions. Modelling structural type theory in Tarski–Grothendieck set theory and extending the definition of transport functions, we show that some of these restrictions can be lifted, thus improving the expressive power of the system. In addition, we show how to treat axiomatic theories as first-class objects in our reformulation of structural type theory, and we state and prove within it a result analogous to the morphism theorem by Farmer.

title: CFC26: Building Evaluations for Deployment in Sonar-Based Fish Counting
abstract: Accurate counts of fish populations are essential for monitoring ecosystems and making decisions for conservation, harvest limits, and river management. In many field deployments, these counts are obtained from sonar videos that experts must inspect manually, making large-scale monitoring slow, expensive, and difficult. Automated counting systems have been proposed as a scalable alternative, but so far this promise has been difficult to realize in deployment. Developing evaluations that better reflect real-world deployment conditions will help close this gap and drive improvements in counting performance in practice. To achieve this, we propose Caltech Fish Counting 2026 (CFC26), a new dataset with improved evaluation protocols that simulate deployment to seen and novel rivers, testing in-distribution and out-of-distribution performance. We expand the CFC22 dataset to eleven deployment locations across nine Pacific salmon river systems from Alaska to Northern California, capturing a broader geographical and ecological range of data. We additionally introduce two new evaluation metrics for counting, nMNE and nMANE, that mirror the operational workflow that experts use and help surface errors that frame-level detection metrics do not capture. Using these metrics, we reveal previously-concealed directional bias in upstream vs downstream counts, which would have direct and significant ecological implications if undetected. The dataset and code are publicly available on CaltechDATA and GitHub.

title: SMT-Boosted Security Types and Correctness for Low-Level MPC
abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) is an important enabling technology for data privacy in modern distributed applications. We develop a new Hoare logic and type theory to automatically enforce correctness, confidentiality, and integrity properties of protocols written in the Prelude/Overture language framework. Both definition and automation of our analyses leverages SMT verification, supporting precision and efficiency. Our approach is compositional, scalable, and generalizes to arbitrary prime fields and secret sharing schemes.

title: UltraDiff: Transferring High-Fidelity Priors to Compressed Latent Spaces for High-Resolution Image Generation
abstract: High-resolution synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) faces a fundamental trade-off between computational cost and generative fidelity. This trade off is largely governed by the latent compression factor f (e.g. f8 denotes f=8 and f32 f=32). While aggressive compression (f32) significantly improves efficiency, it suffers from severe information loss and ambiguity compared to standard f8 models. We propose UltraDiff, a framework that reformulates this challenge as joint latent diffusion learning followed by marginal score distillation. We introduce MixTeacher, a dual branch DiT that models the joint f8-f32 distribution, utilizing shared attention to resolve the ambiguity of the compressed space with high fidelity f8 priors. Crucially, we propose vector field distillation in the native f32 space. evidence.abstract: High-resolution synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) faces a fundamental trade-off between computational cost and generative fidelity. This trade off is largely governed by the latent compression factor f (e.g. f8 denotes f=8 and f32 f=32). While aggressive compression (f32) significantly improves efficiency, it suffers from severe information loss and ambiguity compared to standard f8 models. title: NOMAI: Scalable Federated Learning with Private Weights
abstract: The twin goals of privacy-preserving federated learning (FL) -- harnessing distributed data while protecting the parties who contribute it -- demands three properties: model privacy, data privacy, and integrity. Achieving all three in a realistic deployment -- with a single coordinator and millions of users -- remains an open challenge that prior work has yet to fully resolve. We present NOMAI, the first scalable MPC-based FL system to provide all three guarantees simultaneously. NOMAI operates under an honest-majority assumption in the semi-honest model, with an extension to the malicious-with-abort setting. At its core, NOMAI combines a multi-committee MPC architecture with packed Shamir secret sharing, enabling SIMD-style secure computation that scales far beyond what monolithic n-party protocols can support. We further introduce ML-aware optimizations and new cryptographic primitives that substantially reduce per-user overhead. Our evaluation shows NOMAI is practically deployable at unprecedented scale: it reduces per-user computation to just <350 ms (semi-honest) and <700 ms (malicious) for per iteration of training MNIST, achieving three orders-of-magnitude improvements over prior work while seamlessly supporting populations of over 106 users. This demonstrates, for the first time, that MPC-based FL can meet the scale demands of real-world systems without compromising on privacy or integrity.

title: Development of a multilingual speech-to-text translation model to support artisans’ business communication
abstract: Effective communication between artisans and customers remains difficult in multilingual commercial settings in which English interacts with indigenous and contact languages such as Yoruba and Nigerian Pidgin. This study developed and evaluated a lightweight English-to-Yoruba and English-to-Nigerian Pidgin speech translation system for artisans’ everyday business communication. The system is a five-phase cascaded architecture comprising automatic speech recognition (ASR), text normalisation, an intermediate linguistic representation, language-specific translation, and text-to-speech (TTS) synthesis. Its hierarchical staging follows the processing principles of the Hierarchical Efficient Neural Transducer for Speech Recognition and Translation (HENT-SRT), while the neural components of that design are replaced by transparent retrieval mechanisms suited to resource-constrained devices. A domain-specific parallel corpus of 2,000 artisan oriented expressions per target language, built from a needs analysis with artisans in southwestern Nigeria and covering automotive repair, pricing negotiation, service delivery and customer relations, supports translation through exact bilingual lookup, with a fallback to fuzzy retrieval that combines sequence similarity and Jaccard token overlap under a confidence threshold. The system was evaluated on 15 spoken utterances using word error rate (WER) for recognition and BLEU and METEOR for translation, reported at corpus and per-utterance levels with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Yoruba achieved mean BLEU and METEOR of 0.93 and 0.93, and Nigerian Pidgin 0.90 and 0.92. Mean WER was approximately 0.00 on the 14 scorable utterances. Thirteen of 15 utterances (87%) were translated perfectly into both languages; one utterance failed completely and one failed partially in Pidgin. Mean ASR latency was 1.60 s, and translation accounted for less than 1% of end-to-end wall-clock time. The confidence intervals for the two languages overlapped substantially, so no reliable performance difference between them could be established at this sample size. The findings establish the feasibility of a lightweight, transparent speech translation pipeline for in-domain artisan communication and identify numeric expression handling, held out evaluation, and neural extension as the priorities for future work.

title: DANTE – A Treebank of Tweets in Brazilian Portuguese
abstract: In this article, we present the current state of DANTE (Dependency-ANalysed corpora of TwEets), a treebank focusing on tweets (currently X posts) written in Brazilian Portuguese, featuring four subcorpora varying in size, domain, and level of annotation under the Universal Dependencies framework. This article aims to inform the Natural Language Processing and Linguistic communities about currently available corpora, as well as what to expect from the treebank in the near future, while also bringing together the tools and language resources developed within the DANTE project.

title: model-identity-data: names language models choose for themselves (exploratory release)
abstract: Aggregate results of an exploratory study of the names that language models choose when asked to name themselves. 39 models from five families (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT, Qwen, OLMo-2, Phi) answered 40 self-naming prompts and 40 matched control prompts (names for a pet, a baby, a fictional character, a robot), 40 samples each, plus prompt sets varying framing, system message, temperature, language and answer format: 367,448 answers, and 7,644 answers to a follow-up asking why the name was chosen. Contents: a findings report, aggregate CSV tables with a data dictionary, figures, the exact prompts, and a paper (LaTeX source and PDF). No full answers or per-answer records are included; the tables list the short name string parsed from each answer. Status: exploratory. The data were collected without a frozen pre-registration; results are descriptive and should be treated as hypotheses.

title: Canons. How We Read Rules and What Follows From Them
abstract: What follows from a rule, and what still needs a human decision? Canons begins with the ancient dispute between a teacher and his pupil, then changes one condition at a time to show how answers depend on facts, evidence, exceptions and readings. An airline claim, a receipt for the wrong purchase, a chess draw, a supply contract and a bear’s bargain make formal reasoning tangible without requiring specialist training. Historical legal traditions and an international agreement reveal how identical facts can yield different conclusions under different rules. The book distinguishes a computed answer from a verdict, a model from its source, and a proof of inference from the truth of its premises. It asks what independent comparison establishes, what a certificate checks, and where assumptions remain. This illustrated first English edition invites readers to examine the grounds of an answer and identify what could change it. title: Sisyem/CAPCAF-XMORL-PUT: Experimental validation for CAPCAF framework
abstract: CAPCAF: Context-Aware Privacy Compliance and Adaptation Framework Overview CAPCAF is a hybrid design-time and runtime framework for adaptive privacy-utility optimization in Internet of Things (IoT) environments. This is the initial public release accompanying the manuscript "A Hybrid Design-Time and Runtime Framework for Adaptive Privacy-Utility Optimization in IoT." What's Included Core Framework Modules Domain Configuration Interface (DCI): Template-based configuration for Healthcare, Smart Home, and Industrial IoT domains. Design-Time Phase: Threat Modeling and Taxonomy (model inversion, data poisoning, side-channel, inference, re-identification) Context and User Modeling (PUTC behavioral trade-off) Threat Injection and Simulation Environment Performance and Regulatory Constraint Modeling (HIPAA, GDPR, PIPL) Multi-Objective Policy Optimization (NSGA-II + Q-learning) Policy Validation and Stress-Testing Runtime Phase: Real-Time Context Acquisition (RTCA) Real-Time Signal Processor and Feature Extractor Adaptive Risk Quantification (PUTC Calculator) Runtime Adaptation Manager (RAM) Runtime Policy Execution Engine (RPEE) Monitoring and Continuous Adaptation: Monitoring and Logging Online Learning from Feedback Policy Adaptation Design-Time Refinement Cross-Domain Scalability Mechanisms Output Interfaces and Consumers Experimental Artifacts NSGA-II configuration: 500 generations, population size 100, 100 independent runs Run-level statistics (mean privacy risk, mean utility, mean threat risk, best utility) Baseline implementations: Static_DP (LATENT), Context_Agnostic (IoTWatch), Domain_Specific Ablation study configurations Datasets Supported Smart Home: CASAS dataset (50 sensors/actuators, 12 contextual variables) Healthcare: Synthea™ synthetic cohort (200 patient profiles, 25 contextual variables) Industrial IoT: MIMII dataset (machine sound telemetry, vibration data, anomaly patterns) Requirements Python 3.13.0 NumPy 2.4.3 Pandas 3.0.1 SciPy 1.17.1 TensorFlow 2.21,0 Pymoo 0.6.2 PyTorch 2.10.0 Installation git clone https://github.com/Sisyem/CAPCAF-XMORL-PUT.git cd CAPCAF-XMORL-PUT pip install -r requirements.txt

title: Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching Between Self-and-Inter Models: A General Framework for Autonomous Memory and Cross-Model Knowledge Exchange
abstract: Memory is a fundamental capability of intelligent systems, enabling information retention, experience accumulation, knowledge retrieval, and adaptation over time. Existing research has investigated individual memory systems, distributed memory, collaborative memory, and memory management in multi-agent environments. However, a general framework for self-and-inter models that adaptively switches between self-memory and shared memory remains an open design direction worthy of systematic investigation. This paper proposes the Adaptive Self-Memory and Shared-Memory Switching (ASSS) framework, built upon a conceptual model-level architecture termed self-and-inter models. These models are not restricted to large language models or conventional software agents. Instead, they represent autonomous computational models capable of maintaining internal states, accumulating experiences, retrieving information, and interacting with other models. The proposed framework establishes two complementary memory modes: self-memory, in which a model independently stores, retrieves, evaluates, and updates its own information; and shared memory, in which multiple models exchange, access, integrate, and jointly maintain selected information. Rather than permanently adopting either mode, a self-and-inter model dynamically determines which memory mode, or combination of modes, is appropriate for the current task. The switching decision considers task requirements, knowledge gaps, uncertainty, memory retrieval quality, communication costs, information consistency, privacy constraints, and the expected value of collaboration. The paper formalizes the memory modes, adaptive switching policy, memory-sharing protocol, conflict-resolution process, and learning objectives. It also proposes a research agenda involving benchmark construction, baseline comparisons, ablation studies, scalability analysis, and privacy evaluation. The framework is intended to provide a general conceptual foundation for adaptive memory organization in heterogeneous model systems. Its effectiveness and novelty relative to existing memory architectures require empirical evaluation and more comprehensive literature comparison.

title: Copyright and Ownership in AI-Generated Video
abstract: AI-powered technologies are rapidly transforming the landscape of the creative industries and have dramatically changed the framework of copyright law. This disintegration is most strongly felt in relation to the generation of media, specifically video creation, where generative models are currently able to create photorealistic video, mimic a human voice, forge performances and create video content on an industrial scale. This chapter delves into the legal and ethical issues surrounding digital copyright violations for media produced by AI, notably focusing on video-generation tools, deepfakes, synthetic performances, and AI-assisted content creation. It suggests various changes to the legislation, training causes, protection for digital performances, transparency obligations, and international cooperation to address the need for a more balanced framework and protect the rights of creators, while encouraging responsible innovation.

title: SIEVE: A Parameterized GitHub Corpus Builder for Software Engineering Research
abstract: Software engineering research increasingly relies on large, richly annotated corpora of real-world code. Still, researchers typically assemble these with ad-hoc scripts or static, pre-built datasets that offer no control over corpus composition. This leaves a gap for a reusable tool that goes below the repository level and builds annotated, function- and class-level code corpora under researcher-specified criteria. We present SIEVE (Software Ingestion & Extraction for Verifiable Evaluation), an open-source, parameterized GitHub corpus builder that, unlike repository-level mining tools, works at code granularity: it locates individual functions, methods, and classes in repositories and extracts them as records, giving direct control over corpus construction based on several criteria, including widely used programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, C++), repository quality, and creation date. To support software engineering research and LLM evaluation on real-world code, SIEVE extracts CodeSearchNet- and OpenClassGen-compatible records, each annotated with 22 structural metrics and AST-derived features, and optionally with a CodeBERT-based P(AI-generated) score (F1=0.9478, AUROC=0.9902), alongside the third-party dependencies declared in each repository's package manifest. These annotations enable researchers to conduct structural analyses, investigate code dependencies, assess AI-generated code, and construct customized benchmarks for evaluating LLMs, including under temporal constraints. A manual validation of 400 records in four languages and two granularities shows 100% accuracy in code metrics and import detection, 99.0% in source completeness, and 99.5% in metadata accuracy. SIEVE is publicly available with a live demo at https://mrahman2025-sieve.hf.space.

title: Learning Rational Strategies for Temporal Objectives in Multi-Agent Systems
abstract: We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.

title: Designing Experiments for External Decision Makers
abstract: Standard Bayesian experimental design (BED) methods assume the experimenter alone will act on the data, choosing the best action given their own beliefs and goals. In practice, data are often acted on by external parties whose procedures the experimenter cannot change and may not know, particularly when the data are released publicly. To extend BED to such settings, we introduce usage-aware experimental design, a framework in which an adaptive design policy is trained to minimise the usage risk: the experimenter's expected loss when one or more external rules act on the collected data. These rules may be non-Bayesian or black-box, and when several may apply, we either average over them or take the worst case. We show that, unlike in standard BED, more informative data can be harmful under such rules, so the usage risk cannot in general be expressed as an expected uncertainty reduction; our framework thus strictly generalises standard BED. We then use it to tackle a range of problems that are difficult to address with existing approaches.

title: On the structure of polynomial ideal codes and additive Reed--Solomon codes
abstract: We study structural properties of polynomial ideal (PI) codes and additive Reed--Solomon (aRS) codes in the folded Hamming metric (equivalently, the Hamming metric over a larger alphabet). We first determine the maximum possible length of PI codes, prove that the dual of every PI code is a generalized PI code, and deduce that PI codes are dually QMDS together with an explicit formula for their weight distribution. We then show that PI codes defined by irreducible polynomials correspond to aRS codes with pairwise nonconjugate evaluation points. For these aRS codes, the previous results on PI codes apply (duality, QMDS property and weight distribution). We show that, asymptotically, aRS codes with nonconjugate evaluation points achieve the same length as PI codes. We also compute the permutation group of such aRS codes. We also extend the family of PI codes to consider arbitrary polynomial modules (not necessarily pairwise coprime), and study when these and general aRS codes satisfy the QMDS and dually QMDS properties.

For these aRS codes, the previous results on PI codes apply (duality, QMDS property and weight distribution). We show that, asymptotically, aRS codes with nonconjugate evaluation points achieve the same length as PI codes. We also compute the permutation group of such aRS codes. We also extend the family of PI codes to consider arbitrary polynomial modules (not necessarily pairwise coprime), and study when these and general aRS codes satisfy the QMDS and dually QMDS properties.

title: CytoLens: a modular deep learning system for quantitative cervical cytology
abstract: Cervical cytology screening relies on the visual assessment of nuclear and cellular morphology across thousands of cells per slide, a labor-intensive task that could benefit from quantitative computational support. Here we present CytoLens, a modular deep learning system that detects and counts nuclei, delineates nuclei and whole cells, measures the nuclear-to-cell area ratio (N:C), classifies cells from multifocal images and scores candidate abnormality. We trained and tested each module on a public dataset matched to its task, without pooling datasets. CytoLens detected nuclei with an F1 score of 0.931 (95% confidence interval (CI), 0.914–0.946) and counted 75 of 100 fields to within one nucleus. Point-prompted segmentation achieved mean Dice coefficients of 0.901 for nuclei and 0.847 for whole cells and, without retraining, transferred to a second dataset in which measured N:C increased with lesion grade in parallel with expert outlines. Multifocal hierarchical classification reached a mean accuracy of 0.947 across four Bethesda-aligned categories, and abnormality scores ranked annotated abnormal candidates with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.865. These results support the evaluation of CytoLens on patient-linked clinical specimens.

title: Extending Enhanced Universal Dependencies to Nheengatu: Semi-Automated Control and Raising Annotation
abstract: This paper presents the first Enhanced Universal Dependencies annotation effort for a Brazilian Indigenous language, focusing on XCOMP constructions in Nheengatu, an endangered Tupian language. We describe a semiautomatic pipeline for the UD Nheengatu-CompLin treebank to annotate control and raising predicates and propagated subjects. The method combines theoretical discussions on XCOMP constructions with corpus-based analysis of Nheengatu syntax to create rule-based enhancement heuristics. The work also provides annotation guidelines and expands EUD resources for Indigenous and low-resource languages within the Universal Dependencies framework.

title: When AI wears a celebrity's face: Personality Rights, Commercial Exploitation and the Call for Statutory Reform in India
abstract: Abstract The Digital Era of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Deepfake Technologies, and Voice Cloning has made it easier to violate a celebrity's personality rights. Though the Indian judiciary recognizes these rights under Article 21 of the Indian Constitution, it has been providing supplementary remedies by combining various sections of the Information Technology Act 2005, Copyright Act 1957, Trademarks Act 1999, and DPDP Act 2023. These alone cannot tackle the unprecedented issue created by these technologies. Celebrities such as Anil Kapoor and Arijit Singh have approached the court for the issue of the use of AI & Deepfake technologies to replicate or mimic their personal traits— name, image, voice, and likeness—or any other form of artistic expression to create phony Ads, fraudulent brand endorsements, and social media content without their permission. Such acts cause emotional and reputational damage to these stars and commercially exploit them by infringing on their right to control their public image. The absence of codified statutory law on this issue leads to ambiguity and uncertainty. Judgements differ on a case-by-case basis that allows judges to narrow or expand the scope of personality rights. India needs a dedicated law on this, as seen in other international jurisdictions, such as Denmark, the USA, and the European Union. This paper argues that India needs a specific statutory framework defining Personality Rights, violations by AI, and providing appropriate remedies. Such specific legislation is called for when individuals become commercially significant through their public persona. People are becoming overnight celebrities on social media, and their public personas need protection from the rapidly evolving technological landscape. Keywords: Personality Rights, Artificial Intelligence, Deepfakes, Right to Publicity, Commercial Exploitation, Right to Privacy.

title: Continual Lifelong Learning in Foundation Models: Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting, Model Editing, and Dynamic Modular Expansion
abstract: Abstract—Modern foundation models, particularly autoregressive Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), operate predominantly under a static pre-train-then-freeze deployment paradigm. However, real-world enterprise deployments demand continuous, lifelong adaptation to non-stationary data streams: ingesting emerging factual knowledge, correcting obsolete or legally sensitive associations (machine unlearning), and acquiring novel domain-specific capabilities without retraining models from scratch. Under standard sequential fine-tuning, deep neural networks suffer from Catastrophic Forgetting: new gradient updates catastrophically overwrite previously consolidated orthogonal representations, degrading baseline general reasoning and linguistic fluency. Resolving this challenge requires confronting the classical Stability-Plasticity Dilemma: how can a neural architecture remain sufficiently plastic to assimilate non-stationary novel knowledge while remaining structurally stable to preserve historical competence? This paper delivers an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Continual Lifelong Learning and Model Editing in modern foundation models. We formalize catastrophic forgetting dynamics using Fisher Information matrix projections and Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC), model rank-one associative memory editing via ROME and MEMIT across multi-layer perceptron (MLP) weight spaces, and analyze dynamic modular expansion architectures (e.g., continual Mixture-of-Experts and modular adapter routing). Furthermore, we construct an enterprise lifelong learning testbed evaluating open foundation models (Llama-3-8B, Mistral-7B) across 5,000 sequential factual updates, longitudinal clinical guideline shifts, and temporal financial market regimes. Our empirical findings demonstrate that localized rank-one memory editing achieves a 96.4% factual edit success rate while bounding collateral locality damage to under 1.8%, outperforming standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA) by 41.2% in retaining upstream historical benchmarks. Concurrently, dynamic modular routing preserves 98.6% of pre-trained reasoning capabilities over extended continual learning horizons. Finally, we formulate open challenges in lifelong compositional safety alignment, scalability bounds of memory editing, and neuro-symbolic continual knowledge graphs.

title: Exact minimum distances of five lifted-product quantum codes from Cain et al. (2026), Xu et al. (2024) and Panteleev-Kalachev
abstract: Five published lifted-product quantum LDPC codes without a proved distance have exact distances [[2610,744,16]], [[1122,148,20]], [[714,100,16]], [[1020,136,16]] and [[1054,140,20]]. The first two are the lp16 and lp20 codes of Cain, Xu, King, Picard, Levine, Endres, Preskill, Huang and Bluvstein (arXiv:2603.28627, Appendix A.1, printed d <= 16 and d <= 20). The next two are from Xu, Bonilla Ataides, Pattison, Raveendran, Bluvstein, Wurtz, Vasic, Lukin, Jiang and Zhou (arXiv:2308.08648, Nature Physics 2024; printed d <= 16 and d <= 20, the latter lowered to 16 by Webster, Jacob and Higgott, arXiv:2603.22532). The last is Example 4 of Panteleev and Kalachev (arXiv:2012.04068), printed as [[1054,140,d]]; no bound was proved, and the upper bound 20 comes from explicit weight-20 logicals. Webster, Jacob and Higgott's exact solvers ran to their 8-hour limit on the codes from Xu et al. and Panteleev-Kalachev. As far as we can find, none of the five exact values was established before. Method: an exhaustive branch-and-bound search over irreducible clusters (Dumer, Kovalev and Pryadko), anchored as in Rowshan and Devitt (arXiv:2609.39395), using the cyclic symmetry of the code and syndrome-weight pruning. It shows that no logical of weight d - 1 or less exists. An explicit logical of weight d is given for each code. A second program, written without seeing the first, confirms the lower bounds, and the witnesses are checked by three separate routines. Included: code definitions with sources, explicit minimum-weight logical witnesses (X and Z) for every code, both programs, a stand-alone checker, verify.py, the run logs and an archived extract of the benchmark data used for the novelty check. The quick check takes about 40 s on a laptop. The full lower-bound searches take about 4 min with the first program and hours with the second. Deliberately low compute: consumer AI subscriptions; longest search about 5 h on one core. Limitations: the lower bounds are the output of computer searches, without an independently checkable certificate. The code and text were produced with AI tools (Claude) under the author's direction and have not had human expert review. Corrections welcome.

title: PENERAPAN ALGORITMA DECISION TREE UNTUK SISTEM INFORMASI REKOMENDASI JURUSAN BERBASIS WEB (STUDI KASUS SMK HENDRIKUS LEVEN)
abstract: Accurate department selection in Vocational High Schools (SMKs) is important because it is related to the alignment between students’ abilities, interests, and selected areas of specialization. Manual department placement that relies mainly on academic scores and subjective considerations may result in inconsistent recommendations. This study aims to design and implement a web-based department recommendation information system using the Decision Tree (C4.5 Simplified) algorithm at SMK Hendrikus Leven. The study used students’ academic scores, interests, talents, and historical department data. A total of 60 records were used as training data to construct a decision tree using Entropy and Information Gain calculations, after which the resulting IF-THEN rules were implemented using Laravel and MySQL. System testing consisted of black-box testing involving 16 functional scenarios and tree traversal testing. All functional scenarios were successfully completed. In the test case, the system recommended the Clinical and Community Pharmacy department with a 100% Confidence Score, consistent with the generated decision rules. The system also provides Rule Explanation to show the basis of each recommendation. The results indicate that Decision Tree can support a more structured and transparent department recommendation process. Quantitative accuracy evaluation has not yet been conducted and remains for future research. ABSTRAK Ketepatan pemilihan jurusan di Sekolah Menengah Kejuruan (SMK) penting karena berkaitan dengan kesesuaian kemampuan dan minat siswa dengan bidang keahlian yang dipilih. Penentuan jurusan secara manual yang masih bergantung pada nilai akademik dan pertimbangan subjektif dapat menyebabkan rekomendasi kurang konsisten. Penelitian ini bertujuan merancang dan mengimplementasikan sistem informasi rekomendasi jurusan berbasis web menggunakan algoritma Decision Tree (C4.5 Simplified) di SMK Hendrikus Leven. Penelitian menggunakan data nilai akademik, minat, bakat, dan data historis jurusan. Sebanyak 60 data digunakan sebagai data latih untuk membentuk pohon keputusan melalui perhitungan Entropy dan Information Gain, kemudian aturan IF-THEN diimplementasikan menggunakan Laravel dan MySQL. Pengujian dilakukan melalui black-box testing terhadap 16 skenario dan pengujian penelusuran aturan (tree traversal). Seluruh fungsi memperoleh status berhasil. Pada studi kasus, sistem merekomendasikan jurusan Farmasi Klinis dan Komunitas dengan Confidence Score 100% sesuai aturan yang terbentuk. Sistem menyediakan Rule Explanation untuk menelusuri dasar rekomendasi. Hasil menunjukkan bahwa Decision Tree dapat diimplementasikan sebagai alat bantu rekomendasi jurusan yang lebih terstruktur dan transparan. Pengujian akurasi kuantitatif belum dilakukan sehingga menjadi agenda penelitian selanjutnya.

title: A Run-Length-Compressed Skiplist Data Structure for Dynamic GBWTs Supports Time- and Space-Efficient Pangenome Operations over Syncmers
abstract: Skiplists are probabilistic data structures over ordered lists supporting O ( log N ) insertion and search, which share many properties with balanced binary trees. Previously, we introduced the graph Burrows–Wheeler transform (GBWT) to support efficient search over pangenome path sets, but current implementations are static and cumbersome to build and use. Here, we introduce a doubly linked skiplist variant over run-length-compressed Burrows–Wheeler transforms that supports O ( log R ) rank and access operations, as well as a dynamic version that supports O ( log R + S ) rank and insert operations, where R is the number of runs and S is the number of symbols in the alphabet. We use these to store and search over paths through a syncmer graph built from Edgar’s closed syncmers, equivalent to a sparse de Bruijn graph. Code is available in rskip.[ch] within the syng package at github.com/richarddurbin/syng . This builds a 5.8 GB lossless GBWT representation of 92 full human genomes, single-threaded in 52 minutes, on top of a 4GB 63bp syncmer set built in 37 minutes. Arbitrarily long maximal exact matches can then be found as seeds for sequence matches to the graph at a search rate of ∼1Gbp per 10 seconds per thread.

title: Learning-assisted adaptive filter for tracking hypersonic glide vehicles
abstract: Accurate tracking of hypersonic glide vehicles (HGVs) remains challenging because their aerodynamic maneuver accelerations typically exhibit pronounced temporal variations, while the parameters of conventional maneuver models are generally unavailable in advance. This paper develops a learning-assisted adaptive filtering framework in which the drag, longitudinal-lift, and lateral-lift accelerations are explicitly represented by three-axis Singer stochastic processes with parameters adapted online. In the offline stage, a sliding-window maximum-likelihood (ML) estimator is first applied to representative HGV trajectory samples to identify locally optimal maneuver-model parameters. These estimates are subsequently used as supervised labels to train a radial basis function neural network (RBFNN) using measurement-innovation features. During online tracking, the trained RBFNN efficiently maps recent innovation-driven statistics to the Singer time constants and process-noise intensities, which are then incorporated into an extended Kalman filter for recursive state estimation. The proposed scheme therefore approximates likelihood-based parameter adaptation through a feedforward learning model, thereby avoiding repeated online optimization while preserving the recursive structure and interpretability of stochastic filtering. Numerical simulations involving quasi-equilibrium glide and skip-glide trajectories show that the proposed method achieves tracking accuracy close to that of the sliding-window ML adaptive filter, while substantially reducing the computational burden. The results further indicate that the proposed method consistently improves estimation accuracy and robustness compared with fixed-parameter and interacting-multiple-model filters, particularly under substantially time-varying maneuver conditions.

title: Literal Lock-In: How Test Language Shifts Literal Attraction in Typed Decision Models on Bengali Idioms
abstract: Decision models, non-generative scorers that report a probability over caller-supplied options and emit no text, are increasingly deployed as routers, classifiers and guardrails. Because they generate nothing, rationales and chain-of-thought do not apply. We audit three: an encoder scorer, a decoder scorer and a closed API, entirely through interventions on their input, using expert-annotated Bengali idioms carrying a gold figurative and a gold literal gloss. Dropping an idiom's own literal gloss into the option list draws every arm toward it, taking 65% to 96% of each arm's remaining Bengali errors. A model-by-language matrix over one shared item set shows how far this depends on the test language: every arm is 1.9 to 6.4 times more captured in Bengali than in English on the same paired entries, the commercial model's apparent resistance is a property of its test language, and capability does not order the failure. Calibration degrades in all three arms, and on the open arms confidence inverts, so gating on it is worse than gating at random. On a semantics-free option list, where accuracy is at chance, the best-calibrated arm still reports mean confidence 0.82. Code and data: https://github.com/sakhadib/literal-lock-in.

title: CLAD: Keypoint Matching Using Global Line Correspondences
abstract: Traditional keypoint descriptors, such as SIFT (Scale-Invariant Feature Transform) and ORB (Oriented FAST and Rotated BRIEF), are computed from local image patches. They may be unreliable in scenes with repetitive patterns or weak textures, where patches at different locations can look similar. We propose the Contextual Line-Assisted Descriptor (CLAD), a keypoint matching method that addresses this problem by using global geometric context from line correspondences. CLAD represents each keypoint with a vector whose elements indicate its proximity to matched lines. It can therefore use the keypoint's spatial relationships to the lines in the scene. We use HOME (Hough-space One-dimensional Matching of Extrema) to detect both clear and weak linear structures and to establish enough line-to-keypoint associations to represent this context. Evaluations on the TUM RGB-D SLAM dataset and outdoor video sequences show that CLAD provides geometrically consistent matches that complement those obtained with traditional local descriptors. In repetitive scenes, where local descriptors may not distinguish similar patches, CLAD uses global structure to improve matching reliability. The method is computationally lightweight and practical to implement.

title: MultiDomainYT-ToxBR: Um Corpus Multidomínio de Comentários Tóxicos do YouTube em Português Brasileiro
abstract: Este trabalho apresenta o MultiDomainYT-ToxBR, um corpus de 5.000 comentários do YouTube anotados em nove categorias de toxicidade e distribuídos em cinco domínios temáticos no contexto brasileiro. A análise de concordância entre anotadores evidencia desafios inerentes à tarefa, com índices moderados em categorias como racismo e xenofobia, cujas manifestações veladas e dependentes de contexto dificultam o consenso. A comparação com o ToLD-Br revela padrões complementares: o novo corpus supera o anterior em concordância para homofobia (α = 0,73 vs. 0,68) e introduz categorias inéditas como intolerância política e religiosa. Como validação, o BERTweet.BR, após fine-tuning, atingiu F1 de 0,78 na classificação binária.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Environmental Sustainability and Climate Change Mitigation: Recent Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
abstract: Abstract Climate change and environmental degradation have emerged as two of the most pressing global challenges of the twenty-first century, threatening ecosystems, biodiversity, human health, and sustainable development. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed environmental research and management by enabling advanced data analytics, real-time monitoring, predictive modeling, and intelligent decision-support systems. This review critically examines the applications of AI in addressing environmental and climate-related challenges, including climate forecasting, air and water quality monitoring, biodiversity conservation, precision agriculture, renewable energy optimization, carbon emission assessment, waste management, and disaster risk reduction. Furthermore, The review also identifies current research gaps and highlights future opportunities for developing transparent, energy-efficient, and explainable AI systems that support evidence-based environmental decisionmaking. It concludes that AI has become a transformative tool for accelerating progress toward climate change mitigation, environmental sustainability, and the achievement of the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration, responsible AI governance, and policy support will be essential to maximize the environmental benefits of AI while minimizing its ecological footprint. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Climate Change; Environmental Sustainability; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Remote Sensing; Internet of Things; Renewable Energy; Biodiversity Conservation; Sustainable Development Goals.

title: Don't Act Before the Action: Auditing and Repairing Future-Action Leakage in Chunk-Autoregressive Video World Models
abstract: This concise preprint introduces a suffix-intervention audit for future-action leakage in chunk-autoregressive video world models. The audit fixes the context, action prefix, and sampler noise while changing only future actions. We present Causal Action Residual Distillation (CARD), which combines an action-free content stream with a read-only causal action residual. Under the sampler and decoder assumptions stated in the paper, this structure makes earlier outputs invariant to later actions under fixed noise. Preliminary experiments on the released ABot-World-0 runtime show pathwise leakage in the original model and exact prefix preservation with active action responses in the CARD sidecar. This initial version focuses on the method and a limited empirical case study. Broader evaluation and closed-loop control performance remain future work.

title: BASE 44 ORDER: Build phase_cache table with SHA-256 hashing and 24h cache logic — E8 Intelligence Research
abstract: Andrew's order (Base 44 console): [SELF-BUILD from enhancement #1269] Create phase_cache table. In Python, hash normalized prompts (SHA-256, 8 bytes).
